News.title: Brute knifed pal to death then told cops ‘it happened again’ after he was released for killing his own gran
News.content:
FREE TO KILL Brute knifed pal to death then told cops ‘it happened again’ after he was released for killing his own gran

A CONVICTED killer has admitted knifing his pal to death on New Year’s Eve before handing himself in to cops and saying “it’s happened again”.

Daniel Levy, 48, today pleaded guilty at the Old Bailey to killing Indian national Abdul Kaleem Shaik, 41, at his flat in Vauxhall, south London.



It can now be reported that Levy, who has schizophrenia, had previously been convicted of killing his grandmother by stabbing and setting her on fire in July 2000.

Levy had previously accepted the second killing but denied it was murder due to his mental health at the time.



He dramatically changed his plea as his trial was about to be opened before a jury at the Old Bailey.

At a previous hearing, the prosecution said Levy had stabbed Mr Shaik in the neck with a large knife at his flat some time on New Year’s Eve or early on New Year’s Day.



Police were alerted to an incident after Levy went to Bishopsgate police station, in east London, shortly after 8pm on New Year’s Day.

He confessed that he had killed someone, telling officers: “It’s happened again.”

The comment was understood to be a reference to the killing of his grandmother in 2000.

In a police interview on January 2, Levy gave a detailed account and told officers that he had known Mr Shaik for years and allowed him to stay in his flat.



He said Mr Shaik had become “very depressed” and was not coping well.

He said that as a result of Mr Shaik’s deteriorating mental health, he felt he needed to help him by killing him and securing his passage to heaven.

News.title: Andy Burnham braces for first PMQs bout with Kemi Badenoch as pressure mounts on welfare and defence
News.content:
ANDY Burnham is bracing for his opening PMQs bout against Kemi Badenoch as the two rivals seek to draw first blood.

The pair will face off in the Commons at noon amid mounting issues for the new PM including the economy, welfare and defence.



It follows an initial clash yesterday as Mr Burnham faced a marathon grilling from MPs on his first appearance in Parliament.

The Prime Minister has been under mounting pressure to raise defence spending to three per cent having hinted he wanted to boost funding for the armed forces.



After John Healey’s resignation he said he would reduce the welfare bill to spend more money on defence.

But the next Chancellor has sparked a hypocrisy row after backpedalling on a military cash boost he previously demanded.

The ‘Burnham Bounce’ in the polls has started to flatline as Reform and Labour remain neck-and-neck in the polls.

Labour and Nigel Farage’s party are tied on 23 per cent while the Tories trail in third place on 20 per cent, according to YouGov.

Mr Burnham faces an in-tray from hell as Britain’s welfare bill continues to soar and is expected to cost the taxpayer around £400billion a year by the end of the decade.

Lord O’Neill of Gatley, who has advised the PM on the public finances, said he expected Mr Burnham to bring in public spending cuts to keep the economy ticking over.



Meanwhile Britain’s borrowing costs continue to surge and have risen sharply within the last few months.

The rates hit a multi-decade high and tipped over 5 per cent.

The new PM used his first Commons speech in the job to warn that “Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be”.



He singled out “a series of wrong turns in the 1980s” as well as the decision to leave the European Union as the reason for a lack of UK growth — rather than the record taxes Labour has imposed.

Mr Burnham faced MPs for the first time since entering No 10 six weeks ago and embarking on a summer tour announcing relatively small cost-of-living giveaways.

Ahead of his marathon three-hour grilling by MPs yesterday, the Labour leader was seen working up a sweat during his morning run.

The PM will feel the heat even more, as long-term government borrowing costs rose to their highest level since 1998.



At the dispatch box for the first time in 16 years, Mr Burnham said: “Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should. Life is too expensive and too hard for too many.”

The ex-Manchester Mayor said his decade away from Westminster had given him a “clear diagnosis” of the source of the UK’s troubles.

The Prime Minister took aim at the legacy of former PM Mrs Thatcher and her programme of privatisation, as well as pulling out of the EU.

He said: “Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country deindustrialised, austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this.”

He added: “Then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain.



“For 40 years, too many places have been drifting.”

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch attacked Mr Burnham for living in the past when he should be focused on the future.

She hit back: “The year is 2026, yet the Prime Minister said in his statement that everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. I may not look it, but I’m 46 years old. He is talking about a woman who became Prime Minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.

“On this side of the House, we are for the future, not the past. That is the difference between them and us. His ideas are all about more government control, more spending, more tax, more politicians.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She blamed the £70billion of tax rises under this Labour Government for failing to propel Britain out of the economic doldrums.

News.title: I had my wedding reception at a Spoons for £20 and toasted with Monster Energy pitchers – every couple should try it
News.content:
A BRIDE who hosted her wedding reception at Wetherspoons for £20 is now urging others to try the “cheap and cheerful” hack, with £14.99 small plates and Monster Energy pitchers.

Newlyweds Michelle and Brad Russell tied the knot at Canterbury Registry Office followed by a meal at the local pub with 16 guests on August 8.



The couple, who met on Facebook Dating in 2024, decided to plan a low-key, budget-friendly wedding after getting engaged in December last year.

Michelle, 47, says they just pulled some tables together in the pub and spent £20 all day – including the £14.99 on a small plates deal of halloumi fries, chicken wings and a bowl of chips.



Mum-of-two Michelle bought her wedding dress for £35 from Shein and £20 shoes from Amazon, as well as donning a £22 wig from TikTok shop.

The biggest expense of the day was £590 on the registry office before a further £157 on a hotel room above The Thomas Ingoldsby Wetherspoons in Canterbury.

There they enjoyed a pub meal as well as a first toast with a Monster Energy and vodka pitcher.

Michelle said Spoons is one of her and her new hubby’s favourite eateries for date nights, frequenting the pub chain on a weekly basis.



Civil servant Michelle and Brad, 41, decided to ditch the traditional first dance and speeches for a more “relaxed” nuptials before spending their wedding night upstairs in the pub’s hotel.

The bride said she “can’t speak highly enough of Spoons” – urging other brides to consider a budget-friendly option.

Michelle, who lives in Dover, Kent, said: “We both knew we didn’t want a massive wedding. Brad’s not really one for crowds and making a big display.



“If people are coming to our wedding and paying for their own food, they’re not going to want to pay that much per head.

“We both like going to Wetherspoons every now and then anyway and no one ever complains about the food, and they cater for people who are gluten free and everything.

“It’s one of our favourites. It’s cheap and cheerful. We go three or four times a month.”

Michelle added they decided to book a room above the pub for the night to get ready in.

Speaking on her dress choice, Michelle said: “That was the first dress I bought and I really liked it. I just thought some of the dresses from Shein are amazing.



“Getting married can be done on the cheaper side if you just stick to the bare minimum.

“Just forget about everyone else. At the end of the day, it is just about you two.

“Don’t knock it because it was a good laugh. It was cheap, cheerful and catered for people with dietary restrictions without the stress.”

News.title: What time is PMQs today? When to watch Andy Burnham face first Prime Minister’s Questions live
News.content:
PRIME Minister Andy Burnham is gearing up for a political milestone today as he steps up for his first Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs).

Following a marathon three-hour and 23-minute session at the Commons despatch box on September 1, the new PM is likely to face another test.



While Burnham officially took office more than six week ago, he did so shortly after Parliament entered its summer recess.

Only now has Parliament returned to Westminster for the start of the autumn session.



He’s expected to take questions from Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch on the economy and government spending plans.

Here is everything you need to know ahead of today’s political showdown.



What to expect from Andy Burnham’s first PMQs

Burnham comes into today’s PMQs having laid out his plans for Government.

On Tuesday, he unveiled his strategy to move power away from Westminster and back into the regions, alongside bringing utilities and public services back under public control.

The PM blamed the legacy of Margaret Thatcher, the austerity era, and Brexit for decades of slow growth.

He described the privatised water industry as a “leaking monument to that approach,” arguing the country is currently run in the private rather than public interest.



Burnham has reportedly briefed his Cabinet on three priorities.

They are: slashing the cost of essentials like childcare and mortgages, regenerating local communities, and establishing greater public control over utilities like water, energy, and housing.

What questions will Burnham face?

The Prime Minister will likely face scrutiny from Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch, who is expected to zero in on the UK’s current economic headwinds.

Expect Badenoch to press the PM on the upcoming October 28 Budget.

So far, Burnham has declined to rule out tax rises, though he has hinted that Chancellor John Healey will find the necessary funds to boost defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.



Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson has promised the Government will stick to its fiscal rules, but the Opposition will almost certainly demand more clarity.

What time is PMQs today?

PMQs takes place at its usual scheduled time of 12pm today (September 2).

The session typically lasts for around half an hour, though high-profile sessions like today’s Burnham debut can run slightly over.

How to watch PMQs live

You can stream the entire session through The Sun’s YouTube channel.

It will also be broadcast on the official Parliament TV website.

News.title: Shocking ‘hidden sex scandal’ in penis-filled medieval Bayeux Tapestry that ‘could rewrite European history’
News.content:
THE famed medieval Bayeux Tapestry depicts an alleged secret sex scandal that could rewrite European history, experts claim.

Depicting events leading up to the Norman conquest of England, the embroidered cloth shows battles and bloodshed – but could also contain a hidden royal affair.



The masterpiece was created in the 11th century in Normandy, France and has now returned to the UK for the first time in nearly 1,000 years.

It illustrates 58 events leading up to the Norman conquest of England by William the Conqueror.



The tapestry will be displayed at an exhibition in the British Museum, open to the public from September 10.

Curator Professor Michael Lewis believes an X-rated scene on the tapestry could rewrite our understanding of UK history.



The medieval magnum opus, which contains over 90 penises, also includes a vignette that could endanger the legitimacy of the English King, Norman leader William the Conqueror.

The illustration shows a clergyman caressing the cheek of a noblewoman while a naked man looks on from below a decorative border.



Professor Lewis believes that the woman is Emma of Normandy, who took on the Old English name Aelfgyva during her marriage.

Emma was the great-aunt of William the Conqueror, wife of English King Aethelred the Unready, and mother to Edward the Confessor.

“It undermines the legitimacy of the Norman Conquest,” said British Museum curator Professor Michael Lewis on the HistoryExtra podcast.

In 1066, Edward the Confessor died without an heir, which led to William making a claim to the English throne through his family connections and paving the way for his conquest.



At the time there were rumours that Emma cheated on King Aethelred with a prominent religious figure, and Professor Lewis believes that this vignette hints at this alleged affair.

By alluding to the affair, artists were able to subtly question William’s legitimacy as King.

The popular theory was that Emma was having an affair with Alfwin, the Bishop of Winchester, according to Professor Lewis.

He added: “That [naked] figure at the bottom, and the sexual scandal… then it kind of switches it completely against her…it undermines her legitimacy and therefore the legitimacy of the Norman Conquest.”



The alleged slander against Emma could have weakened William’s claim to the English throne by consanguinity.

Nonetheless, the name Aelfgyva was extremely popular in 11th century England and the identity of the woman in the tapestry will likely remain a mystery.

Historians have speculated whether she could have been Aelfgyva of York, first wife of King Aethelred, or Aelfgyva of Northampton, wife of King Cnut — the English/Danish king whom Emma of Normandy married after King Aethelred’s death.

The tapestry will be on display at the British Museum in the Sainsbury Exhibitions Gallery from from September 10, 2026 until July 11, 2027.

It comes as The Bayeux Museum, where the tapestry has been since 1983, closed on September 1, 2025, for a two-year refurbishment.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Measuring 70 metres long and containing 626 characters and 202 horses, it will be the first UK showing of the tapestry since it was made.

The masterwork holds great historical significance as it portrays key moments in the UK’s history, moments that reshaped the country’s ruling class, transformed the national language from English to French, and bound the two countries closer together for centuries to come.

News.title: Moment bodybuilding influencer has ‘bag stolen’ in broad daylight outside London station – would you have noticed?
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a bodybuilding influencer says she had her bag stolen in broad daylight outside a busy train station.

Colleen Bankston, 62, shared the clip of a man she claims snatched her suitcase outside London St Pancras International.



British Transport Police (BTP) confirmed they are investigating after the incident was reported.

Footage shows a man wearing wired earphones, glasses and a cap approach Colleen as her back was turned loading luggage into a boot.



The man then looks around to see if anyone is watching him before he appears to discreetly pinch the case and walk away.

Colleen, an influencer and personal trainer, seems none the wiser as the man disappears into the station.



The video was captured by a passerby who claimed to recognise the man, and uploaded to socials by the bodybuilder.

She penned: “This guy just stole my bag at St Pancras Train station.

Sunday morning 10am.



Shocked users flocked to the comments as one wrote: “Keep on sharing it. He has definitely done this before… he is a pro.

“Has the innocent guy demeanour down like the pro he is. I bet he has stolen countless bags from tourists.”

Another added: “Happened two weeks ago to my friend at St Pancras.”



A spokesperson for BTP said: “Officers are aware of a video showing a man taking a suitcase from outside St Pancras International railway station on Sunday (30 August).

“Enquiries are ongoing, and anyone with information is asked to contact British Transport Police by texting 61016, quoting reference 447 of 1 September.”

News.title: Cops release CCTV in search for man with shaved head and earrings after early hours ‘sexual assault’ in street
News.content:
STREET 'ASSAULT' Cops release CCTV in search for man with shaved head and earrings after early hours ‘sexual assault’ in street

COPS have released CCTV of a man with a shaved undercut and earrings after an alleged early hours sexual assault in a street.

Police launched a probe after the reported attack happened in Birmingham at 3am on April 18.

Officers have been combing through footage and shared an image of a man wearing a green stud earring and a gold hoop.

He is described as having long hair with it shaved underneath.





They are yet to identify the man they believe could help their enquiries, and urge anyone who recognises him to call 101.

A spokesperson for West Midlands Police said: “Officers are asking for the public’s help to identify a man following a sexual assault in Charlotte Street, Birmingham.

“We’ve been carrying out a thorough review of all CCTV in the area since it happened, but have still been unable to identify the man who we believe could help us and have information about the incident which happened at 3am on 18 April.

“The man is described as having long hair with it shaved underneath and was wearing a green stud earring and a gold hoop as pictured.

“Anyone who recognises him or has any information is asked to call 101 or use the Live Chat option on our website quoting crime number 20/218495/26.

“You can also make an anonymous report to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.”

News.title: Four charged with murder after baby stabbed to death
News.content:
Two men and two women have been charged with murder after a baby girl was found stabbed to death at a house in Sheffield.

The newborn was found at the property on Holywell Heights in the Wincobank area on Sunday morning, after police were called to reports of concern for her safety.

South Yorkshire Police said two men, aged 19 and 38, and two women, 20 and 37, had been charged with murder, causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant.

A fifth person, a 15-year-old girl, has also been charged with perverting the course of justice.

Police said all five had been remanded in custody and were due to appear at Sheffield Magistrates' Court later.

They are:

Peter Horvath, 19, of Holywell Heights, Sheffield

Andrea Skopova, 20, formerly of Robey Street, Sheffield

Nina Horvathova, 37, of Holywell Heights, Sheffield

Peter Horvath, 38, of Holywell Heights, Sheffield

The 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons

Two women, 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remain on bail, police added.

Det Ch Insp Tom Woodward said: "This is a significant step in our investigation into the tragic circumstances that resulted in the death of this baby girl.

"I would like to thank our communities, who I know will have been deeply impacted by this traumatic incident, for supporting us as we work through this intricate investigation.

"We would ask the public to avoid speculating and posting information online about this case while the legal process takes it course.

"Protecting the integrity of the criminal justice process is crucial to us securing justice for this little girl."

Police said officers would continue to be in and around the Holywell Heights area carrying out inquiries.

News.title: Watch: What we know about reported strike on Iran wedding celebrations
News.content:
Iran has launched missile and drone attacks at US targets across the Middle East, after American forces resumed strikes against Iran.

The Iranian Red Crescent said four people - including a child - were killed at wedding celebrations when a US missile hit a building in southern Iran.

BBC Verify has analysed footage released of the aftermath of the strike and spoken to a weapons expert to identify munition remnants.

The US military says it is aware of the reports but that it never targets civilians, and was striking Iranian targets in response to "recent attempted attacks" on American forces and commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Merlyn Thomas reports.

News.title: UK aid worker says he was mistaken for survivor in Nepal
News.content:
A British aid worker says he was mistaken as a survivor of Nepal's flash floods, after it was incorrectly announced he had been rescued.

Alastair Chambers, from Gloucester, said the mix-up happened when he returned to Kathmandu after flying back in a humanitarian aid helicopter from a village near the Trishuli river.

The 45-year-old told the Press Association: "I got dropped off at the army barracks, and when I got dropped off one of the police officers came up to me and asked for my details. Then they presumed that I'd been rescued. It's been a bit of a weird one, really."

On Tuesday Nepal officials had announced 119 people, including a British man, had been rescued through the use of air resources.

Chambers said he gave police his details to abide by the rules but realised later they assumed he had been rescued.

"News spreads - I was contacted by about 15 different journalists in the last few hours, just asking how I was and how I'm feeling after being rescued, and I had to say: 'Well sorry, I haven't been rescued.'"

Chambers flew to Nepal last week after seeing the disaster that hit both Nepal and neighbouring Tibet, killing more than 1,000 people, with 3,900 still missing.

On Tuesday, Under-Secretary of State at the Foreign Office Lord Wood of Anfield told the House of Lords 36 British people were unaccounted for, up from the previous total of 33.

The Foreign Office has been contacted for comment.

Chambers said he worked with volunteers to distribute sleeping bags, water purification tools, food and essentials to communities cut off by collapsed bridges, travelling to the area by helicopter.

"It's quite dangerous, and we've got a lot of landslides, trees across the roads in front of us," he said.

News.title: Watch: Amol Rajan says goodbye to Today programme
News.content:
Amol Rajan has said goodbye to BBC Radio 4's Today programme as he presented his final show on Wednesday morning.

Speaking at the end of the programme, he thanked his co-presenter Emma Barnett, as well as his wife Charlotte and his children.

Rajan became emotional as he paid tribute to father, who died shortly after he began his role on Today in 2021.

Colleagues gathered in the radio studio's gallery for his exit, and the programme played highlights from his time on Today as well as well wishes from his co-presenters.

Rajan announced his intention to step down from the role in January to "jump into the great digital Narnia of the creator economy" by launching his own company.

News.title: Gary Glitter pleads not guilty to historical sex offence charges
News.content:
Gary Glitter, the former singer whose real name is Paul Gadd, has pleaded not guilty to eight allegations of sexual abuse against a girl when she was aged between eight and 11.

Gadd, 82, is accused of offences against the girl between 1978 and 1981, after allegedly giving her chocolate and inviting her to his home in Kensington and Chelsea, west London.

It is alleged he caused the girl to touch his genitals and "engaged in unlawful sexual intercourse" with her.

At Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, Glitter appeared via video-link from prison to enter his pleas.

He denies four charges of indecent assault with a girl under the age of 13, two counts of sexual intercourse with a girl under the age of 13, and two counts of indecency with a child under the age of 13.

All charges relate to the same individual, and are alleged to have taken place between 12 March 1978 and 31 December 1981.

Gadd was wearing blue headwear, a blue shirt and a navy jacket, and was sitting next to a member of his legal team whilst on the call.

He spoke first to confirm his name. Then, he spoke again with his arms folded to deny the eight counts against him.

Gadd said he was "absolutely not guilty" to two of the eight charges, and repeated "not guilty" to the remaining six.

Judge Tony Baumgartner adjourned the case for a three-week trial starting on 22 November 2027.

The allegations were first reported to the Metropolitan Police on 9 January 2025 and an investigation into the circumstances was launched.

Gadd was first interviewed on 22 July last year in relation to the investigation.

The Met said in July that the alleged victim was being supported by specialist officers and had been made aware that Glitter had been charged.

The 82-year-old was one of the biggest pop stars of the 1970s with a string of number one hits.

News.title: Khan convicted in car tax 'scam' for vehicle he denies owning
News.content:
Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan has been convicted and fined in a fast-track court system after being accused of not taxing a 24-year-old Nissan Micra in what his team has called a "scam".

The Labour politician, 55, was found guilty by a magistrate last month of keeping an unlicensed vehicle, in a criminal prosecution brought by the DVLA.

Court documents show that DVLA letters addressed to the mayor about the unpaid tax bill were sent to Gordon Ramsay's east London restaurant, instead of the nearby Transport for London (TfL) offices.

City Hall officials said the car did not belong to the mayor or TfL.

A spokesperson for the mayor said: "This is a scam, which is a crime. It's not the first time the mayor has been victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle.

"Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware."

The mayor's adviser told BBC London the DVLA was "urgently" looking into reopening the case, with a view to withdrawing the prosecution.

The DVLA will also investigate the false registration, the adviser said.

The magistrate, sitting in a private hearing of the Single Justice Procedure in Herefordshire, convicted Khan in his absence and ordered that he pay a Â£220 fine, Â£85 in costs, and settle the Â£35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.

After the mayor expanded the Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez) to cover the whole of London he faced a wave of protests, including from motorists who said they planned to register their car in his name - supposedly to make him liable for the Â£12.50 daily charge.

News.title: Ariana Grande makes emotional tour exit and steps back from public life
News.content:
Ariana Grande made an emotional exit on Tuesday night, as she wrapped up her Eternal Sunshine tour, and prepared to step back from public life.

The singer was occasionally close to tears - most notably during One Last Time, the song that took on extra meaning as an anthem for survivors of the 2017 Manchester terror attack.

"London, I'm going to need you to help me on this one," she said, kneeling down to be near the audience throughout the performance.

Last month, Grande announced a break from all future public-facing appearances following months of intense speculation about her health and appearance.

The step-back includes Grande's withdrawal from a production of Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George at London's Barbican next summer.

She was due to appear alongside her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey. He also pulled out of the production on Tuesday.

On stage in London, Grande showed no signs of fragility or poor health - other than a foot injury that required her to swap her trademark stilettos for a succession of knee-high platform boots.

Nonetheless, she sprang across the stage in sync with her dancers, often on tip-toe to compensate for the lost height of her high heels.

But her voice faltered again during the song Nowhere, Nobody, as she sang the line: "Hard to believe in a perfect ending."

The blip was short-lived, though. Professional to the core, Grande regained her composure and was never less than magnetic on stage.

News.title: Kids eat free and loyalty points - six ways to eat out but not break the bank
News.content:
Restaurants often want to fill seats outside of peak lunch and dinner hours so opting for earlier or later sittings can be rewarded by a cheaper bill.

Apps such as First Table, which operates across 21 UK cities, as well as Ireland, New Zealand and Australia, give diners 50% off food when they book a participating restaurant's first or last dining slot. In exchange, diners pay a small booking fee.

EatClub is another, giving walk-ins up to 50% off the whole bill at thousands of venues when they redeem an offer within its app. The biggest discounts are at off-peak times.

Shokofeh Hejazi, director of foresight and innovation at global trends agency The Food People, says earlier dining appeals because it tends to be quieter and calmer, people drink less and it allows them to get home sooner.

Meeting up for breakfast also tends to be a bit more wallet-friendly as it's usually just one course and diners get the same catch-up time with friends and family, she adds.

News.title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
News.content:
Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget next month.

The yield on a 30-year gilt â a loan to the British government â rose to 5.89% on Tuesday, the highest since 1998.

Borrowing costs in the US, Japan and Europe have hit similar highs in recent days, reflecting investors' concerns about inflation, state borrowing levels and spending levels by large tech companies on AI.

Burnham told the House of Commons his government's "bedrock", as it seeks to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, would be "fiscal responsibility".

All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor, John Healey.

Burnham told the House of Commons the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".

Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living.

Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs.

"Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of "living in the past".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong," she told the House of Commons. "His theory of growth is completely wrong. He thinks that if Government spends more money, we will all get richer.

"That is not how this works."

The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.

The more that is forecast to be spent on interest payments, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.

On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.

The prime minister was already facing a tough balancing act with taxing and spending, due to pressures on defence and the cost of living.

Burnham's ex-economic adviser Lord Jim O'Neill told BBC News that high government borrowing costs would force Labour to "get real" about "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Lord O'Neill, who recently turned down the offer of a formal position in the prime minister's team, said that current market pressure would force changes over "some of the things that no political figures ever seem to want to deal with".

As well as the rise to 30-year gilt yields, the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to 5.22% on Tuesday. This is its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis.

Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.

News.title: Children as young as six going to A&E in mental health crisis
News.content:
There has been a sharp rise in children and young people - some as young as six - attending A&E units in England in a mental health crisis, NHS doctors are warning.

The number of six to 17-year-olds turning up in significant distress for things like self-harm and eating disorders, or in emotional crisis, rose by 36% between 2019 and 2025, according to the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health analysis.

Some faced waits of more than 12 hours once there. The college said A&Es were not the best place for them, but a lack of support in the community meant they often had nowhere else to turn.

The government said it was looking to improve services and would be setting out plans soon.

The analysis â based on figures provided under the Freedom of Information Act by NHS England â found there were 75,491 attendances at A&E by children and young people for a mental health concern in 2025.

That is up from 55,525 in 2019 with some of the biggest rises seen in very young children aged six to nine. The increases far outstrip the overall jump in attendances, which has risen by just over 8% over the period.

Doctors said the cases included children and young people brought in by families, carers and police â some of those in emotional crisis become aggressive or have challenging behaviour.

In total, more than 6,200, around 8%, waited over 12 hours in A&E.

News.title: Menopausal women pose as men to buy testosterone online after prescription difficulties
News.content:
Women are posing as men to buy testosterone from online pharmacies because of difficulties getting NHS prescriptions in Wales, according to a consultant.

There has been a "very sharp increase" in testosterone referrals to the NHS for post-menopausal women, but access varies between health boards.

Menopause specialist Dr Michelle Olver said she had seen women with up to 12 times the safe level of the hormone - risking permanent side effects - because they have bought online.

She would like to see an equitable all-Wales approach to testosterone prescribing, with it used to help with things such as libido.

The Welsh government said: "All health boards are expected to provide individualised care."

While testosterone is proven to help with libido after menopause, many women also claim it helps with energy levels and cognition.

Olver, a consultant in sexual and reproductive health, said it was "incredibly sad" to see women lying to get hold of the drug online, because they were being "denied access to something they need", but urged proper counselling and monitoring was needed.

"We want to maintain women in female physiological range for testosterone. We don't want them to have sky-high levels," she said.

"When you persistently have very high testosterone levels you can get undesirable permanent side effects.

"Nobody wants to have baldness, deepening of the voice or enlargement of the clitoris."

News.title: Fake 10 Downing Street listing exposes 'unfit' Booking.com, says consumer group
News.content:
Consumer group Which? says it was able to create a fake listing for 10 Downing Street on travel giant Booking.com.

The UK watchdog said its researchers were able to book a bogus stay at the prime minister's address - as well as leave a fake review noting "hanging out" with resident mouser Larry the cat as a highlight.

It said despite clear signs it was fake, Booking.com did not remove the listing until two months after it was uploaded.

"This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings or reviews published on our platform," a Booking.com spokesperson told the BBC.

They said because Which?'s listing was not "live" on its site across the two months it was present, "some of our automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the closed listing".

People could only see the listing and request to book the property during a 20-minute window opened by Which? so its researchers could try to book it.

Booking.com's spokesperson added "a range of checks and verification measures" help secure the site, and technologies such as AI "help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours".

But Which? Travel editor Rory Boland said its checks had been shown to be "unfit for purpose".

"If Booking.com's so-called sophisticated AI systems can't spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it's no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily," he said.

"It would be laughable that we were able to list the UK's most famous address for rent, if the consequences weren't so devastating for holidaymakers, who risk losing thousands of pounds to bogus listings and phishing links."

It is not the first time the site has faced criticism over its security efforts and customer service.

News.title: No compulsory redundancies from health board cuts - Swinney
News.content:
The first minister has promised his plans to reduce the number of health boards in Scotland will not result in compulsory redundancies.

John Swinney would not be drawn on the scale of job losses likely following his proposals to cut the number of mainland boards from 14 to two.

He told BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast he would "work collaboratively" with trade unions on a reform programme that will mean a reduction in public sector jobs.

Swinney said: "I will maintain the no compulsory redundancy commitment. There is no question about that in my mind."

The pledge came after Matt McLaughlin, head of health at the union Unison Scotland, said officials would be pressing ministers to ensure the NHS redundancy commitment was honoured.

News.title: Temperatures to touch 27C despite more rain on the way for some
News.content:
A bust of early autumn warmth will see temperatures rise as high as 27C in south-east England by the weekend, whilst more rain is on the way further north.

Temperatures will be a few degrees above average across the UK for most, with Thursday and Sunday looking particularly warm in the south.

The unsettled theme also continues, with low pressure systems bringing rain at times, focused towards the north-west.

Higher pressure keeps things much drier across the southern half of England and Wales, where drought conditions and hosepipe bans continue.

News.title: Bus journeys in west of Scotland to be capped at £2 from Monday
News.content:
Bus fares in the west of Scotland will be capped at Â£2, First Minister John Swinney has announced.

The move takes effect from Monday morning for journeys in Glasgow, Renfrewshire, Ayrshire, Dunbartonshire, Lanarkshire and Inverclyde.

In his programme for government, Swinney also confirmed plans to cut Scotland's health boards from 14 to two in what he said was the "most significant structural reform in the NHS in the era of devolution".

He vowed that by 2031, no patient will wait longer than 26 weeks for the treatment they need - an apparent downgrade on a promise in 2011 that patients should not wait longer than 12 weeks for inpatient or day-case treatment after diagnosis.

This is the first programme for government in the seventh session of the Scottish Parliament and outlines the government's policy and legislative goals.

News.title: Israel warns it will retaliate if UK imposes sanctions
News.content:
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has warned his country will retaliate if the UK imposes sanctions against it over the potential expansion of settlements in the West Bank.

Addressing Parliament for the first time as foreign secretary, Ed Miliband said he would introduce a "comprehensive reset" of policy on Israel "in the coming weeks".

He said the government would examine how to stop UK companies "financing, constructing or advertising new settlements" in the occupied West Bank.

Responding, Gideon Saar told Hebrew-language news website Ynet: "If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain."

"If they act, I think they will be making a big mistake," he said.

Last month, Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation.

The development would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

Miliband said the plans are "illegal under international law" and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also warned that Israel's statement about the E1 area could "imperil or end" the two-state solution in the Middle East.

All settlements are illegal under international law and, under global pressure, Israel held off for decades on plans to build in the area.

Argentina’s president has issued a fresh warning to the UK over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, saying his country would defend its interests “with tooth and nail, no matter who it bothers”.

Javier Milei said he was preparing to make what he billed as a national announcement on Thursday night, saying the islands were “sacred” to his people and his country’s national sovereignty had been ”violated”.

On Tuesday, Downing Street said Britain’s commitment to the Falkland Islands was “unwavering” after Donald Trump suggested the US could review its position on the archipelago.

open image in gallery Argentine president Javier Milei is to make a ‘national announcement’ on the Falkland Islands onThursday ( Reuters )

James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, hit back at President Milei, saying the Falklands “are British and they will remain British”.

“British soldiers fought and died to defend our sovereignty and the freedom of the Falkland Islanders. That sacrifice will never be forgotten, and we will always stand by the people of the Falklands and their overwhelming desire to remain British.”

In a statement on X, formerly Twitter, Argentina’s president said: “We announce a national broadcast for Thursday at 9:00 PM on a SACRED topic for Argentinians... a historic claim of the Argentine people that to this day continues to see its national sovereignty violated.”

He added: “What more important and strategic cause for the vital interests of the Nation could there be more important than the Malvinas cause?... We will continue defending the interests of the Argentine Nation with tooth and nail, no matter who it bothers. LONG LIVE FREEDOM, DAMMIT...!!!”

open image in gallery Downing Street said Britain’s commitment to the Falkland Islands was “unwavering” ( PA Wire )

The US’s stance is formally neutral, although Washington provided support for Britain’s campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.

However, reports last week suggested the US could revise its position if the UK government does not increase defence spending.

Asked about the reports on Monday, Mr Trump told reporters in the Oval Office: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”

The next day the PM’s official spokesman said the UK’s position on the Falklands was “long-standing and unwavering”.

“Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders’ right to self-determination is paramount,” he said. “The UK’s position is clear. The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory.”

open image in gallery Donald Trump suggested the US could review its position on the archipelago ( AP )

Falkland Islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory in a 2013 referendum, with 99.8 per cent voting in favour - and just three votes against.

But the issue hit the headlines this summer when Argentina’s football team controversially waved a banner in support of their country's claim to the islands while celebrating their World Cup win against England.

Players held a banner after the semi-final match that read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas", which translates as "The Falklands are Argentine".

Four people were killed and dozens injured after US forces bombed a wedding ceremony in Iran, local authorities have said as both sides traded heavy strikes.

Iran’s Red Crescent Society said 67 people were injured after a missile hit a building in Sirik, a coastal area in the Strait of Hormuz. A four-year-old child was among those killed in the strike on Wednesday, they said.

Tehran vowed to inflict a “crushing and devastating blow” in response, hours after retaliating with strikes on US bases in Jordan.

US CENTCOM said it was aware of reports of the attack but that the US did not target civilians.

open image in gallery At least 50 people were injured in the strike ( Iranian Red Crescent )

The US and Iran have returned to all-out war following the collapse of a short-lived truce last month, with no end in sight to the conflict despite mediation efforts by Pakistan and Qatar.

You can follow our live blog here.

Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson accused the US of “cruelty” and claimed it formed part of a pattern of attacks on civilians, which CENTCOM denies. It cited a strike on a school in Minab earlier this year that allegedly killed 156 civilians, including 120 children.

"American evil in the region will be met with heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences,” Iran’s joint military command said on Wednesday.

“In the new list of war crimes and attacks by the US army on civilian targets in Iran, after schools, stadiums, and residential homes, now add wedding ceremonies to this list too,” the Iranian Red Crescent said in a statement.

It added that the Hormozgan Province Red Crescent Society, the local branch, had reported that most of the injured were women and children.

The Pentagon is also yet to issue an official finding on the Minab strike, but sources told Reuters that it may have been the result of the use of outdated targeting data, with other sources telling CNN that senior military commanders bypassed warnings that some of the targeting was severely out of date.

open image in gallery Rubble lies around damaged houses following a reported attack near a wedding gathering in Kuhistik, Sirik ( Iranian Red Crescent Society )

Another seven people were killed and eight injured in US missile attacks in Iran's Khuzestan province overnight, state media cited the province's deputy governor as saying.

CENTCOM said it had hit air defences, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites on Tuesday.

Tehran says it has struck US targets across the region including in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, and Iraq. US officials told The Independent that reports regarding a ballistic missile attack on a US base in Jordan were false.

The IRGC also claimed a missile and drone attack on Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base that it said targeted the accommodation of a US commander.

open image in gallery Vessels remain stranded near the Strait of Hormuz as the US and Iran return to full-scale war ( Reuters )

The clashes spell the end of a stalemate lasting over a month, during which both sides have launched only limited strikes while making no progress towards peace.

US president Donald Trump has claimed that Tehran is “playing out the inevitable” despite the unpopularity of the war at home.

"I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing," Trump said. "They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?"

Tehran’s foreign ministry vowed to respond to "these savage crimes with firmness”.

"Those governments and international institutions that remain silent in the face of such barbarism, or seek to justify such acts, must understand that their silence is not neutrality," Iran said.

"Those who remain silent today will not be immune to its consequences tomorrow."

Ten years after his protest against racial injustice made headlines across the sports world and beyond, former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick says his personal mission continues, but his affection for the NFL is long gone.

In an interview with NBC News, the 38-year-old acknowledged that he no longer tunes in to professional football games, saying, "I'm not gonna support an organization that one, is actively blackballing me, but two, has targeted my brothers who have been protesting as part of this as well. I watch college football."

During the 2016 preseason, Kaepernick and then-49ers teammate Eric Reid took a knee during the national anthem before a game. Although he had sat on the bench during the anthem earlier in that preseason, the image of him and Reid kneeling while teammates stood quickly circulated worldwide.

Colin Kaepernick speaks after receiving the newly-established ACLU Ralph Ellison Award for Defenders of Civil Rights and Civil Liberties in the Arts, Business, Science and Sports ( Getty )

At the time, he told the NFL Network, "I am not going to stand up to show pride in a flag for a country that oppresses Black people and people of color. To me, this is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way. There are bodies in the street and people getting paid leave and getting away with murder."

Kaepernick, who guided San Francisco to the Super Bowl to finish the 2012 season, was out of the league following the 2016 season and never played again. He and Reid later sued the NFL, alleging collusion to keep them out of professional football, reaching a settlement in 2019.

Since then, Kaepernick has committed his time to initiatives such as Know Your Rights camps, which aim "to advance the liberation and well-being of Black and Brown communities through education, self-empowerment, mass-mobilization and the creation of new systems that elevate the next generation of change leaders," while also helping pay for independent autopsies in police-involved deaths.

Asked by NBC if he reflects on his football legacy, Kaepernick said, "I don't think about legacy a whole lot. What I think about is what are the areas that I can do work that I think are going to have an impact and help us move towards that future together. At the end of the day, people will decide what that legacy is, and hopefully that's a positive one."

Kaepernick has authored a memoir, titled "The Perilous Fight," which will become available on Sept. 15.

Bonnie Engstrom believes a long-deceased TV priest helped save her son’s life after he was born in 2010 without a pulse.

The Catholic Church agreed, declaring the boy’s resuscitation a miracle after Engstrom and others sought the heavenly prayers of the late Archbishop Fulton Sheen, who died in 1979. That determination made Sheen — a towering presence in 20th-century Catholicism, with pioneering broadcasts on radio and TV — eligible for beatification.

Now after years of delays to his formal beatification, Engstrom and many others from around Sheen’s hometown of Peoria are eagerly preparing for a service on Sept. 24 that will designate the late prelate as “Blessed Fulton Sheen” — one step away from sainthood.

“We will all be at the beatification, and we’re super excited,” said Engstrom, of nearby Washington, Illinois. Her son James Fulton, who is now a healthy teenager, will carry a relic of Sheen at the ceremony.

“The whole family will accompany him, which is special because in a lot of ways the whole family has walked with him through this whole process,” Engstrom said.

Tens of thousands are expected to join them. Too large for Peoria, where his tomb is a worldwide draw for pilgrims, Sheen’s main beatification ceremony is being held across the state line in St. Louis. Smaller events will be held in Sheen’s hometown.

Pope Leo XIV — a native Illinoisan like Sheen — greenlighted the beatification in February after years of delays.

‘The first televangelist’ was a pioneer in religious broadcasting

With the rise of television in the 1950s, Sheen entered millions of American living rooms with his show, “Life is Worth Living.” Dressed in a cassock, cape and skullcap, he stood at a chalkboard and delivered moral and religious lessons without a narrowly Catholic focus.

The show competed favorably against entertainers Milton Berle and Frank Sinatra on other networks. In an Emmy acceptance speech, Sheen thanked his writers — Gospel scribes Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.

“He was probably the best and, in many ways, the first televangelist in the United States,” said Monsignor Jason Gray, executive director of the Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen Foundation, which advocates for his sainthood.

Sheen’s devotees from far beyond Peoria are also hoping to attend the beatification.

“He’s the TV saint,” said Patricia Stephen of Edmonton, Alberta, on a July visit to Sheen’s tomb with her husband. “I’ve heard about him since I was a young kid. His message is very relevant to today.”

The foundation and the diocese are working on a major, high-tech expansion of the Sheen museum, which already displays his books, holy objects and other memorabilia.

“Sheen plays in Peoria!” proclaims a foundation newsletter headline encouraging pilgrims to visit. It’s a takeoff on the old expression, “Will it play in Peoria?,” which locals trace to the city’s reputed role as a Middle America proving ground on the vaudeville circuit.

John Kelly, a city councilor who recalls how his parents admired Sheen, says his beatification demonstrates the potential for anyone to become holy. “Being a hometown boy, he’s a regular guy. He didn’t walk on water,” Kelly said.

Sheen's prayers sought during a childbirth crisis

Engstrom knew little about Sheen as she grew up in the same Central Illinois region. That changed while she was pregnant with James, the third of her eight children.

She discovered online videos of Sheen’s broadcasts and began asking for his prayers during her pregnancy — in keeping with Catholics' practice of seeking the intercession of those they believe are in heaven.

“That was kind of the beginning of a beautiful relationship,” Engstrom recalled.

Her prayers became urgent on Sept. 16, 2010, when Engstrom gave birth to James at her home with the help of a midwife.

The baby was born without a pulse. Attendants quickly began chest compressions, and he was rushed to a Peoria hospital.

Dr. Juanita Aguila-Corrales, a specialist in neonatal perinatal medicine, was on call and hurried there as resuscitation efforts continued for some time.

They prepared to record the time of death but then detected a faint heart tone, she said. The heart began beating normally. The baby was put in therapeutic hypothermia, which helps prevent damage from extended oxygen loss, she said.

“I think it’s a miracle he survived without major setbacks,” said Aguila-Corrales, a Catholic.

Engstrom waited for James to successfully reach various developmental milestones before calling the Sheen Foundation, triggering the lengthy, formal inquiry that prompted the church to call his survival miraculous.

“I attribute the miracle to Jesus Christ,” Engstrom said. “But I firmly believe that Jesus allowed Fulton Sheen’s prayers and presence to play an integral part in it.”

James enjoys basketball, bike rides and studying meteorological reports. He also remains devoted to Sheen. “He’s my protector,” the teen told Catholic media.

Sainthood recognizes a “heroic witness of faith,” Peoria Bishop Louis Tylka said. The church typically requires authentication of one miracle for beatification — such as what it deems a medically unexplainable cure attributed to prayers to the candidate.

“We have five potential miracles to investigate” for a second one attributable to Sheen, which would qualify him for sainthood, the bishop said.

A long road to the beatification ceremony

Sheen was born in 1895 in the small town of El Paso, Illinois, and raised in Peoria. After seminary, ordination and a doctorate in philosophy, he had a short pastorate in Peoria before becoming a professor at The Catholic University of America in Washington.

He became known both for his academic lectures and his plainspoken addresses from the pulpit and the studio, first on radio and then on TV.

Sheen appeared in a Time magazine cover article. He guided celebrities and others converting to Catholicism.

He met with popes and spoke at the reformist Second Vatican Council. He railed against communism, though he opposed the Vietnam War.

Sheen raised funds and traveled the world on behalf of Catholic missions. He served as a bishop in New York state, retiring as an archbishop. After his death at 84, he was buried at St. Patrick’s Cathedral in New York until his niece won a court battle in 2019 to move his body to Peoria’s Cathedral of St. Mary of the Immaculate Conception.

Pilgrims today place crucifixes and other items on his marble tomb, giving them status as relics.

Although Pope Francis confirmed the Engstrom case as a miracle attributed to Sheen’s intercession, the Vatican postponed a scheduled 2019 beatification ceremony.

The Diocese of Rochester — which Sheen led in the late 1960s — requested the delay due to legal investigations into the oversight of priests accused of sexual abuse across New York state.

Church officials later concluded that Sheen’s record gave no cause for further delay, and plans for the ceremony resumed.

The Engstroms have found an informal community of those who believe they’ve also experienced Sheen’s miraculous interventions, even if the church hasn’t formally designated them as such.

Their new friends include Joe and Lizzy Taggart of Bloomington, Illinois.

After being told it was “nearly impossible” medically for Lizzy to conceive and carry a child to term, Joe said he prayed before a crucifix: “Fulton Sheen, if you’re up there, we could really use a miracle right now.”

Soon afterward, Lizzy conceived their oldest child — named Fulton, now a healthy 8-year-old boy.

The Taggarts firmly believe they’re not alone in experiencing a miracle.

“We’re hoping to meet some more Fultons when we go down to the beatification,” Joe Taggart said.

French President Emmanuel Macron arrives in London on Wednesday to meet new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and visit the Bayeux Tapestry at its temporary home in the British Museum.

The two leaders and their spouses will join King Charles III and Queen Camilla for a private viewing of the 230-foot (70-meter) tapestry, a 1,000-year-old symbol of Anglo-French relations that depicts the Norman conquest of England in 1066.

France loaned the embroidery, insured for 960 billion euros ($1.1 billion), for a 10-month exhibition that opens to the public on Sept. 10. It was spirited from Bayeux in northwest France to London by road and rail in a clandestine high-security operation in July, the first time since the 11th century that it has touched British soil.

Burnham said the tapestry’s return “is a landmark moment in the history of our two nations.”

Macron and the king will deliver speeches at a reception in the museum’s Great Court for representatives from Britain and France involved in the loan and schoolchildren from both countries.

Stitched in wool thread on linen fabric, the artwork depicts events leading up to the Battle of Hastings in October 1066, when William, Duke of Normandy defeated King Harold’s Anglo-Saxon army. The invasion ended Saxon rule, made William the Conqueror the first Norman king of England, and bound Britain and France together in a close and complicated relationship.

The loan was announced during Macron’s state visit to the U.K. in July 2025. In return, the British Museum is lending items including Viking and Anglo-Saxon treasures to museums in Normandy.

Burnham, who took office six weeks ago, will host Macron for talks at 10 Downing St. on Thursday. Burnham’s office said efforts to stop migrants crossing the Channel in small boats will top the agenda. The U.K. says stepped-up law enforcement cooperation between the two countries has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing in 2026 by more than 40% compared to last year.

The U.S.-Iran conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war are also likely to feature. France and the U.K. have led efforts to bolster European support for Ukraine during its more than 4-year war against Russia’s invasion, and Burnham has vowed to maintain British backing for Kyiv.

The prime minister also wants to forge closer ties with the European Union to end what he has called a “decade of low growth” caused by Britain’s departure from the now-27-member bloc after a 2016 referendum.

News.title: King and Macron unite for historic Bayeux Tapestry viewing in London
News.content:

On Wednesday, the King, the Queen, French president Emmanuel Macron and Prime Minister Andy Burnham are scheduled to view the Bayeux Tapestry together in London.

Highlighting warm diplomatic relations between the UK and France, the monarch, Camilla, Mr Macron and Mr Burnham will walk along the full 70-metre masterwork at the British Museum.

They will be accompanied by Brigitte Macron, France’s first lady, and Marie-France van Heel, the wife of Mr Burnham.

Serving as a woven record of the Norman conquest, the Tapestry has returned to the UK for the first time in nearly 1,000 years. It stays on loan until September 2027 under a trilateral agreement between Britain, France and the museum.

open image in gallery The almost 1,000-year-old tapestry is on display at the British Museum until September 2027 ( British Museum )

The party will pause at key sections of the 11th century artwork to hear from curators about historical events, such as Harold Godwinson’s coronation and the disputed portrayal of his death via an arrow to the eye at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Both the King and Mr Macron will give speeches marking the loan at a reception in the Great Court, attended by British and French representatives and schoolchildren from both nations.

Welcoming the royals and the Macrons will be museum director Nicholas Cullinan and chair, former chancellor George Osborne.

The monarch and president share a warm rapport, with the King hosting the Macrons for a state visit last July. Charles famously rebranded the entente cordiale as the entente "amicale" in a Windsor Castle banquet speech.

Mr Macron is the first European leader to visit the UK since Mr Burnham took office.

The visit indicates Mr Burnham is likely to maintain his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer’s policy of a "reset" in UK-EU relations. During a recent visit to Kyiv, Mr Burnham pledged to be "bolder" regarding closer ties, maintaining that "greater co-operation" was required across all areas.

open image in gallery King Charles and Queen Camilla hosted the Macron’s for a state visit last year ( AFP/Getty )

Mr Burnham said: “The return of the Bayeux Tapestry to England is a landmark moment in the history of our two nations, and I want people everywhere in the country to be able to enjoy it.”

He added: “As we celebrate our shared heritage, President Macron and I will continue to strengthen the relationship between our two nations.”

The Labour leader also said the Bayeux Around Britain programme, which will see the digital exhibition displayed in museums, galleries and castles in all four nations, would “give communities across the UK the opportunity to learn about one of the defining stories of our past”.

A live national history lesson on October 14 will teach thousands of schoolchildren about the significance of the tapestry.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: “This will be the first generation in 1,000 years who will be able to see this unique part of our heritage and we are determined that children from all backgrounds across every part of Britain have the chance to see it. The British Museum has pulled out all the stops to ensure that a generation of British children will remember it for the rest of their lives.”

British Museum director Mr Cullinan said the initiative to ensure the exhibition was not confined to London marked “the most ambitious and inclusive programme we or any museum in the UK has ever done”.

News.title: Collapsing child vaccination in South Africa ‘a public health emergency’
News.content:
Plummeting child immunisation rates are now a public health emergency in South Africa and risk causing outbreaks of preventable but potentially deadly childhood diseases, the government has said.

The proportion of children under one who have received no vaccinations has trebled in the past decade to nearly a third of infants in South Africa.

Mistrust of vaccines and growing ignorance about the benefits of childhood immunisations risk undoing years of progress made by one of the continent’s most effective health systems.

Outbreaks of measles, diphtheria and whooping cough this year have all been linked to poor immunisation rates and are evidence that herd immunity is breaking down, officials warned.

An alert from the department for health said the proportion of unvaccinated infants had hit 36.3 per cent in the first four months of 2026, up from 12.1 per cent in 2017.

The department warned the jump was “effectively tripling the number of completely unvaccinated children and leaving hundreds of thousands of infants at risk of life-threatening illnesses”.

Coverage of the six-in-one hexavalent infant vaccine that protects against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, meningitis, and hepatitis B declined from 87 per cent to 60.5 per cent over the same period.

Officials said the shortfall was caused by a lack of people coming forward to bring their children for jabs and was not due to any shortage of vaccines.

Dr Nonhlanhla Ndlovu, deputy director general of South Africa’s health department, told the state broadcaster that parents had a poor understanding of the public health benefits of childhood jabs.

She said: “The second one that comes out is the issue of public trust, in terms of the safety of the vaccines, but also the trust in terms of our systems.”

“Theses vaccines are very safe and we have seen the gains that we have had in our years before and now that is changing.

“The benefit of vaccines far outweigh anything we can talk about in public health. We need them to come back and bring the children for immunisation.”

News.title: Man City sign Enzo Fernandez for £125m to end transfer saga of the summer
News.content:
It is expected to be another busy deadline day in the Premier League, with many clubs still hoping to finalise deals before the transfer window shuts at 11pm. Here, Telegraph Sport identifies 10 potential high-profile moves that could yet go through.

Julian Alvarez to Barcelona… or Arsenal

This has been the most dramatic and relentless saga of the European transfer window. The situation, as far as we understand it, is as follows: Barcelona want Alvarez and Alvarez wants Barcelona, but Atletico Madrid refuse to sell him to Barcelona. Arsenal want Alvarez, and Atletico are more open to selling him to Arsenal, but Alvarez only wants Barcelona. For a move to happen, it will require one party to change their mind. Either Atletico decides to sell to Barcelona, or Alvarez decides he will join Arsenal.

Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City

Another long-running saga. Chelsea are well aware of City’s interest in Fernandez but want a massive fee for the Argentina international, having initially valued him at £120m. City have the cash and the space in the squad after saying goodbye to Rodri, Tijani Reijnders, Nico Gonzalez and Bernardo Silva this summer. Fernandez has not featured in Chelsea’s last two games.

Lamine Camara to Chelsea

As reported by Telegraph Sport last week, Chelsea have identified Monaco midfielder Camara as a target amid the uncertainty over Fernandez’s future. French reports on Monday suggested the move may have stalled, however. The clock is ticking.

Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City

Spurs had been working on a deal to sign Ndiaye from Everton but they now appear to have fallen behind City in the race for the winger, as a consequence of City failing in their attempt to sign Cody Gakpo from Liverpool. City are ready to complete the hijack on deadline day.

Ismaila Sarr to Liverpool

A deal that, as of Monday night, is regarded as unlikely to happen. As with their interest in Brighton’s Yankuba Minteh, Liverpool have so far been unable to strike a deal with Crystal Palace for Sarr, who scored 21 goals in 45 games last season. Liverpool would only allow Gakpo to leave if a replacement, such as Sarr, can be signed.

News.title: Borrowing cost surge leaves Healey with £10bn headache
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs have surged at one of the fastest paces in the world in a move that threatens to blow a near £10bn hole in Chancellor John Healey’s fiscal plans.

Interest rates on 10-year gilts, a benchmark for Treasury borrowing costs, rose to the highest level since 2008 on Tuesday amid a global bond market rout.

Britain’s cost to borrow over 20 years rose to its highest level since 1998, signalling growing stress in the market.

Government borrowing costs around the world have climbed sharply in recent weeks, amid concerns about unsustainable debts and persistent inflation.

However, Britain suffered the biggest increase in bond yields in the G7 on Tuesday as economists warned that investors were particularly nervous ahead of Mr Healey’s first Budget.
