World.title: US sailors arrive at Thailand's Pattaya after record 250 days at sea
World.content:
After a record 250 days at sea without a port stop, the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has docked in Thailand, giving its nearly 5,000 crew members a much-needed break.

The ship is docking close to the beach resort of Pattaya, known for its raucous nightlife and for sex tourism. For the US it also carries strong historical echoes.

When the weary sailors walk into the city's bars and restaurants, they will literally be treading in the footsteps of the hundreds of thousands of US troops who came here for R&R â rest and relaxation - during the Vietnam War.

They transformed it from a sleepy fishing village to one of the world's most famous and frenetic party towns.

Today the neon-lit alleys running down to the beach are much quieter than usual. The bars in the city's famous Walking Street still screen videos on their walls of pole-dancing women, trying to lure customers inside.

But there are not many of those customers, and most seem to be family groups from the Middle East more interested in the Turkish ice-cream vendor than the go-go bars.

The Iran War, which has affected tourism and consumer spending, has hit businesses hard here. The prospect of thousands of American sailors, with nine months of salary unspent while at sea, offers a rare opportunity to local businesses.

World.title: Why US troops have a history in this raucous Thai city
World.content: After a record 250 days at sea, the USS Abraham Lincoln has docked in Thailand close to the city of Pattaya. Known for its raucous nightlife and sex tourism, the BBC's South East Asia correspondent Jonathan Head explains the history between US troops and the beach resort.

World.title: Thousands still missing as Nepal-Tibet flood relief and recovery intensifies
World.content:
A massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, wiping out villages.

Nearly 12,000 people have since been rescued, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

But thousands more, including hundreds of foreign nationals - from India, the UK, Australia, the US, Malaysia, and more - are still missing. A week on, fears are growing that the death toll will only rise.

Chinese state media has not reported any survivors on the Tibetan side of the border, but the search continues. Beijing, which annexed Tibet in the 1950s, tightly controls the region. All information comes from state media and foreign journalists cannot travel there without permission.

Rescuers using heavy machinery, working around the clock, have been able to re-open the route to the Gyirong border crossing between Nepal and Tibet and clear the road of debris, which will accelerate the search for the missing, Chinese state media said.

Rescue operations continue in challenging conditions, and experts from China and India are helping build temporary bridges to reach remote areas. Drones are being deployed over hard-to reach areas to scan for survivors.

The UN's humanitarian agency said the main challenge is now access, with more than 40 bridges destroyed.

The most remote communities are relying on army helicopter flights for supplies, and villages are still struggling for fuel and electricity.

World.title: BBC travels inside occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel expanding positions
World.content:
The drive on the highway by the Mediterranean in southern Lebanon, near the border with Israel, is scenic and, these days, desolate. Crops lie abandoned and buildings destroyed by Israeli air strikes, too many to count, are in ruins.

Near the town of Naqoura, a Lebanese military checkpoint, painted in the white-and-red colours of the national flag, is the last visible sign of the state's presence. Soldiers are positioned behind concrete walls, but the road is empty. A few minutes further south, around a dozen Israeli flags indicate the start of occupied territory. Unless authorised by Israel, no-one can enter.

This part of the country is the heartland of Lebanon's Shia Muslim community, from which Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed militia and political party, gets most of its support. It has seen three invasions by the Israeli military in wars against the group in the last two decades alone. The most recent started in March, after Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel following the killing of the Iranian supreme leader, at the start of the US and Israel's war against Iran.

Last month, a BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, known as Unifil, which is one of the only ways to visit the area under Israeli control. There, as it did in Gaza, Israel has flattened entire villages, and air strikes and demolitions have continued even after a ceasefire was announced in June.

World.title: Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations
World.content:
Ukraine's president has told airlines that Russian airspace will be "effectively closing" as his country escalates its drone strikes.

"We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports: the Russian sky is becoming completely dangerous," Volodymyr Zelensky said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin responded by saying that Zelensky's comments amounted to a "declaration of state terrorism". Russia, he added, would continue its attacks on Ukraine which have intensified in recent weeks.

Most Western commercial airlines do not fly over Russia as a consequence of the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, but carriers in countries such as Turkey and China do.

Explaining the elevated airspace risk in his nightly video address on Tuesday, Zelensky said that "Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such - not a single civilian aircraft" and did not want the loss of innocent lives.

"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said.

Zelensky directed the warning to airlines continuing to operate flights to Russian airports, especially in major cities like St Petersburg and Moscow.

Ukraine has targeted energy facilities deep inside Russian territory and there have been repeated attacks on depots belonging to Russia's two biggest online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon.

Its drone attacks have for months led to disruption at some of Russia's biggest airports, especially in Moscow where at times all four major airports have been forced to halt arrivals and departures.

Several cancellations were reported on Wednesday.

Ukraine does not have to target airports to cause disruption.

Under Russia's air defence "Kovyor" (carpet) plan, flights are suspended if a drone is detected in the relevant area.

Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were almost certain to continue this year.

"There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russian territory," the alert added. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict."

Speaking to reporters at the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said: "They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists."

His comments come as Russia's attacks on Ukraine continue, with heavy strikes killing 12 people on Tuesday and further attacks on Odesa, Sumy and Kyiv on Wednesday. Russia's military has said it is preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian power stations.

The Ukrainian capital and its surrounding region have come under attack for seven days in a row.

A few weeks ago, Zelensky said Russia was attacking Ukraine every day, and Ukraine's military had "begun the process of bringing the war back to Russia". At the weekend he said the same, that Russia had to feel the war was "returning to where it came from".

Putin acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes had damaged infrastructure inside Russia, while insisting that "only 10%" of oil refineries were left to repair.

Chinese, Turkish and Gulf state airlines are among those using Russian airspace, with savings in time and fuel on routes between Asia and Europe.

Other carriers have largely avoided the eastern European region since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February, 2022.

Ukraine has closed its airspace to civilian aircraft throughout that period.

The risks of civil aviation during a war are clear. A few months after war broke out in eastern Ukraine in 2014 between Russian-backed separatists and the Ukrainian military, a Russian-made missile brought down a passenger plane, killing all 298 people on board.

Last year, the UN aviation agency ruled that Russia was responsible for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014.

The Kremlin has always denied any responsibility for the air disaster.

In 2024, Putin apologised to the president of neighbouring Azerbaijan over the downing of a commercial airliner in Russian airspace, in which 38 people were killed.

He said the "tragic incident" had occurred when Russian air defence systems were repelling Ukrainian drones.

World.title: Bus crash on Egypt's Red Sea coast kills 16
World.content:
At least 16 people have been killed in a bus crash in eastern Egypt, the country's health ministry has said.

Another 28 people were injured on the road between Red Sea towns of Dahab and Nuweiba in the South Sinai governorate on Wednesday morning.

Reports in Egyptian and Jordanian media say Jordanian nationals were among those killed in the accident.

As many as 20 ambulances were sent to the crash scene to provide first aid and evacuate the injured, the Egyptian health ministry said. The cause of the crash remains unknown.

The area is a popular tourist destination, attracting visitors from around the world.

Deadly road accidents are common across Egypt, with the authorities reporting nearly 6,000 fatalities in 2025.

Such accidents are often blamed on reckless driving and poor road maintenance.

Last month, 18 people were killed and 30 injured when two lorries collided in the north-eastern Ismailia governorate.

World.title: Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial
World.content:
The defendant, wearing a grey suit and occasionally consulting with his lawyers, appeared in court in the city of Provo on Tuesday.

Kirk's widow, Erika, the mother of their two children, and his parents, â Robert and Kathryn, were also at the hearing.

In a statement shared afterwards, the Kirk family said the judge's decision "marks an important step" in their "pursuit of justice".

"Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father," the statement added.

Closing arguments followed a five-day preliminary hearing in July, during which prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial.

That included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs.

"There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court on Tuesday, outlining video that he said showed Robinson "dressed to kill" on campus on the day of the shooting.

"We know that the defendant is the shooterâ¦ first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said.

Prosecutors said the accused, a former apprentice electrician, was in a relationship with his roommate and regarded Kirk's conservative views, particularly on transgender issues, as "repugnant" - which they argued was the motive.

World.title: South Korea jails care home head for sexually assaulting disabled residents
World.content:
A South Korean court has jailed the former head of a disabled care home for sexually assaulting multiple residents, in a case that shocked the nation.

The man, surnamed Kim, was handed a 15-year prison term for abusing three residents at the Saekdongwon facility in Incheon City, west of Seoul. The ruling is subject to appeal.

Police started investigating Kim after one of his victims, a woman with a severe intellectual disability, came forward in February last year.

The case has prompted the government to inspect 1,507 care facilities for disabled people across the country, where 33 cases of suspected abuse were found.

South Korean Prime Minister Kim Min-seok had described the abuse at Saekdongwon as "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".

An in-depth assessment of residents commissioned by Ganghwa County found that 20 current and former female residents may have experienced sexual abuse.

Many in South Korea have asked how such a case could still occur, especially after laws were strengthened in 2011 to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.

Some have also raised questions on how the director's actions could have gone undetected for so long.

Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close, while Incheon City officials revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.

However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed.

The foundation has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence.

World.title: Ghana, Nigeria set for African Unity Cup in Estonia
World.content:
Ghana and Nigeria will renew their rivalry in a different setting on Saturday as members of the African community in Estonia come together for the African Unity Cup – Friendship Match in Tallinn.

The friendly, scheduled for 3 p.m. at Sportland Arena, Jalgpalli 21, Tallinn, aims to promote unity, community engagement and a positive representation of Africa in the diaspora.

The event is being organised by African Expats MTÜ in collaboration with the Association of Ghanaians in Estonia (AGIE), with support from Afro Empire.

Speaking on the decision to support the initiative, the CEO of Afro Empire, Tamara Adu, said the event goes beyond the football rivalry between the two countries.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I decided to support this Ghana versus Nigeria friendly because it represents much more than football. It is about unity, identity, culture, and bringing our community together. As Africans living in the diaspora, events like this give us an opportunity to connect, celebrate our heritage, and create a stronger sense of belonging.

And for the Black community in Estonia, I believe this is a powerful moment. It creates visibility, encourages unity, and shows that we can come together to build meaningful platforms for our people. Football may be the reason we gather, but the bigger purpose is community connection and empowerment,” she said.

Ms Adu also expressed optimism that the initiative could become an annual event and eventually bring together more African communities in Estonia.

“I truly believe this can grow into a yearly event. My vision is for it to become bigger than just Ghana versus Nigeria, and eventually include other African communities in Estonia.”

President of AGIE, Benny Baiden, said the event was intended to strengthen relations between the two communities rather than fuel the traditional football rivalry between Ghana and Nigeria.

“Nigeria is our brother any day, anytime. Even though our jollof rice is better, we just want to play and bond together as brothers that we are. This is not a competition, but the kind of friendly that we need here in Estonia,” Mr Baiden said.

He added that the Ghanaian community was prepared to turn out in numbers to celebrate the occasion with Nigerians.

The Media Coordinator of the event, Seun Agbabiaka of African Expats MTÜ, said the initiative was also designed to promote networking and challenge stereotypes about Africans in Estonia.

Mr Agbabiaka, a former Nigerian television editor who worked with Galaxy Television and Calivision under the umbrella of AIT “Livebeat”, and an organiser of the Nigeria Music Video Awards (NMVA), said football provided a platform for Africans who might otherwise have little opportunity to interact.

“The purpose is bigger than football. We want to promote unity among Africans in Estonia, fight stereotypes and show a positive image of Africa, and create networking. Many Nigerians and Ghanaians here don’t know each other. Football brings us together,” he said.

He also pointed to the presence of Nigerian and Ghanaian players in the Estonian league as an example of how football can transcend national rivalries.

“What makes this special is the Estonian league itself. At FC Levadia Tallinn – current champions of the Estonian Premium Liiga who were recently eliminated from the Conference League by Swedish side IFK Göteborg – we have Nigerian players like Abraham Nwankwo and Victory Iboro Sunday playing side-by-side with Ghanaian winger Enock Otoo. In AFCON they are rivals, but in Estonia they wear the same jersey. That is the spirit we want to bring to Sportland Arena.”

Mr Agbabiaka also urged Nigerians living in Estonia to conduct themselves responsibly and remember that their actions could shape perceptions of the wider Nigerian community.

“Wherever we find ourselves, we carry Nigeria on our head. In a country like Estonia where we are few, what one Nigerian does, they say Nigerians did it. So we must be good ambassadors. Be disciplined, be punctual, respect the host country’s rules and play fair.”

The organisers said the arena has been booked from 3 p.m. to 5:30 p.m., with vendors, cultural exhibitions, music and other community activities planned around the match.

The event is open to Africans and friends of Africa living in Estonia.

World.title: Katsina health workers to begin 7-day warning strike 8 Sept
World.content:
The Assembly of Health Care Professionals in Katsina State says its members will begin a seven-day warning strike from 8 September over unresolved demands.

The assembly announced this in a statement jointly signed on Tuesday in Katsina by the Chairman of the assembly, Ibrahim Balange, chairmen and secretaries of three other unions.

The unions include the Health Workers Union of Nigeria, National Association of Nigeria Nurses and Midwives, Association of Hospital and Administrative Pharmacists of Nigeria, and the Association of Medical Laboratory Scientists of Nigeria.

The notice, addressed to the State Head of Service, followed the expiration of a 21-day ultimatum issued to the Katsina State government on 11 August.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Balange said the ultimatum expired without serious commitment by the government towards addressing the union’s longstanding demands.

He said that the assembly’s members unanimously resolved to begin the warning strike at 12 midnight on Tuesday, 8 September.

According to him, the unions will proceed on an indefinite strike if the government fails to address their demands at the expiration of the seven-day warning action.

“For the avoidance of doubt, over the years that we have been on this struggle, the state government has never demonstrated any form of seriousness on our long overdue legitimate demands, despite admitting the justification of our cries,” he said.

Mr Balange appealed to members of the public to understand the situation and hold the government responsible for inconveniences that might arise from the industrial action.

He said that the assembly had exhausted all available avenues for an amicable resolution of the issues.

World.title: Osinbajo, African lawyers seek accountability from tech firms over risks to children
World.content:
Former Vice President Yemi Osinbajo and African legal experts have called for greater accountability from technology companies over digital products and platforms that expose children to harmful content, exploitation and other online risks.

They made the call on Monday at a high-level session on children’s digital rights during the 16th Annual Conference of the Pan African Lawyers Union (PALU) taking place in Cairo, Egypt, between 31 August and September.

The session, titled “Guardrails, Not Gates: Protecting Children in the Digital Age,” was convened by the Justice Research Institute (JRI) in collaboration with the African Alliance for People-Centred Justice and with support from Luminate. The Director of People-Centred Justice at JRI, Foluso Idumu-Shado, shared the details with PREMIUM TIMES in a statement on Wednesday.

The experts examined a proposed Cairo Declaration on Child Rights and Design Accountability in the Digital Age, which seeks to establish common standards for the design and regulation of digital products used by children across Africa.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Osinbajo, who chaired the session, noted that companies should not shift the responsibility for risks built into their products to children and their parents.

“We cannot build digital environments in which the risks are engineered into the product and then expect children and parents to carry the responsibility for managing those risks,” he said.

He said the focus should be on creating digital environments that let children benefit from technology without unnecessarily exposing them to its dangers.

“The objective is not to build gates that exclude children from technology. It is to establish guardrails that ensure technology works for children rather than exploiting their vulnerabilities,” he said.

The discussion comes amid growing concern over children’s exposure to harmful content, exploitation, manipulation and misuse of personal data online.

The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child addressed children’s rights in the digital environment in General Comment No. 25, issued in 2021. The guidance covers issues arising from technologies including artificial intelligence, algorithms, data analytics and connected devices.

In 2024, the African Union adopted its Child Online Safety and Empowerment Policy, which recognises children’s rights to safety, privacy and participation online and calls for their best interests to guide efforts to improve the digital environment.

The proposed Cairo Declaration seeks to build on those efforts by placing greater emphasis on the obligations of companies that design and develop digital technologies.

According to the statement, delegates discussed emerging threats facing children and the difficulty of regulating digital platforms while preserving access to their benefits and avoiding excessive surveillance.

They reviewed and prioritised six proposed pillars for the declaration.

These include safety-by-design requirements for digital products used by children, restrictions on exploitative targeting and manipulative practices, age-appropriate design standards, and greater transparency around algorithms capable of amplifying harmful content or behaviour.

The proposals also include stronger safeguards for children’s personal data and age-assurance systems designed to protect minors while respecting privacy and other fundamental rights.

JRI said African countries should have a stronger voice in determining the rules governing technologies increasingly used by children on the continent.

“Children in Africa are entering a digital environment largely designed elsewhere. We must ensure that African children are not merely protected from the consequences of technology but that their rights and interests are considered in how digital technologies are designed, deployed and regulated,” the statement stated.

It added that the declaration could give African lawyers, regulators, civil society organisations and technology stakeholders a common continental position while allowing individual countries to develop laws suited to their circumstances.

Following the session, a consolidated draft of the Cairo Declaration, incorporating amendments and priorities raised by delegates, was presented to the PALU leadership for consideration.

The initiative also proposes model laws and regulatory instruments that national legislatures, data protection authorities and other regulators could adapt to their jurisdictions.

JRI said a working group on child-centred digital governance had been established following the Cairo meeting. The group will include PALU delegates, member bars and other relevant experts, while JRI will serve as its technical secretariat.

Further consultations on the declaration and proposed legal instruments are expected to continue, with progress scheduled for review at PALU’s 17th Annual Conference.

The initiative ultimately seeks to move responsibility beyond parents and children and towards the companies that design the digital environments in which children increasingly live and learn.

World.title: Parents accuse teacher of extortion, absenteeism at Nasarawa nomadic school
World.content:
Parents in Wuro Auta, Gitata area of Karu Local Government Area of Nasarawa State, have accused teachers at the Wuro Nomadic School of absenteeism and extortion.

The parents, under the aegis of the Parent-Teacher Association (PTA), said teaching staff had been inadequate in the school despite serving more than 200 children from different Fulani settlements in the area.

The PTA chairman, Saleh Isah, alleged that the head teacher, who was posted to the school in March, had not visited the school since his posting.

Mr Isah claimed that instead of reporting to the school, the head teacher had repeatedly called him to demand money.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“He will call and ask me to send him money, which I refused because he has never come to teach our children,” he alleged.

Mr Isah said the school was built through community efforts, but the government had failed to provide adequate learning materials and teachers.

According to him, the situation worsened after the previous teacher was transferred, with the replacement allegedly refusing to report for duty.

“Since the last teacher was transferred, the present one has refused to come.

“No government officials have come despite several complaints to the authorities in the Panda Development Area,” Mr Isah alleged.

Reacting to the allegations, the supervisor in charge of the area, Joseph Auta, promised to intervene and ensure that the matter was investigated and addressed.

Mr Auta also appealed to Governor Abdullahi Sule to recruit more teachers for schools in the area, which he said were experiencing serious shortages.

Also speaking, Kande Adamu, Special Assistant to the Governor on Nomadic Education, said the state government would invite the teachers involved in the allegations and investigate the matter.

Mrs Adamu promised that anyone found culpable would be sanctioned, adding that the administration of Governor Sule was committed to ensuring access to education for all.

She said the government was also working to restore sanity and improve the standard of education in nomadic communities across the state.

World.title: JAMB, WAEC fix one-off fee for WASSCE result verification
World.content:
The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) and the West African Examinations Council (WAEC) have introduced a one-off N4,000 fee for the verification of West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE) results for candidates seeking admission into Nigerian tertiary institutions.

The two examination and admissions bodies said the new arrangement is designed to prevent candidates from paying multiple verification fees to different institutions during the admission process.

Under the arrangement, candidates whose admissions are regulated by JAMB will verify their WAEC results through a JAMB-provided verification platform. The verified outcome will then be made available to the tertiary institution where the candidate seeks admission.

The development was announced in a joint statement signed by both examination bodies and shared with PREMIUM TIMES.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“This collaboration underscores the commitment of both JAMB and WAEC to putting the interests of candidates first, reducing unnecessary costs and simplifying the admission process while maintaining the integrity and security of candidates’ academic records,” the statement said.

According to the new arrangement, candidates can initiate the verification process from home or any location with internet access.

The agencies encouraged prospective students to take advantage of the arrangement by completing the verification once, with the assurance that the verified result would subsequently be made available to all other institutions concerned.

One verification for multiple institutions

The agencies said candidates will be required to verify their WASSCE results once through JAMB, after which the verification outcome can be used by the relevant institution for screening, admission processing and other administrative purposes.

“Candidates are to pay N4,000 only, once, for the verification of their WASSCE O’ Level results on the specified platform and not through their desired institutions,” the statement said.

The tertiary institutions that the applicants are seeking admission to are not permitted to demand another verification payment from candidates whose results have already been verified through the JAMB platform, the statement clarified.

“Tertiary institutions are to utilise the verified results shared by JAMB for screening, processing candidate admission and other administrative purposes…Candidates shall not be required to pay for another verification,” the statement said.

READ ALSO: WAEC defends 2026 WASSCE results amid social media criticism

O’level verification for admissions

O’Level results are a key requirement in Nigeria’s tertiary admissions process. Candidates seeking admission typically use results from examinations such as WAEC’s WASSCE, the National Examinations Council (NECO) Senior School Certificate Examination and the National Business and Technical Examinations Board (NABTEB) examinations to demonstrate that they possess the required secondary-school qualifications.

The prerequisites usually include at least five credits in relevant subjects in the candidate’s discipline, including English and Mathematics.

JAMB coordinates admissions into universities, polytechnics, colleges of education and other tertiary institutions through the Central Admissions Processing System (CAPS).

World.title: Lassa fever: Young adults most affected as Nigeria records 1,035 cases, 252 deaths
World.content:
People aged 21 to 30 years remain the predominant age group affected by Lassa fever in Nigeria, as the country recorded 1,035 confirmed cases and 252 deaths in 2026.

This was revealed in the latest situation report for epidemiological week 33, released by the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) on Tuesday.

According to the NCDC’s report spanning 10 to 16 August, the confirmed cases were reported in 23 states and 117 local government areas (LGAs)

The report shows that confirmed cases were recorded among people aged between one and 93 years, with a median age of 30 years. The age and sex distribution showed that people aged 21 to 30 accounted for the largest share of confirmed cases among both males and females.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The distribution between men and women was relatively close, with a male-to-female ratio of 1:0.9 among confirmed cases.

Cases rise in one week

The latest report showed a sharp increase in new confirmed cases from four in week 32 (3 to 9 August) to 14.

In week 33, the 14 new confirmed cases were recorded in Ondo, Edo, Bauchi and Benue states. Two deaths were also recorded during the week, compared with one death in week 32.

The week 32 report had recorded 140 suspected cases and four confirmed cases, with one death.

Cumulatively for 2026, Nigeria recorded 7,426 suspected cases, 1,035 confirmed cases and 252 deaths. The case fatality rate (CFR) also increased from 23.5 per cent in week 32 to 24.4 per cent in week 33.

Five states account for most cases

Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue accounted for 87 per cent of all confirmed cases as of week 33, while the remaining 18 affected states accounted for 13 per cent.

Ondo recorded the highest share, accounting for 33 per cent of confirmed cases, followed by Bauchi with 25 per cent, Taraba with 13 per cent, Edo with 10 per cent and Benue with six per cent.

The same five states accounted for 86 per cent of cases in week 32. The number of affected LGAs remained at 117 between weeks 32 and 33.

The report shows that health workers continue to be affected, with 54 infections recorded as of week 33. It also noted that 783 cases had been managed at treatment centres in 2026.

Late presentation remains a challenge

The NCDC identified late presentation of cases as one of the factors contributing to the high case fatality rate.

It also listed poor health-seeking behaviour linked to the high cost of treatment and clinical management, poor environmental sanitation in high-burden communities, poor awareness and healthcare worker infections among the challenges affecting the response.

It also urged healthcare workers to maintain a high level of suspicion for Lassa fever, ensure timely referral and treatment, and adhere to standard infection prevention and control procedures.

The NCDC said it would continue to collaborate with partners to strengthen state capacity to prevent, detect and respond to Lassa fever promptly.

The latest situation report also listed several ongoing response activities, including the deployment of rapid response teams to seven high-burden states, active case search and contact tracing, training of frontline healthcare workers, pre-positioning of personal protective equipment, and community engagement activities in affected states.

Lassa fever

Lassa fever is an acute viral haemorrhagic illness caused by the Lassa virus, which is transmitted to humans primarily through contact with food or household items contaminated by the urine or faeces of infected rats.

It can also spread from person to person through contact with bodily fluids.

The disease often begins with fever, weakness, and headache, and may progress to more severe symptoms such as bleeding, difficulty breathing, swelling, and organ failure.

World.title: Living and surviving the Black woman’s curse
World.content:
From childbirth to menstruation, pain has often been treated as an unavoidable part of womanhood. It is regarded as something to be managed quietly rather than investigated. It also is often said that, women are built to endure. For many Black women living with fibroids, that expectation of endurance can become particularly costly.

Uterine fibroids are benign growths that develop from the muscle tissue of the uterus. They are common and may cause no symptoms at all. For some women, they can result in heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, severe cramps, pelvic pain and pressure, anaemia, pain during sex, and difficulties with fertility.

What makes the conversation more urgent for Black women is the disproportionate burden. Research consistently shows that fibroids occur more frequently in Black women, tend to appear at younger ages and can be larger, more numerous and more symptomatic. A 2024 review noted that fibroids may affect up to 70 per cent of women by age 50, with Black women experiencing a significantly higher burden than White women.

The disparity has become so familiar that fibroids are sometimes described as the “Black woman’s curse.” But while the phrase captures the frustration of women who have lived with the condition, it can also make fibroids sound like an inevitable fate which, they actually are not. What is undeniable, however, is that many women continue to live with symptoms for years before seeking or receiving appropriate care.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Moyo Awotile knows what that experience can look like.

Her journey began in 2018 when she missed her period and consulted a doctor. An ultrasound revealed that she had fibroids, alongside another reproductive health condition. At the time, she did not fully understand how significant the diagnosis would become. She continued with her life, but over the years, her periods became increasingly difficult. The pain intensified, her menstrual cycle became irregular, and there were occasions when the cramps were so severe that she could barely eat. Eventually, she found herself returning to Avon Medical in search of a lasting solution.

Moyo’s experience reflects one of the less discussed realities of fibroids: Women, gradually adapting to their lives around their symptoms. A period becomes something to plan for and the heavy bleeding dictates what clothes can be worn and how long one can stay away from home. Pain affects work, social activities and relationships. Fatigue may be accepted as normal, even when it is related to blood loss and anaemia.

Medical guidance is clear that heavy or painful periods that disrupt normal activities warrant medical attention. Yet, conversations about menstrual health remain uncomfortable in many communities, leaving some women to normalise symptoms that should prompt a medical consultation.

There is also a wider gap in what is known about fibroids among Black women in Africa. A review of research on Black women in sub-Saharan Africa found significant gaps in evidence on prevalence, incidence and risk factors, highlighting the need for more research on the condition within African populations.

For women who eventually require treatment, the decision can come with its own fears. Fibroid treatment is not one-size-fits-all. Depending on the size and location of the fibroids, severity of symptoms, age, reproductive plans and other individual considerations, options can include medication, monitoring, uterine artery embolization, minimally invasive procedures or surgery. Myomectomy, for example, removes fibroids while preserving the uterus, while hysterectomy involves removing the uterus and is generally considered when other options are unsuitable or have not worked.

For Moyo, surgery became the eventual choice and she underwent an open abdominal myomectomy. During the procedure, doctors found multiple fibroids weighing more than 1.5 kilograms in total. Herstory did not end when the surgery was over because, recovery became another important part of her experience.

She recalls the support she received from her family, colleagues and others around her, and describes community as an important part of the process. The medical team at Avon Medical also continued to follow up with her after the operation, including a scheduled review two weeks later.

That emphasis on care beyond the procedure is significant because recovery is often missing from public conversations about fibroids. A successful operation may remove the immediate physical problem, but the patient still has to navigate pain, mobility, anxiety, follow-up appointments and the gradual return to everyday life.

Moyo’s most striking reflection came after she had recovered. She realised an improvement in her quality of life and a renewed sense of peace of mind.

Her story also illustrates why conversations about fibroids need to go beyond diagnosis. Avon Medical’s documentary, “Overcoming Fibroids: A Journey of Care and Compassion”, attempts to make that shift by focusing not only on what fibroids are, but on what it means to live through diagnosis, treatment and recovery. Its role in Moyo’s story provides one example of how healthcare can extend beyond a procedure to include communication, reassurance, follow-up and support.

But the larger issue extends beyond one woman, one hospital or one treatment. For women, especially, black women, fibroids remain an important health concern that deserves more open discussion, better research and earlier intervention.

Calling fibroids a “curse” may describe how the condition has felt for generations of women, but it should not define what the future looks like. A diagnosis does not have to become a life sentence, and treatment should not be measured only by whether a fibroid has been removed. It should also be measured by whether a woman can return to work without fear, move through her day without pain, manage her life without anxiety and regain the quality of life she may have slowly surrendered to the condition.

Perhaps that is the conversation worth having now and not simply how many women have fibroids, but how many have spent years adjusting their lives around them, and how many could live differently if they had the information, support and care to seek help earlier.

World.title: Infantino: FIFA ready to support Nigeria’s football reform drive
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino says the world football governing body is working with Nigerian authorities on reforms aimed at strengthening the country’s football structures and creating more opportunities for young players.

Infantino disclosed this on Tuesday after meeting a Nigerian delegation led by National Sports Commission (NSC) Chairman Shehu Dikko at FIFA House in Zurich, Switzerland.

The meeting came days after the mass resignation of the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) leadership, including President Ibrahim Gusau, General Secretary Mohammed Sanusi and members of the federation’s Executive Committee.

Mr Infantino said the discussions focused on the institutional, governance and developmental challenges facing Nigerian football, as well as FIFA’s ongoing collaboration with the country.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I was pleased to sit down with a delegation from 🇳🇬 Nigeria, led by National Sports Commission (NSC) Chairman Shehu Dikko, at the Home of FIFA in 🇨🇭 Zürich to hold important discussions and align on our vision for football in the country. 🤝” Infantino said in a post on his social media account.

“We had a detailed talk on institutional, governance and developmental topics, as well as our ongoing collaborations.”

He said the discussions also examined ways to strengthen Nigeria’s football structures and create more pathways for young players.

“While stressing the need to create stronger structures and pathways to provide even more opportunities for the youth, we explored areas where FIFA can further support the growth of our beautiful game in this football-passionate country,” the FIFA president said.

Infantino also wished Nigeria’s women’s youth teams success at the upcoming FIFA U-20 and U-17 Women’s World Cups.

“I also wished luck to @ng_superfalcons for the upcoming FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup and the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup and thanked the entire team for their time, ideas and positive intent to work together in taking Nigerian football forward. 👏” he added.

The meeting in Zurich also provided an opportunity for FIFA to formally engage with Nigerian football authorities following the leadership crisis that resulted in the mass resignations at the NFF.

In a statement issued after the meeting, the NFF said FIFA had accepted the resignations of the federation’s principal officers and pledged to continue engagements with the Nigerian government, the NFF administration and the Confederation of African Football (CAF) on a roadmap for comprehensive reforms.

The NFF said the meeting agreed to continue discussions aimed at fine-tuning a roadmap covering the short, medium and long term, with the objective of producing a more inclusive NFF and creating a peaceful and stable environment for the development of Nigerian football.

Mr Dikko led the Nigerian delegation, which included NSC Director-General Bukola Olopade, former NFF President and ex-FIFA Council member Amaju Pinnick, Acting NFF General Secretary Emmanuel Ikpeme and NFF Director of Legal Services Okey Obi.

Mr Pinnick attended in his official capacity as Special Adviser to the CAF President and Deputy Chairman of the FIFA Men’s National Teams’ Competitions Committee.

CAF 2nd Vice President Kurt-Okraku and FIFA Director of Member Associations for Africa Gelson Fernandes were also present.

ALSO READ: NFF exposes fake FIFA letter as Nigeria delegation meets football body

Mr Dikko described the engagement as an important step towards restructuring Nigerian football.

“Mutual engagement among the National Sports Commission, the NFF administration and the Confederation of African Football is ongoing with FIFA on the comprehensive reforms of Nigeria football, including agreeing a roadmap going forward in accordance with the relevant rules, regulations and Statutes, and indeed there is no doubt Nigeria Football will emerge much better and properly-structured after the conclusion of this process,” he said.

The Zurich meeting followed President Bola Tinubu’s directive for comprehensive reforms of Nigerian football after a difficult period for the country’s national teams and football administration.

The president had directed that the reforms address governance, administration, stakeholder representation, development pathways, domestic competitions and accountability.

The NFF subsequently suspended the electoral process for its elective congress, which had been scheduled for September 27 in Lafia, Nasarawa State.

Mr Ikpeme was appointed to oversee the NFF Secretariat as Acting General Secretary, while Ademola Olajire was named Acting Deputy General Secretary.

The leadership crisis followed Nigeria’s failure to qualify for the 2026 FIFA World Cup and the Super Falcons’ failure to qualify for the 2027 Women’s World Cup, ending their record of appearing at every edition of the women’s tournament since its inception in 1991.

With FIFA now directly engaged in the reform process, attention will turn to the roadmap for restructuring the NFF and the eventual emergence of a new leadership under an electoral process agreed by the relevant football authorities.
