The electoral body also dismissed claims of improper staff changes, saying deployment and redeployment of employees was part of its normal administrative functions and was guided by its human resource policies and public service regulations.

"The Commission complies with its Human Resource policies, guidelines and other relevant instruments under the larger public service when engaging employees," the statement read in part.

It further denied allegations of malpractice against the chairperson and vice-chairperson, describing them as fabricated claims intended to damage the reputation of the commissioners and the commission.

Magarini by-election

On the Magarini by-election, IEBC said the poll was conducted in a free, fair and credible manner and was not challenged through an election petition. The commission added that it had successfully conducted several by-elections and was prepared to oversee the 2027 General Election.

At the same time, IEBC also defended its procurement process for election technology and ballot papers, saying all tenders were being conducted in accordance with Chapter 12 of the Constitution and the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015.

"Two key tenders, one for the Integrated Elections Management System, hardware and accessories, and another for ballot papers and other election materials, have temporarily been halted following a request for review filed before the Public Procurement Administrative Review Board," IEBC stated.

According to IEBC, documents for the technology tender were uploaded on its website and the Public Procurement Information Portal on August 11, 2026.

The commission said the technical specifications were generic and performance-based and open to all qualified suppliers. It stressed that the procurement process was still at its initial stages and that no company had been awarded the tender.

Voter register protected

The commission also dismissed claims that voter registration data could be manipulated or shared with external parties, insisting that the Register of Voters remained under its exclusive custody.

"Voter registration involves several stages, including in-person registration, verification of identity, collection of biometric and biographical data, transmission to a central database and automated biometric deduplication," IEBC added.

Flagged records are subjected to data cleaning, validation and adjudication before valid records are incorporated into the register.

The register will subsequently undergo a 30-day biometric verification exercise, followed by an independent audit before it is finalised and certified for use in an election.

IEBC said allegations of bribery, predetermined tender awards and voter suppression were false and potentially harmful to public confidence in the electoral process.

World.title: Ruto hands Sh2.6bn to Mau Forest evictees
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto also announced the lifting pf the caveat that had been placed on land bordering the Mau Forest. [PCS]

President William Ruto has announced the payment of Sh2.6 billion to 13,000 families evicted from the Mau Forest in Narok six years ago, marking what he described as the closure of a long chapter.

Each beneficiary received Sh200,000 through M-Pesa to help them resettle and rebuild their lives away from the water tower.

Speaking at Sogoo in Narok South Constituency on Wednesday, during the final day of his two-day tour of Narok County, Ruto said the Government had taken steps to address the longstanding Mau Forest resettlement problem.

He noted that in 2023, the Government gave Sh300,000 each to 2,000 families living in tents in the Mau Forest to enable them to leave the water tower and purchase land elsewhere.

“We are today officially closing the long and painful chapter of people who were removed from the Mau Forest, which the County Government of Narok will now manage,” Ruto said.

The President criticised politicians who, he said, had continued to politicise the Mau Forest issue without providing lasting solutions.

“Many politicians have talked of the Mau question, but I talked of the Mau answer. This is why we are here today closing this chapter,” he said.

Ruto also announced that the Government had purchased 5,800 acres of land to settle families who have been living as squatters on property previously owned by the family of former Provincial Commissioner Isaiah Cheluget.

“We are processing title deeds of the people living on the land after buying the Cheluget farm,” he said.

Construction of Johanna Ng'eno University

The President also announced the allocation of Sh1.2 billion for the construction of Johanna Ng’eno University in Emurua Dikirr Constituency.

Speaking during the laying of the foundation stone, Ruto said the institution would fulfil a pledge to residents while expanding access to higher education for students from across the country.

“You told me, as residents of Emurua Dikirr, that you want a university. Today, I have brought KSh1.2 billion to construct the university that will be named after our brother Johana Ng'eno,” he said.

He said the university would create employment opportunities and attract new investments to the region.

At the same time, Ruto maintained that his administration had fulfilled at least 80 per cent of the pledges contained in its 2022 campaign manifesto.

“Kenyans will elect leaders based on their development record. Sloganeering will not make Kenyans vote for them. They have a long way to go,” he said.

The President further launched the construction of the 18-kilometre Mogondo-Cheramgoi-Mogor-Soit road in Emurua Dikirr, saying the project would improve connectivity and unlock economic opportunities in the region.

“This new road will strengthen connectivity and unlock greater economic opportunities in the region,” Ruto said.

World.title: Gachagua to Duale: You don't own pastoralists
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua and delegates from Isiolo and Marsabit at Wamunyoro, Nyeri County on August 25, 2026. [Ali Abdi, Standard]

Democracy for Citizen Party (DCP) Leader Rigathi Gachagua has accused Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale of allegedly doing nothing for pastoralist communities in the country.

Mr Gachagua said Duale, while being the only CS from northern Kenya and claiming to be the spokesperson of the group, had instead been a liability to pastoralists.

“You, the Borana who are here, along with the Turkana and Somali, are all complaining like other Kenyans. You suffer from runaway insecurity and widespread underdevelopment. We must join hands to vote out this rogue government (in next year's general election),” the former Deputy President told a delegation of grassroots leaders and residents from Isiolo and Marsabit who paid him a courtesy call at his Wamunyoro rural home in Nyeri.

“Duale thinks that the pastoralists are his property, his children or servants. What has he done for the people of Isiolo and Marsabit? (He has) only rhetoric, shouting pastoralists everywhere, every day,” he said.

Gachagua questioned how Duale would be able to marshal ‘millions’ of votes for President Ruto in the 2027 General Elections while he (Duale) could only raise 7,000 votes for the UDA presidential candidate in the 2022 polls in his Garissa Township Constituency backyard.

Despite his little contribution to the Kenya Kwanza administration's victory, Gachagua said Duale was appointed as the only CS from northern Kenya but had ended up doing nothing for the region and pastoralist communities.

“He only gave him (Ruto) 7,000 votes in Garissa Township. It's Central Kenya that propelled this government,” Gachagua told the gathering.

“Duale was appointed CS and he has nothing to show apart from empty words, going round shouting (the name of) pastoralists, and you (the pastoralists) are suffering. If you love them, then why are their livestock stolen every day?” He asked the CS.

“These pastoralists are killed every day and their cows and goats stolen. What have you done for them and you are in the government?” Gachagua posed.

The Opposition leader claimed that the government was ill-prepared for the heavily forecasted El Niño rainfall, pointing out that those living in flood-prone areas like the Tana Delta and Garissa are exposed to danger.

“Now, going into El Niño, what plan has been put in place to save people from death as a result of floods and how livestock will survive?” he asked the State.

During the event, Gachagua revealed that Yusuf Huka Jillo from Isiolo would represent Upper Eastern at the DCP secretariat and serve as a member of the National Executive Committee (NEC) in an acting capacity.

Gachagua said the mountain was now complete, with Isiolo and Marsabit forming Mt Kenya North.

The locals alleged that the Health CS was interfering in Isiolo County politics, with elder Hussein Jama claiming that Duale and the Office of the DCI were shielding a section of leaders accused of corruption and criminal activities.

Speakers claimed that there was massive corruption at the local lands registry office, while Mr Jillo faulted the State for the slow pace of registration of community land in Isiolo.

Jama said Isiolo International Airport, which was constructed during the administration of President Kibaki to help in the export of miraa and horticultural goods from the Mt Kenya region and livestock products, mainly meat and hides, lies idle because the expansion of the runway from 1.5 metres to 3 metres had not been done.

In response, Gachagua said the airport was meant to create employment and wealth, but the Kenya Kwanza administration had instead left it in ruin deliberately, claiming the move was aimed at sabotaging the economy of Mt Kenya and pastoralists’ economies.

“What was the good about destroying the Imenti forest to construct an airstrip for an individual while there is an international airport meant partly to serve the entire region just a few kilometres from Meru town?” Asked the DCP leader.

World.title: Relief for schools as government releases Sh18.5b capitation
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Education CS Julius Ogamba. [File, Standard]

The government has released Sh18.5 billion in capitation to support operations in public basic education institutions during the third term of 2026, as schools reopened across the country on Monday.

Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba said the funds have already been released and will support learners in pre-primary, primary, junior and senior schools.

The allocation is intended to facilitate smooth school operations and ensure learning activities continue without disruption.

The Sh18.5 billion has been distributed across three major capitation programmes, with Free Day Secondary Education (FDSE) allocated Sh10.963 billion, accounting for the biggest portion of the Term Three capitation.

The money will support operations in public day and secondary schools and comes as institutions prepare learners for a busy academic term.

Free Day Junior School Education has received Sh6.1 billion, to support learners in the second tier of basic education and help institutions meet operational requirements as the Competency-Based Education system continues to expand.

Meanwhile, Free Primary Education has been allocated Sh1.4 billion to support learning in public primary schools.

The funds come as a relief to school heads who had raised concerns on the insufficient funds disbursed to schools this year.

However, Ogamba said the disbursement demonstrates the Government's commitment to ensuring that learners have access to free and compulsory basic education as provided for under Article 53(1)(b) of the Constitution.

“The Government affirms its commitment to fulfil its duty to learners and educational institutions,” said the CS.

Ogamba also warned school heads and principals against misuse of the funds, directing them to ensure the money is spent prudently and for the benefit of learners.

School administrators have further been cautioned against imposing unauthorised levies on parents and learners.

Ogamba said the Ministry would take firm action against institutions found to have misappropriated public resources or imposed illegal charges.

“We will deal firmly with any verified cases of misappropriation of resources and the imposition of unauthorised levies,” he said.

The warning comes as schools reopen for the third term, a period that is expected to be particularly demanding for institutions and learners because of the academic activities and assessments scheduled for the school calendar.

The Ministry has maintained that capitation is meant to ease the financial burden on families and enable schools to provide essential services without passing prohibited costs to parents.

Ogamba reiterated that school administrators must remain accountable for the public funds entrusted to them, warning that verified cases of misuse will attract action from the Ministry.

The Government has also reaffirmed that every child is entitled to free and compulsory basic education, placing the responsibility on education officials and school managers to ensure capitation achieves its intended purpose.

World.title: Ndindi Nyoro begins nationwide political mobilisation ahead of 2027
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro after attending service at Gathuki-ini ACK Church on August 23, 2026. [Boniface Gikandi, Standard]

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro has said he will take his campaign for national transformation across Kenya as he positions himself for the 2027 presidential race.

Ndindi said he was interested in leadership committed to addressing concerns in education, health, youth and unemployment, among other needs.

Nyoro, who is the People’s Party of Kenya leader, spoke at St Michael Gathuki-ini ACK Church in Kiharu on Sunday, where he called for respect and political maturity.

Addressing residents in Kiria-ini (Mathioya) and Gakira (Kangema), he urged politicians to engage in a responsible manner.

“I trust in God that after next year Kenya will be able to have leadership that will be responsible for improving citizens' standards of living,” he said.

He regretted that hundreds of university graduates in the area were yet to secure employment.

“I plead with Kenyans to support my course that is geared to transform the nation and ensure equality and transparency,” said the PPK leader.

Nyoro said that after engaging Murang'a residents, he will take his transformation campaigns to all parts of the country.

Speaking at Kiria-ini market, he said he would engage the people to seek their blessings.

“All along had been feeling the urge to lead the country, thus the need to come out in the open and fight for position,” he said.

On Monday, the MP announced his exit from the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA), declaring that he will join the opposition ahead of the 2027 General Election.

Nyoro, an economist serving his second term as Kiharu MP, said he will work with opposition leaders to push for what he termed real change in Kenya.

The legislator said all opposition presidential aspirants are welcome at rallies organised by the PPK.

His move marks a significant political shift as parties and leaders begin positioning themselves ahead of the 2027 polls.

World.title: Tehran still seeks negotiated solution with Washington, says Iranian President
World.content:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian announced Monday that Tehran still seeks a negotiated solution to the conflict with the US, following renewed strikes between both countries.

Pezeshkian added, during his meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit Kyrgyzstan that “the continuation of the war is not in anyone’s interest.

“Dialogue and cooperation are the way to resolve the existing problems,” he emphasized.

This comes after Pezeshkian said, before departing Tehran for Kyrgyzstan, that “Iran is not seeking war, and this is a clear message we have made to the world until now.”

“But we will not stand idly by in the face of any aggression, and we will respond decisively to the aggressors,” considering that “instability and turmoil in the region are not in the interest of any country and will present challenges for everyone.”

In the first direct military escalation between Washington and Tehran in weeks, Iran announced it had targeted US forces in Jordan and the UAE in retaliation for US airstrikes targeting the Iranian island of Larak.

World.title: US Federal Trade Commission to sue Amazon for deceiving advertisers: Wall Street Journal
World.content:
The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday – citing officials at the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) – that the FTC plans to file a lawsuit against Amazon, accusing it of manipulating advertising prices on its e-commerce platform.

Amazon shares fell 2.8 percent on Monday following the Wall Street Journal report.

According to the report, the commission plans to file a lawsuit in federal court in Seattle, alleging that Amazon manipulated the prices companies paid for advertising on its platform over a seven-year period.

More than 20 state attorneys general from both parties are expected to join the case.

World.title: Sisi: Egypt-China relations become model of partnership
World.content:
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi sent a welcoming message to the event held in Cairo on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, to mark the 70th anniversary of the establishment of Egyptian-Chinese diplomatic relations.

The event was jointly organized by the State Ministry of Information and China Media Group.In his message, read by Minister of State for Information Diaa Rashwan at the opening of the ceremony, al-Sisi warmly welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to Egypt, describing him as a dear guest and a close friend of the Egyptian people.

Sisi greeted the Egyptian and Chinese peoples on the 70th anniversary of the establishment of the diplomatic relations between the two countries.

He said that he and President Xi have been working for more than 12 years to strengthen the bonds of friendship between Egypt and China, with their joint efforts helping elevate bilateral relations to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership.He noted that the partnership has contributed to increased trade, investment, tourism flows and people-to-people exchanges, as well as scientific and cultural missions, particularly among Egyptian and Chinese youths.

Sisi said that over seven decades, Egypt-China relations have developed into a model of partnership based on mutual respect, solidarity and shared interests.

The two countries also promote cooperation among nations; uphold the principles of truth, justice and equality; and work toward comprehensive development and a just peace, he added.

Welcoming Xi to his second home Egypt, Sisi expressed hope for a new phase of more advanced relations, with the two countries working together in a wider range of fields to achieve mutual benefit and greater prosperity and progress for their peoples, as well as development and peace for the world.

World.title: PM, Spanish firm discuss investment opportunities in renewable energy
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly met with Gonvarri Industries Chairman and CEO Jon Riberas to discuss the Spanish company’s potential investments in Egypt, particularly in automotive components, renewable energy, metal structures, and logistics.

Madbouly highlighted Egypt’s plans to expand renewable energy projects, especially solar and wind power, and stressed the country’s potential as a regional manufacturing and export hub serving Middle Eastern and African markets.

The meeting also explored establishing a major Gonvarri manufacturing facility in Egypt for automotive components, as well as partnerships with local investors. The company, which specializes in steel and aluminum processing, said it is studying several investment models and views Egypt as both a key market and a potential regional base.

The two sides agreed to continue discussions, with the government aiming to reach a concrete investment framework in the coming weeks.

World.title: ‘Flee quickly’ – Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps threatens Israeli citizens
World.content:
The senior advisor to the commander-in-chief of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Mohammad Reza Naqdi urged Israelis to return to their countries and “flee quickly,” adding that those who remain will be treated “as Banu Qurayza were treated,” according to Iranian media.

Naqdi added, “They should know that the method the Islamic forces will use once they arrive there will be the same method used with Banu Qurayza.”

He continued, “Therefore, they must flee quickly, and those who remain will be treated according to the way the Banu Qurayza were treated, according to the rulings of the Torah, not according to Islamic mercy.”

On the 76th day after the signing of the Memorandum of Understanding between Washington and Tehran, and 185 days after the outbreak of war between the two sides, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that if the US returned to fulfilling its commitments under the Memorandum, his country would immediately reciprocate.

US President Donald Trump meanwhile threatened, “We will strike Iran hard and will respond to the Iranian attack on US forces in Jordan,” emphasizing that the Strait of Hormuz was in excellent condition and that the average number of ships passing through was 30 every night.

The Iranian presidency meanwhile announced that President Pezeshkian had assured the Pakistani Prime Minister of Iran’s readiness to implement the Memorandum of Understanding, provided the other party also adheres to it.

World.title: FM: Egypt, Burkina Faso ties gains momentum recently
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty, on Tuesday September 1, 2026, said that the relations between Egypt and Burkina Faso have gained increasing momentum recently, reflecting the fraternal ties between the two countries and their political will to strengthen bilateral relations and encourage businessmen to establish joint investments.

Abdelatty made the remarks during a joint press conference with Burkina Faso’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Regional Cooperation Karamoko Jean Marie Traore, following their talks at the Foreign Ministry headquarters in the New Capital.

Abdelatty welcomed his Burkinabe counterpart and his accompanying delegation during their current visit to Cairo, saying the visit reflects the depth of relations between the two countries.

The foreign minister praised the distinguished relations and close cooperation between Egypt and Burkina Faso in several domains.

He said the talks focused on bilateral cooperation and ways to strengthen it, in line with the directives of President Abdel Fattah El Sisi and Burkina Faso President Captain Ibrahim Traore.

Abdelatty added that he reaffirmed during the talks Egypt’s support for Sahel states — Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger — in their efforts to combat terrorism.

Meanwhile, the two sides condemned the failed coup attempt that took place in Niger.

Abdelatty affirmed that Egypt, under the direct guidance of President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, has not and will not hesitate to provide all possible support to its brothers in the Sahel in their efforts to combat terrorism, restore stability and advance development in the region’s countries.

He said that, alongside ongoing efforts to strengthen political, military and security relations, the talks addressed Egypt’s full readiness to provide Burkina Faso with all possible support in counterterrorism efforts, whether through training courses or capacity-building programmes.

Abdelatty added that terrorism is a global, cross-border phenomenon that no country can confront alone. He noted that there was agreement on the soundness of Egypt’s vision and comprehensive approach to combating terrorism. Talks also addressed Al-Azhar Al-Sharif’s readiness to provide training for young imams from Burkina Faso and other Sahel countries, as well as to strengthen Al-Azhar’s mission and receive students from the Sahel region for study in Egypt.

Talks also covered the Aswan Forum, scheduled to hold its next edition in Aswan in November. Abdelatty said he had invited his Burkinabe counterpart to participate in the forum.

The foreign minister said the two sides also discussed economic and investment cooperation. A business forum between the two countries is currently being held, with the participation of around 80 senior business leaders, to explore investment and trade opportunities and establish partnerships between the private sectors of Egypt and Burkina Faso.

Abdelatty also referred to the tour he made last year of the three Sahel countries, accompanied by a delegation of Egyptian business leaders. He said he would invite Burkinabe business leaders to participate in the El Alamein Business Forum, to be hosted by the city of El Alamein from October 2 to 4. The forum will coincide with the mid-year African Union summit and will bring together a number of African presidents, along with major African companies and business leaders, as part of Egypt’s vision of finding African solutions to the continent’s economic challenges.

He stressed that Egypt is seeking to expand its investments across Africa, which currently amount to nearly $14 billion and continue to grow steadily.

For his part, the Burkinabe foreign minister expressed his thanks and appreciation to his Egyptian counterpart for the invitation to visit Egypt, noting that this was his second visit to the country, which, he said, reflected the depth of relations between the two countries.

He praised the close cooperation between Burkina Faso and Egypt, noting that his accompanying delegation included a large number of business leaders seeking to build on the progress made during the Egyptian foreign minister’s visit to Burkina Faso last year. He stressed the importance of the economic partnership between the two countries, saying efforts would be made to further strengthen it.

The Burkinabe foreign minister conveyed the appreciation and thanks of the Burkinabe president to President El-Sisi, praising the Egyptian president’s efforts and vision in promoting peace.

Responding to a question from the Middle East News Agency (MENA) on whether the talks had resulted in agreement on specific investment projects, Foreign Minister Abdelatty said discussions held during the talks, as well as those at the business forum with high-level participation, focused on doubling trade between the two countries. He added that a number of specific projects had been identified for implementation in the food, energy and pharmaceutical sectors.

Abdelatty noted that the Burkinabe minister would visit the Egypt Pharmaceutical City during his stay in Cairo.

He explained that a number of Egyptian companies were interested not only in exporting pharmaceuticals to Burkina Faso but also in establishing manufacturing facilities there, particularly for pharmaceutical packaging, as well as cooperating in the production of various vaccines.

He also pointed to cooperation in infrastructure, noting that the Arab Contractors Company is operating in Burkina Faso, as well as cooperation in the agricultural sector. He described all these areas as important sectors, adding that the two sides had discussed various financing models, including payments in foreign currency, barter arrangements involving goods, and payment through projects.

In response to journalists’ questions, the Burkinabe foreign minister stressed the need to intensify efforts to combat terrorism and confront terrorist organizations through an integrated approach combining security measures with economic and cultural development.

He said combating terrorism required security operations on the ground alongside efforts to address economic and cultural dimensions in ways that tackle the underlying factors contributing to the spread of extremism. In this regard, he highlighted the role of the Confederation established by Burkina Faso in 2024 with Mali and Niger to cooperate in combating terrorism.

Regarding the future of partnerships and projects between Egypt and West African and Sahel countries, Abdelatty affirmed that Africa represents one of the main pillars of Egyptian foreign policy. He said President El-Sisi had repeatedly directed the government to pursue greater engagement with the African continent, to which Egypt takes pride in belonging.

The foreign minister announced that he would undertake African tours in the coming months, including visits to countries in Central and West Africa as well as Southern Africa, as part of Egypt’s efforts to strengthen its presence and reposition itself on the continent.

He said Egypt had established a number of new mechanisms to support its presence in Africa, including an investment entity that will be announced soon to promote Egyptian investments across the continent, particularly in manufacturing, agriculture and education. He also pointed to a financing mechanism worth around $100 million from the Egyptian budget to support development in Africa, in addition to the Egyptian agency for guaranteeing trade and investment on the continent.

Abdelatty highlighted the role of the Egyptian Agency of Partnership for Development in providing training and capacity-building programmes across Africa and dispatching medical convoys.

The foreign minister stressed that the security and stability of the Sahel region are a major priority for Egypt due to its geographical proximity. He noted that Libya and Sudan, which are neighbouring countries of Egypt, are also neighbours of Sahel countries. Therefore, he said, strengthening state institutions in Burkina Faso and other Sahel countries in their fight against terrorism is of utmost importance, and Egypt will continue to provide support in this regard.

Regarding relations with Egypt, the Burkinabe foreign minister described cooperation between his country and Egypt as “fruitful” across all fields, particularly the political sphere, noting that diplomatic relations between the two countries date back to 1960.

World.title: FM reaffirms Egypt’s full support for counterterrorism efforts in West Africa, Sahel
World.content:
Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt’s full support for counterterrorism efforts in West Africa and the Sahel, stressing the need for a comprehensive security and development approach.

Abdelatty made the remarks during talks on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, with Burkina Faso’s Foreign Minister Karamoko Traore on strengthening bilateral relations and regional issues of mutual concern.

He highlighted the potential role of the Aswan Forum for Peace and Development in the Sahel and expressed Egypt’s interest in closer coordination with Sahel countries.

The two ministers discussed efforts to promote regional stability and security, particularly under Burkina Faso’s presidency of the Alliance of Sahel States. Abdelatty invited Traore to attend the sixth Aswan Forum for Peace and Sustainable Development in November.

Abdelatty praised the growing momentum in Egyptian-Burkinabe ties and called for stronger trade, economic and investment cooperation, particularly in energy, infrastructure, healthcare and pharmaceuticals, in line with the political consultation agreement signed in July 2025.

He expressed hope that the Egyptian-Burkinabe Business Forum, held alongside Traore’s visit, would produce tangible results to boost trade and investment.

He also stressed the importance of security and military cooperation and capacity-building programs provided by Egyptian institutions and Al-Azhar Al-Sharif.

Traore, for his part, praised the growing Egyptian-Burkinabe partnership and stressed the importance of continued high-level exchanges and cooperation in counterterrorism, training and capacity building.

He expressed Burkina Faso’s interest in expanding cooperation and benefiting from Egypt’s expertise and capabilities to strengthen the country’s national institutions.

World.title: Tariff elimination opens Chinese market to Egyptian goods: Chinese news channel
World.content:
China’s CGTN news channel highlighted Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt on Tuesday, stating that relations between the two countries are at their best point ever.

It noted that official data indicates China has remained Egypt’s largest trading partner for 14 consecutive years, with bilateral trade reaching a record high of US$ 20.79 billion in 2025.

Egypt’s imports from China are concentrated in engineering equipment, textiles, and building materials, while its exports to China consist mainly of agricultural and food products.

Frozen strawberries, beets, raw flax, natural dyes, and natural calcium phosphate accounted for 46.1 percent of Egypt’s exports to China.

The channel added that trade figures have strengthened this year.

Since May 1, China has eliminated tariffs on products from 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations, including Egypt.

Surging exports

Egyptian exports to China surged 199.8 percent year-on-year to reach $ 840.8 million in the first half of 2026, compared to $ 280.5 million in the same period last year, according to the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics.

This policy is also changing how some Egyptian companies approach the Chinese market.

At the “Export to China” event held in Cairo on August 17, Chinese and Egyptian companies signed trade agreements worth nearly US$ 170 million.

More than 10 Chinese companies held talks with Egyptian firms.

The executive vice president of the Egypt-China General Business Association, Ma Guanghui, said that Egyptian companies are paying closer attention to the demands of the Chinese market.

The linen factory in Sadat City, with a total investment of US$ 58 million, produced approximately 3,800 tons of linen yarn annually, previously exporting its products only to the European Union market.

Ma said the factory is currently seeking Oeko-Tex certification and preparing to enter the luxury home textiles market in China, anticipating an 8-10 percentage point increase in its profit margin.

World.title: Liberia Wraps Up Rwanda Study Mission on Proposed Peace and Reconciliation Museum
World.content:
KIGALI, RWANDA — Liberia has concluded the Rwanda phase of a high-level study mission designed to gather practical lessons for the establishment of the proposed Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum.

The initiative is intended to preserve Liberia’s history, promote national healing and ensure that lessons from the country’s civil conflict are passed on to future generations.

The delegation, headed by Minister of State without Portfolio, Hon. Hadja Mamaka Bility, engaged with Rwandan institutions involved in reconciliation, historical preservation, archives, education and post-conflict recovery.

Supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the mission forms part of efforts to translate President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s vision for reconciliation and historical preservation into a lasting national institution.

Minister Bility said Liberia’s objective is to move reconciliation beyond speeches and discussions by establishing institutions capable of preserving the country’s experiences and helping future generations understand its past.

“This study tour is part of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s vision for national reconciliation, with the support of UNDP. We want to move Liberia beyond simply talking about reconciliation to building strong institutions that can preserve our experiences, tell our story, and pass the lessons of our past on to future generations,” Minister Bility said.

The initiative comes amid President Boakai’s broader reconciliation efforts, including his July 2025 public apology on behalf of the Liberian State to victims and families affected by the country’s civil conflict.

During the Rwanda phase, the Liberian delegation studied the country’s approaches to unity, reconciliation, citizenship education, community resilience and the preservation of historical memory.

The team visited and examined the Gacaca archives and their digitization, Rwanda’s National Archives, the Campaign Against Genocide Museum, the University of Rwanda’s Centre for Conflict Management, the Rwanda Peace Academy and the Mutobo Demobilisation and Reintegration Centre.

The engagements provided lessons on how Liberia could collect, authenticate, digitize and preserve photographs, films, documents, testimonies and other historical materials currently scattered across government institutions, private collections and archives within and outside the country.

The mission also underscored the need for a credible memorial institution to go beyond the construction of a museum building, with education, research, documentation, reconciliation and community engagement forming key components of its mandate.

UNDP Liberia Resident Representative, Amb. Aliou Mamadou Dia, said the initiative forms part of a broader effort to strengthen peacebuilding, reconciliation and national unity.

“UNDP is working with the Government of Liberia to support the establishment of a Peace and Reconciliation Museum as part of the President’s broader reconciliation agenda.

“This study mission gives us an opportunity to learn from the experiences of other countries, document lessons that can be adapted to Liberia, and engage partners who can support the Government in moving this vision forward,” Amb. Dia said.

Amb. Dia stressed that lasting peace requires Liberia to confront difficult issues from its past, pursue genuine reconciliation and strengthen accountability, while building an institution that preserves history, promotes healing and educates future generations.

As the Rwanda phase concluded, the leadership of Rwanda Cooperation emphasized experience-sharing and the prospects for continued technical partnership with Liberia.

The discussions identified potential areas of cooperation, including museum development and management, training for Liberian heritage professionals, preservation and digitization of historical records and testimonies, peace education and technical exchanges, including potential collaboration with Aegis Trust Rwanda.

The Liberian delegation will now proceed to South Africa to continue studying African experiences in national healing, peacebuilding, reconciliation and memorialization.

A central lesson emerging from the Rwanda experience is that Liberia cannot simply replicate another country’s model. Instead, it must develop an institution rooted in its own history and informed by the voices, photographs, documents and experiences of Liberians.

Such an institution, the mission emphasized, would help acknowledge the country’s past, educate new generations and contribute to preventing Liberia from returning to conflict.

World.title: 2026 COUNTY SPORTS MEET: Grand Kru Reappoints Emmanuel Kehkeh Following Full Exoneration by LFA
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Grand Kru Sports Steering Committee has reappointed experienced football tactician Emmanuel “Emo” Kehkeh as head coach of the county’s men’s football team ahead of the 2026 National County Sports Meet.

By Christopher C. Walker | [email protected]

The decision comes immediately on the heels of a major ruling by the Liberia Football Association (LFA) Grievance and Disciplinary Committee (GDC), which officially rescinded a five-year ban previously handed to the coach and cleared him of match manipulation charges.

With his suspension set aside, Kehkeh returns to lead Grand Kru in their preparations for the tournament scheduled for November, providing much-needed technical continuity to the squad.

Full Exoneration Clears Path for Return

Kehkeh’s path back to the Grand Kru bench was cleared after the LFA GDC completed a thorough re-evaluation of evidence connected to an alleged match of convenience between Margibi County and Grand Kru County at the Samuel Kanyon Doe Sports Complex during the 2025/2026 tournament.

The GDC had initially handed down five-year suspensions on July 1 against several individuals, including Kehkeh and Margibi County head coach S. Warmann Yeafapolee, citing violations of the FIFA Disciplinary Code.

However, upon reviewing intercepted cell phone records and additional communications, the disciplinary body established that while Kehkeh was informed of an arrangement to fix the match, he explicitly opposed it.

“After a careful review of the evidence produced indicating that Coach Kehkeh did inform other people through cell phone communication about playing of a match of convenience/manipulation, that he was strongly against,” the GDC noted in its final ruling.

The committee subsequently ordered his suspension lifted in a July 18 communication to LFA Secretary General Emmet Crayton, signed by GDC Co-Chairman Jenkins D. N. Pelenah Sr., fully reinstating Kehkeh’s eligibility to take charge of football activities.

Background to the Appointment

Kehkeh previously guided Grand Kru during the last edition of the County Sports Meet, earning a reputation within the county administration for tactical discipline and squad organization and guided the team to the final but lost to Nimba County.

When the Grand Kru Sports Steering Committee met to finalize its technical leadership for 2026, the administration chose to stand by Kehkeh, citing both his familiar knowledge of local players and his proven resistance to corruption during the LFA inquiry.

Rather than starting from scratch, Kehkeh now assumes full responsibility for technical preparations, player recruitment, and match planning.

His immediate priority will be screening emerging local talent alongside experienced players to build a competitive squad ahead of November’s kickoff.

“Joining Grand Kru again is a commitment to the people of the county,” Kehkeh said following the confirmation of his role. “With our name cleared and our focus restored, the objective is to build a disciplined, hardworking team that can compete for the title.”

World.title: One Woman, half a Billion Dollars: The Question Liberia’s Drug Investigation hasn’t Answered
World.content:
As former President George Weah touches down in Monrovia, the two record-breaking drug busts that started this saga — nearly half a billion dollars combined — have quietly gone still. A vessel authorities once chased across Liberian waters was recently brought ashore, and nobody in government has said a word about it since. Somewhere in that silence sits a question this newspaper thinks Liberia must ask out loud: is one former Vice President really the whole story?

By Rodney D. Sieh | [email protected]

Monrovia — As former President George Manneh Weah touches down in Monrovia Wednesday, the fate of his former Vice President, Jewel Howard-Taylor, lingers in a state of uncertainty, as the ruling Unity Party-led government worked through an audio recording and what it calls mountains of evidence tying the former First Lady to a litany of charges in the ongoing investigation into cartel-driven drug trafficking in Liberia. Weah’s arrival, months after he pledged from abroad to return home and “rally the CDC along with all well-meaning Liberians” against what he called a politically motivated prosecution, adds a charged political backdrop to a week already centered on his former running mate’s fate.

But there is a version of this story Liberians could be forgiven for believing, if all they did was follow the headlines of the last two weeks: that a former Vice President ran a cocaine empire more or less by herself, that she has been caught, and that the case is now simply a matter of scheduling hearings and arguing over a recorded phone call. It is a tidy version of events. It also happens to leave out most of what happened this summer, and nearly everyone else who was standing in the room when it did.

A Summer That Started with Two Busts, Not One

Long before anyone in Liberia was arguing about a Dubai hotel meeting or a foundation called Jewel Star Fish, the story began with customs officers and a number nobody wanted to believe: US$19.2 million in cocaine, seized at Roberts International Airport in June. It should have been the year’s biggest story on its own. Instead, it was a preview. Weeks later, authorities raided a stash house in Paynesville and pulled out somewhere between US$317 million and US$319 million in narcotics — an estimated 238 kilograms to nearly 4 metric tons, the largest seizure in Liberia’s history, and enough to make the June bust look, in hindsight, like a warning shot nobody heeded in time.

Add the two figures together, and Liberia is sitting on almost half a billion dollars in drugs that moved through, or nearly through, its ports and airport in the space of a single summer. That is the number that should anchor every conversation about this case. Instead, it has quietly receded behind a single name.

The Ship Nobody Talks About Anymore

Somewhere in between the two seizures sits a vessel that, for a few uncomfortable days in June, became the most-watched ship in West Africa: the IB Atlantic IV, which sat off Liberia’s coast for the better part of a week while the government worked out what to do about it, before slipping away from patrol boats that were, by multiple accounts, too small to catch it. This newspaper has since learned that a vessel matching that description — or one very much like it, caught up in the same broader case — was eventually brought ashore in Liberia. What was aboard it, what has been done with it, and whether anyone has been charged in connection with it has not been made public. A ship that once dominated the national conversation has become, in the span of a few months, a footnote nobody in government seems eager to revisit.

How the Story Narrowed to One Name

The path from those two seizures to a former Vice President in prison runs through a 2022 meeting in Dubai, arranged, prosecutors say, by a middleman named Sheikh Bassirou Kante, who later became a cooperating witness after running into his own legal trouble in the United States. A wiretapped phone call in which Kante told Jewel Howard-Taylor that the “investors” she met in Dubai had sent her a “gift” became, by the government’s own account, the piece of evidence that turned years of quiet financial ties into a formal arrest. She was stopped at Roberts International Airport on August 19, charged five days later with nine felony counts spanning trafficking, importation, conspiracy, money laundering and abuse of office, and has remained in custody since, her preliminary hearing delayed once already and now set to resume in the coming days. It is, by any measure, a serious and detailed case. It is also, notably, the only piece of this entire saga that has moved with anything resembling urgency.

The Arrests So Far: A Short List for Such a Big Number

Set the charge sheet against Jewel Howard-Taylor next to everyone else this investigation has touched, and the list gets uncomfortably short, uncomfortably fast. Beyond Howard-Taylor herself, only two people connected to this saga have been charged and sent toward trial: LDEA officer Moses Jallah and Paynesville bar owner George Harris, both swept up months ago in the early stages of the case. That is the entire list of people Liberia has formally accused of a crime in connection with nearly half a billion dollars in narcotics.

Everyone else occupies some quieter, murkier status. Mark Egon Kuiah, the former operations chief at Roberts International Airport, was named in a writ of arrest back in June and fired from his job in late July — but two months later, he has not been charged with anything a judge could rule on and is reportedly cooperating with investigators rather than facing them. Jonathan Momolu, a security officer at the airport tied to both this year’s case and a 2023 methamphetamine shipment disguised as tea leaves, was questioned once and sent home. Fitzgerald Biago, the Officer-in-Charge of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency, recused himself months ago over an unresolved allegation involving vehicles, and that recusal has never been followed by a public resolution one way or the other. Two currently serving Liberia National Police officers, alleged to have physically escorted the drug shipment at the center of the Paynesville case, remain unnamed by the government to this day. Gerald Smith, a former NSA deputy director, was called in for questioning and, as far as the public record shows, nothing more. And the five-person European network this newspaper has identified as the operational core of the entire scheme — Croatians Nikola Ivancic and Mihovil Vrovac, Ukrainian Taras Zadereiko, and a Serbian national and a Spanish national charged earlier in the same case — have all been charged in absentia, and all remain free, spread across Dubai, Ghana and destinations unknown, precisely because a network built to survive the loss of any single member was never going to be dismantled by one arrest in Monrovia.

Is She the Only One Responsible?

Put plainly, because the question deserves a plain answer: no. Nothing in the public record supports the idea that Jewel Howard-Taylor single-handedly moved nearly half a billion dollars in cocaine through Liberia. The government’s own charging documents describe a five-person foreign network with a financier in Dubai, an operator running logistics from Ghana, and a technician structuring the money laundering — a structure that, by design, requires local facilitation at multiple levels to function inside Liberia’s ports, airport and government circles. Names tied to that facilitation — an airport operations chief, an airport security officer, a drug enforcement chief, unnamed police officers — have all surfaced in this newspaper’s reporting over the past two months. Only one of those threads has produced a former official sitting in a prison cell facing trial. The rest have produced recusals, questionings, and silence.

That is not necessarily evidence of a cover-up. Some of it may simply reflect where the evidence is strongest, or where a cooperating witness has made a prosecutor’s job easier. But intent matters less here than pattern, and the pattern is now impossible to miss: the case that moved fastest, hardest and most publicly is also the case attached to the most politically recognizable name. Every other thread — including two seizures worth, combined, more money than the charge against Howard-Taylor alone — has moved slowly enough that most Liberians could be forgiven for forgetting it was ever a separate story.

Where the Silence Is Loudest

Ask the Ministry of Justice today for an update on the broader investigation into the June airport seizure, separate from the Howard-Taylor case, and there is no recent public answer. Ask what happened to the vessel recently brought ashore, and there is no public answer. Ask whether Liberia has made any real progress toward extraditing the five foreign nationals charged in absentia, and there is no public answer beyond a general promise of cooperation with Interpol. Each of these silences might have an innocent, procedural explanation. Together, they describe an investigation whose public face has narrowed to a single defendant, while the machinery that moved nearly half a billion dollars in narcotics through this country continues to operate largely out of view.

President Boakai has pledged “no sacred cows” in this fight, and this newspaper has held him to that standard before. The test of that pledge was never going to be how thoroughly Liberia prosecutes the one defendant whose arrest generated the most headlines. It was always going to be whether the government keeps chasing the money, the network and the local facilitators after the cameras move on to the next hearing date. Right now, on the evidence available to the public, that chase looks like it has largely stopped at one name — and nearly half a billion dollars in drugs says that cannot be where the story ends.

World.title: Liberia: They Were Found Guilty in Liberia’s Biggest Human Trafficking Trial But Noone Has Been Charged Over a Death in the Case. Now the Family Wants Justice
World.content:
Ophelia Melway, 32, who victims say died after ill treatment at a compound where as many as 150 trafficking victims were detained. Credit: Ophelia Melway’s family.

Summary:

The family of Ophelia Melway, a trafficking victim whose death helped expose Liberia’s largest human trafficking case, wants the investigation into her death fast-tracked.

Prosecutors are investigating whether her death warrants homicide charges.

Melway’s family, survivors and anti-trafficking advocates are demanding a swift and transparent investigation.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

It was Liberia’s biggest human trafficking trial to date. At the end of 22 days of hearings in June and July, a jury took just 23 minutes to decide eleven defendants were guilty of a range of crimes against 57 victims who were trafficked, starved, forced to work and deceived into handing over more than US$100,000 in total in the belief they would travel to jobs in Canada.

Eleven traffickers are now serving sentences as long as 50 years and have been ordered to pay US$131,500 in restitution and fines. (15 defendants have yet to face trial because they have not been apprehended.)

But victims say there is one major crime for which no one has faced justice: the death of Ophelia Melway, one of the victims, who fell seriously ill and was finally released by the traffickers only to die soon after.

Melway’s family has been joined by survivors of the trafficking ring who say determining whether anyone bears criminal responsibility for Melway’s death is essential to delivering full justice.

“I just want transparency,” said Melway’s younger brother, who FrontPage Africa/New Narratives is identifying only as M. to protect him from retaliation.

Anti-trafficking advocates have also called on the government to act.

“With that kind of gravity where somebody died, I don’t think the case can die, because if it dies, it puts the government in a very bad situation because that means they are compromising justice,” said Adolphus Satiah, head of the anti-human trafficking secretariat at the Ministry of Labor during the Weah administration. “When somebody dies, it’s not an easy case for anybody to play with, not even the government people.”

Melway’s death did not appear on the charge sheet against the 12 original defendants in the case drawn up by Enoch Dunbar, the head of the Anti-Human Trafficking Unit at the Liberia National Police, in October 2025.

That charge sheet – which had substantially downgraded most of the charges and dropped them against three of the defendants – was revised in April by Sumo C. Kutu Akoi, the senior human trafficking prosecutor. This came after FrontPage Africa/New Narratives revealed allegations by numerous victims that Bestman Juah, now head of public defenders, had offered a bribe on behalf of the traffickers to a prosecutor to downgrade the charges.

Victims allege Dunbar accepted a bribe to downgrade the charges. The case drew international attention and became a national test of Liberia’s willingness to prosecute organized trafficking networks. Previously the state had secured just six human trafficking convictions since 2020 and was on the US State Department’s Trafficking in Persons watchlist, risking aid cuts. When the charges were reinstated and the case went to trial there was still no charge related to Melway’s death even though numerous victims had detailed it in their statements to police.

The traffickers convicted in Liberia’s largest human trafficking case head into the sheriff’s room shortly after being sentenced.

At the start of the trial, Akoi told FrontPage Africa/New Narratives that the prosecution had opened an investigation into Melway’s death. He has not responded to questions about the investigation since.

Two family members of Melway—her younger brother and nephew who were also recruited from Nimba by the trafficking ring – said Melway was healthy when she was recruited in early 2025.

“She was not sick. She was well moving,” said M. speaking in Liberian English. “She was hustling on own her. She had her home.”

The jury found the traffickers forced victims to make repeated recruitment calls to family and friends lying that they were in Canada. M. said traffickers forced Melway to recruit him, and he in turn was pressured to recruit their younger sister. Melway resisted. Victims who failed to recruit new members were routinely punished. M. said food was withheld from his sister because she would not recruit more people.

“When I get there, she was not eating,” said M. “From morning all the way up to the evening, you will not eat because they will still press her to call somebody.”

The compound where Ophelia Melway and other victims were held in captivity. She fell ill there before her traffickers released her to her family for treatment shortly before she died. Credit: Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

Melway’s deteriorating condition and death came up repeatedly during the trial, with nearly every victim mentioning it in their testimony. But still it was not proposed as a charge. Akoi did not answer questions as to why.

Another survivor, L., testified that Melway became progressively weaker, and traffickers ignored repeated warnings that Melway’s condition was worsening.

“She was sitting down the whole day, tired,” said L. “In the night when the people finished packing their chairs, we used to [sit] on the cool ground. She used to tell them she not well, but they never believe her.”

L. said that as Melway’s appearance changed dramatically, she was subjected to the same punishments as the other victims, including being forced to hold rocks in her outstretched hands, do squats until she collapsed and drink dirty water.

Although he did not testify during the trial, Melway’s nephew, identified as A., said in an interview that he watched helplessly as traffickers tried to force his aunt to continue recruiting others despite her deteriorating condition.

“I was feeling discouraged because seeing your family member in that kind of condition, I felt bad,” A. said. After learning of her death, he said he begged to leave.

“The people said, ‘No way. When they put me out, I was going to expose their secret.’”

Another relative of Melway, who testified during the trial and whom FrontPage Africa/New Narratives is identifying only as J., said Daniel Davis, one of the convicted traffickers, told victims he had given Melway US$20 to travel home to Nimba County for treatment. J. said Davis’ girlfriend, Shelly Suah, another convicted trafficker, later told them, “Oh, Ophelia na make it.”

A male victim identified only as M. testified that “she was killed.” He said Melway became seriously ill before traffickers removed her from the compound for medical treatment.

Z. said Melway was sent to the family who later took her to Ganta United Methodist Hospital.

One of the rooms of the compound.

There doctors diagnosed her with dangerously high blood pressure M. said. After three days she died.

Her death, on top of the thousands the family gave to the traffickers, had dealt a devastating blow to the family. M. said Melway was the primary provider for the family, selling rice to support her parents and paying his school fees. Melway also left behind her partner, and their 17-year-old daughter.

“I was going to school. But since she passed away, I don’t have different sponsor,” said M. “That thing, it’s paining me. Because when I think about the things that we did to do together, when I am jammed, the things she was doing, the sad moment will come over me. I am feeling discouraged.”

When news of Melway’s death reached the compound, victims testified, it sparked desperation and fear. Victims believed she had been killed and feared that the traffickers planned to kill them one by one. The victims made loud banging and screaming noises and drew the attention of security guards at the neighboring home of Vice President Jeremiah Koung who freed them. From there the victims made their way to the Paynesville magistrates’ court where they reported the crimes.

Inside the compound where Melway and other victims were held in captivity. Credit: Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

Under Liberian law, the Ministry of Justice, which supervises the police, has the authority to initiate criminal investigations without the police. Police and prosecutors will determine whether the evidence supports charges of murder, negligent homicide or manslaughter.

Experts said the Melway case was another test of the government’s willingness to hold traffickers to account. Liberia has remained on the U.S. State Department’s trafficking watch list for two consecutive years and risks cuts to aid if it remains there again on this year’s report which is due to be released any day.

Zokerseh B. Saye, executive director of the Liberia Anti-Trafficking Scam and Victim Support Initiative, which helps expose human trafficking and scam operations and reports perpetrators to the government, said investigators should build on the evidence already presented during the trial.

“It’s clear and it’s because of the act that caused that woman to die,” he said. “We want the government to be fast with the result that the people can see the impact of human trafficking.”

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Cooperation Development Agency. The funder had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-VP Jewel Howard Taylor’s Drug Case Delayed as Defense Seeks Medical Records, Cardiologist
World.content:
MONROVIA — The preliminary hearing in the government’s drug trafficking and money laundering case against former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor has been delayed as her defense team seeks access to her medical records and an independent medical evaluation before she returns to court.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The Monrovia City Court has reassigned the preliminary examination for Friday, September 4, 2026, at 10:00 a.m., according to a notice of assignment issued by Stipendiary Magistrate L. Ben Barco.

Taylor’s lawyers had initially asked the court to continue Tuesday’s proceedings to Wednesday, September 2, at a time convenient to the court, citing their client’s ongoing health condition.

The request was filed at approximately 7:54 a.m. on September 1, according to a handwritten notation on the document.

In their communication to the court, Taylor’s lawyers said she remains unwell but is willing to participate in all stages of the preliminary examination.

They said Taylor had a medical consultation scheduled for September 1 and had requested permission from the Ministry of Justice to be examined by a physician familiar with her medical history.

The lawyers argued that a brief postponement would allow the former vice president to receive necessary medical attention before returning to court.

The communication was signed by Cllr. Laveli Supuwood, Cllr. Kabineh Ja’neh, and Cllr. Finley Y. Karngar.

Defense Seeks Medical Records, Cardiologist

FrontPage Africa has gathered that Taylor’s defense team is also seeking a continuance to allow her lawyers to obtain her medical records and arrange for an independent doctor to assess her condition.

A source told FPA that Dr. Gomez of GIMS Medical Center requested Taylor’s medical records based on a notarized authorization signed by the former vice president.

The source said efforts were also underway to have a cardiologist examine Taylor as her defense team seeks a clearer assessment of her condition before she faces further proceedings.

Taylor was previously taken to GIMS Medical Center while in police custody after reportedly experiencing an unstable medical condition, including elevated blood pressure.

She was later returned to custody at the Monrovia Central Prison, where she remains detained.

Facing Serious Drug Charges

Taylor’s detention followed her arrest in connection with the government’s investigation into a massive cocaine seizure in the VOA community in Paynesville.

Authorities have valued the seized cocaine at more than US$317 million, making it one of the largest narcotics seizures in Liberia’s history.

The case has drawn significant public and political attention because of Taylor’s status as a former vice president and the identities of others named in the investigation.

The latest notice of assignment lists Taylor alongside Teras Zadereiko, alias Tony; Mitovil Vrovac, alias Michael; Nikola Ivancic, alias Sheikh; and others to be identified.

The charges listed include importation of controlled drugs, unlicensed exportation of controlled drugs and substances, abuse of office, illicit trafficking, criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation, criminal solicitation, and money laundering.

The Government of Liberia, through the Ministry of Justice, is listed as the plaintiff.

The matter is before Magistrate Barco at the Monrovia City Court at the Temple of Justice.

Taylor Denies Allegations

Taylor has denied the allegations against her, while her lawyers have continued to challenge aspects of the government’s handling of the case.

Her arrest and detention have also triggered political controversy, with supporters and opposition voices questioning the circumstances surrounding the case.

The government’s prosecution stems from the broader investigation into the cocaine shipment seized in Paynesville, which authorities say was linked to an international narcotics trafficking operation.

Health Now Central to Proceedings

Taylor’s medical condition has emerged as the latest hurdle in the case.

With the defense seeking her medical records and an independent evaluation by a doctor, including a possible cardiology assessment, the question of whether she is medically fit to participate in court proceedings is now likely to feature prominently when the case returns on September 4.

For now, the former vice president remains in custody as her lawyers work to establish the full state of her health before the preliminary examination proceeds.

World.title: Liberia: GAC Clears Liberia’s 2025 Accounts, Flags US$76.9M Year-End Cash Balance
World.content:
Monrovia – Auditor General P. Garswa Jackson has released the General Auditing Commission’s (GAC) audit of the Government of Liberia’s Consolidated Fund Account for the 2025 fiscal year, giving the government’s financial statements an unqualified opinion while urging lawmakers to urgently act on recommendations contained in the report.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The audit, covering the period January 1 to December 31, 2025, examined the government’s statement of cash receipts and payments, comparison of budgeted and actual amounts, and accompanying financial notes.

In his report dated August 2026, Auditor General Jackson said the financial statements “present fairly, in all material respects” the government’s receipts and payments as of December 31, 2025, and conform with the 2017 International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) Cash Basis of Accounting.

The audit was conducted in accordance with the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAIs) and Section 2.1.3 of the General Auditing Commission Act of 2014.

GAC Urges Legislature to Act

Despite issuing a favorable audit opinion, Jackson warned that matters raised during the audit require the attention of the Legislature.

In a transmittal letter addressed to the Speaker of the House of Representatives and the President Pro-Tempore of the Liberian Senate, the Auditor General said the findings had been formally communicated to the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning through a Management Letter.

He said responses provided by the Ministry were reviewed and incorporated into the final audit report.

“Given the significance of the matters raised in this report,” Jackson urged lawmakers to consider implementing the audit recommendations with urgency.

The report now places responsibility on the Legislature to scrutinize the findings and follow up on the government’s implementation of the recommendations.

Government Managed US$955.2M in Cash Receipts

According to the financial statements, the government recorded US$955.20 million in total cash receipts during fiscal year 2025, a substantial increase from the US$685.56 million recorded in 2024.

The increase of approximately US$269.64 million, or 28 percent, was attributed largely to improvements in revenue administration, digital transformation and enhanced revenue collection and compliance.

The government said the integration of the Liberia Tax Administration System (LITAS) with commercial banks and mobile money platforms, along with the expansion of ASYCUDA and LITAS across major customs and tax offices, contributed to the improved performance.

Total cash expenditure also increased significantly, reaching US$902.77 million, compared with US$660.57 million in 2024.

That represents an increase of approximately US$242.20 million, or 27 percent.

The government attributed the increase partly to the settlement of outstanding commitments from the previous fiscal year’s 90-day window period and adjustments to budgeted expenditure.

US$76.89M Remained at Year-End

The financial statements show that Liberia closed fiscal year 2025 with a reconciled cash balance of approximately US$76.89 million.

The reported balance comprised funds held across government accounts, including consolidated accounts, escrow accounts, the Road Fund escrow accounts, mobile money accounts, and transitory and other accounts.

The report lists approximately:

US$14.37 million in Consolidated Accounts;

US$7.04 million in Other Escrow Accounts;

US$902,000 in Road Fund Escrow Accounts;

US$53,000 in Mobile Money Accounts;

US$58 million in Transitory and Other Accounts; and

approximately US$3.48 million in foreign currency gain/loss adjustments.

The government stated that the reconciled balances were controlled by the government and held at the Central Bank of Liberia, commercial banks and electronic platforms.

Revenue Outperformed Budget

The audit report also highlights stronger-than-projected revenue performance during the year.

The government had approved a US$880.66 million resource envelope for fiscal year 2025, representing a 19.2 percent increase over the FY2024 recast budget of US$738.86 million.

Actual overall revenue reached US$885.10 million, exceeding the approved budget by approximately US$4.44 million, or 0.5 percent.

Domestic revenue was particularly strong, reaching US$847.05 million against a budget projection of US$804.63 million—an overperformance of approximately US$42.43 million.

However, the government fell short of its projected external revenue after approximately US$40 million expected from the World Bank was not realized during FY2025 because of unmet disbursement conditions.

US$880.66M Expenditure Envelope

The FY2025 budget authorized total expenditure of US$880.66 million.

Of that amount, recurrent and non-PSIP capital expenditure accounted for US$773.95 million, or 87.9 percent, while the Public Sector Investment Program (PSIP) accounted for US$106.72 million, or 12.1 percent.

Actual cash spending, however, reached US$902.77 million, exceeding the approved expenditure envelope.

The government said the higher expenditure was influenced by the payment of outstanding commitments carried over from the previous fiscal year’s 90-day window and upward adjustments to expenditure during the reporting period.

Government Claims Stronger Financial Controls

In its statement of responsibility, the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning maintained that the government had upheld its obligations under the Public Financial Management Act and Regulations.

The government said it had systems of internal control and risk management designed to safeguard public resources against loss, misuse and fraud, ensure transactions comply with applicable laws and regulations, and maintain reliable financial records.

The Comptroller and Accountant General also certified responsibility for the accuracy, completeness and reliability of the financial information contained in the consolidated financial statements.

The financial statements were approved for issuance on April 30, 2026, while the Auditor General’s report was issued in August 2026.

Audit Opinion Does Not Mean No Problems

While the Auditor General’s unqualified opinion represents a positive assessment of the financial statements, the report makes clear that an audit opinion is not a guarantee that every instance of fraud, error or internal-control weakness will be detected.

Jackson noted that an audit provides reasonable assurance, rather than absolute assurance, that financial statements are free from material misstatement.

The Auditor General said the audit procedures were designed based on assessed risks of material misstatement, including those arising from fraud or error, and included an evaluation of accounting policies, estimates and the overall presentation of the financial statements.

The release of the report comes amid heightened public scrutiny of government spending, revenue collection and financial accountability, making the Legislature’s promised consideration of the GAC’s recommendations a key next step in determining whether the identified issues will result in corrective action.

World.title: Liberia: Court Puts $8M Bail Bond Under Microscope, Gives Ex-Presidential Protocol Officer 30 Days to Cure Defect, Passport Seized
World.content:
Nora Finda Bundoo Survives Bid to Revoke Bail, But Judge Feika Rules AUG Insurance Over-Exposed; Orders Augmentation and Travel Ban.

Monrovia – Former Executive Mansion Chief of Protocol Nora Finda Bundoo is making another legal effort to secure her temporary release, filing a new criminal appearance bond backed by two insurance companies after the Criminal Court “C” rejected two previous attempts to satisfy its bail requirements.

By Victoria G Wesseh and Willie N. Tokpah

The latest move places Bundoo’s constitutional right to bail and the State’s demand for adequate security at the center of a continuing legal battle before Criminal Court “C,” presided over by Assigned Circuit Judge Ousman E. Feika.

Court records show that Bundoo has not abandoned her effort to comply with the court’s requirements. Instead, following the rejection of two earlier bond arrangements, her legal team turned to insurance companies licensed to issue criminal appearance bonds in Liberia.

For Nora Finda Bundoo, the fight for temporary freedom has become a legal journey marked by repeated setbacks, escalating financial requirements, and yet another challenge from the State.

The former Executive Mansion Chief of Protocol is now before Criminal Court “C” seeking approval of a new criminal appearance bond after two previous attempts to secure her release were rejected.

This time, Bundoo has turned to two insurance companies, Accident and Casualty Insurance Company and American Undertakers Group International Insurance Company (AUG, in what appears to be another effort to meet the court’s requirements and regain her liberty while she awaits trial.

But once again, the prosecution has objected.

The development has placed Bundoo in an increasingly difficult position. She must defend herself against serious criminal allegations while simultaneously finding a way to satisfy a bond requirement that the court has set at US$8 million.

The situation is becoming bigger than the value of a bond for her defense.

It is about whether bail, which is intended to secure an accused person’s appearance in court, is being transformed into an obstacle so difficult to overcome that it effectively keeps an accused person behind bars before trial.

Two Attempts, Two Rejections

Bundoo’s present predicament follows two previous attempts to secure her release.

The first bond was set aside by Judge Ousman E. Feika after the court found that the proposed sureties were insufficient and did not meet the legal requirements to file the bond.

The court then gave Bundoo 72 hours to present another criminal appearance bond.

She did.

Two sureties, Kai Garlo Farley and John Moses Gbetee, submitted property valuation bonds on her behalf. Again, the prosecution objected.

On July 21, Judge Ousmam Feika ruled on the property-backed guarantees and set the bond threshold at US$8 million.

That ruling for Bundoo dramatically changed the challenge before her.

The issue is no longer simply finding individuals willing to stand as sureties. She is now confronted with a financial threshold running into millions of United States dollars.

However, rather than abandoning her effort to secure release, Bundoo’s legal team searched for another lawful mechanism, which produced the latest insurance-backed bonds.

A Different Route to the Same Goal

ACICO and AUG subsequently filed separate criminal appearance bonds for Bundoo.

The move can be viewed as an attempt to address concerns surrounding the earlier property valuation bonds by relying instead on insurance companies licensed by the Central Bank of Liberia to issue criminal appearance bonds, but the State has again objected.

The prosecution argued that the latest bonds remain inadequate and do not sufficiently satisfy the statutory objectives of bail under Section 13.2 of the Criminal Procedure Law.

Bundoo’s lawyers disagree, arguing that bail is intended to accomplish two fundamental things: to prevent unnecessary pretrial incarceration while ensuring that an accused person remains within the jurisdiction of the court and appears whenever required.

Bubdoo’s position goes to the heart of her struggle, and she is not asking the court to terminate the criminal case against her, but asking to face the allegations while temporarily outside detention.

The defense argued that if bail is intended to guarantee an accused person’s appearance, the amount should be set at a level that an accused person has little realistic ability to meet.

Bundoo’s lawyers argue that although the court has discretion in determining the sufficiency of bail, that discretion should not result in a bond so excessive that it exceeds the accused’s financial capacity.

For Bundoo, the US$8 million threshold is therefore not merely a number on a court document.

It represents a potentially formidable barrier between her and temporary liberty.

After two earlier bonds were rejected, the latest prosecution objection means she faces yet another hurdle in an already prolonged effort to secure release.

The State’s Pursuit Under Scrutiny

The government’s prosecution of Bundoo is being conducted through the Assets Recovery and Property Retrieval Task Force, AREPT, and the Ministry of Justice.

The State has a legitimate responsibility to prosecute allegations of financial crimes and to ensure that defendants appear before court.

But the intensity with which Bundoo’s release has been contested also raises questions about proportionality.

Bundoo stands indicted on allegations including money laundering, theft of property, misuse of public money and records, criminal conspiracy, forgery and criminal facilitation.
