World.title: Trump is closing an asylum loophole legal immigrants have watched others exploit
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A tourist visa should not become a Trojan horse for permanent immigration. While Washington has spent years focused on the southern border, one of the most consequential loopholes may begin at a consulate, where someone promises to visit temporarily and later files for asylum to remain. That is why the Trump administration is preparing to revoke the visitor visas of up to 200,000 foreign nationals who later sought asylum. Critics will call this anti-immigrant, but enforcing the terms of a visa defends every immigrant who entered legally and honestly. It is also how the United States protects the integrity of legal immigration.

A visitor visa begins with a representation that an applicant is seeking permission to enter the United States temporarily. A B-1 visa permits limited business activities, such as attending meetings or conferences, while a B-2 visa covers tourism, vacations, visits with family or friends and certain medical treatment. Applicants must complete a visa application, establish a legitimate purpose for the trip and persuade the government that they intend to leave when their authorized stay ends. Permanent residence is not a permitted purpose of a visitor visa.

Asylum, by contrast, protects people who have suffered persecution or have a well-founded fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group. Filing for asylum does not grant permanent residence, although someone granted asylum may later become eligible for a green card. An asylum claim filed after entering on a visitor visa is not automatically fraudulent. An applicant may face changed circumstances after arriving or develop a legitimate fear of persecution. Allowing someone to seek asylum does not prevent the government from investigating whether the applicant fraudulently obtained a visitor visa by concealing an intention to remain permanently once their entry was granted.

IMMIGRANT BUSINESS OWNER WHO BUILT THE AMERICAN DREAM SAYS BIRTH TOURISM IS A 'SLAP IN THE FACE'

This distinction matters to me personally because I came to America legally as a child and later practiced immigration law. My family, like millions of legal immigrants, filed the appropriate paperwork, paid the fees, attended government interviews and waited for the privilege of becoming American citizens. We followed a process that demanded patience, honesty and respect for the rule of law, often requiring families to spend years separated from loved ones and make enormous financial and personal sacrifices. They should not be told that those sacrifices were optional while others used a visitor visa as a loophole to cut the line and remain permanently.

Further, false asylum claims hurt the people genuinely fleeing persecution. Manufactured claims divert limited resources from legitimate asylum seekers who may be facing imprisonment, torture or death. This is why the Trump administration should apply this policy carefully, rather than presume that every asylum applicant lied. Visa holders should receive notice and an individualized opportunity to explain how their circumstances changed, identify any new threats and present evidence supporting a legitimate claim. The government can enforce immigration law without abandoning due process.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ORDERS GREEN CARD APPLICANTS TO LEAVE THE US, APPLY FROM THEIR HOME COUNTRIES

Revocation matters because many visitor visas allow multiple trips to the United States over several years. Once revoked, the visa can no longer be used to enter or reenter the country, preventing someone who has applied for asylum from continuing to travel under a temporary visitor classification. However, revoking a visitor visa does not deny a pending asylum claim or result in immediate deportation. It just closes the door to future entry while the government separately determines whether the asylum claim is legitimate.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Washington presents a false choice between enforcing immigration law and treating immigrants with compassion rather than hostility. That argument ignores the millions of legal immigrants who respected the rule of law and want a system that refuses to tolerate abuse. The greatest threat to legal immigration is a two-tiered system that rewards those who manipulate the law while disregarding the sacrifices of millions who followed it.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

President Trump is asking the question Washington should have asked from the beginning: Was the United States government told the truth, or did the applicant conceal an intention to remain permanently? America must continue protecting people who genuinely face persecution, but this protection must be preserved through careful vetting and honest enforcement. Compassion does not require accepting abuse or injustice. A strong nation can enforce its laws, protect due process and offer refuge to those who truly need it.

World.title: Democrat establishment flexes dominance as insurgents fall and GOP bench thins in deep blue stronghold
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Massachusetts Democrats rewarded incumbency in marquee primaries Tuesday, but the clearest message came in the state’s generational showdown, with 80-year-old Sen. Ed Markey routing moderate Democratic Rep. Seth Moulton, 47, after Moulton argued it was time for the party to "pass the torch."

Tuesday night's results underscored Democratic dominance in the deep-blue state rather than a single ideological sweep. Voters backed established incumbents across the party’s factions and selected a Biden-Harris-backed former White House aide in the closely watched open-seat contest to take over Moulton's House seat after he abandoned it to run for Senate. Meanwhile, Republicans failed to nominate House candidates in four districts — the first, second, fifth and seventh — while only fielding write-ins for the blue stronghold's secretary of state race.

Markey’s victory over the more moderate Moulton, however, stood out as the night’s clearest win for the party’s progressive wing.

TOP ELECTION SCHEMES ROILING KEY MIDTERM RACES AS BOTH PARTIES ACCUSE RIVALS OF TRICKERY

"Its very clear that the dem voters care more about policies and having a progressive represent them in the senate, than age!," controversial Twitch streamer and far-left activist Hasan Piker said after the Associated Press projected Markey would win. "Another w for our movement!"

Moulton highlighted the difficult battle he faced trying to unseat a longtime incumbent like Markey following his concession, but said the effort was not for nothing, noting "we started conversations that needed to happen" and adding that he is "confident ... others will be inspired to buck the system when they’re told to wait their turn."

Markey faced attacks during the campaign over his far-left positions, including his support for transgender athletes' participation in women's sports, but the progressive bona fides of the Massachusetts lawmaker, who has represented the state in Congress for nearly five decades, were not a significant enough sticking point for voters to abandon him.

SCANDAL-PLAGUED 'SQUAD' REP CRUISES TO DEMOCRATIC NOMINATION WITH NO GOP ROADBLOCKS IN VIEW

"Ed Markey has spent decades fighting for LGBTQ+ equality, for working people, and for a more livable world," said Human Rights Campaign (HRC) President Kelley Robinson following Markey's win. "He knows why equality matters. He’s stood with us no matter what. We were proud to endorse him this year, and when a pro-equality majority takes back the Senate this fall, we will continue to count on him as a champion for our community."

The incumbent success Markey saw carried into the House during Tuesday night's Massachusetts primaries, where Reps. Richard Neal and Stephen Lynch fended off younger challengers, while Reps. Katherine Clark and Jake Auchincloss also advanced. The string of wins offered little evidence of broad anti-incumbent turbulence in the state’s Democratic delegation.

Massachusetts Democrats also picked former Biden White House aide Dan Koh to succeed Moulton in the open 6th Congressional District. Koh’s victory gives the delegation a new face, but it did not come at an incumbent’s expense as Moulton vacated the seat for his unsuccessful Senate bid, creating the district’s first open-seat contest without an incumbent on the ballot in decades.

TOP DEMOCRAT SURVIVES DOUBLE-BARRELED CHALLENGE AS PARTY’S ISRAEL DIVIDE HITS HOME

Massachusetts Republicans, meanwhile, failed to field nominees in several House districts, including the Boston-area 7th District, leaving Democrats such as Rep. Ayanna Pressley without GOP opposition in November. Pressley ran unopposed in Tuesday's primary.

Republicans will still have a statewide standard-bearer in November after businessman Michael Minogue defeated Brian Shortsleeve for the GOP gubernatorial nomination and advanced to face Democratic Gov. Maura Healey, who won her primary unopposed Tuesday night.

The GOP also nominated House candidates in five of the state’s nine districts: the third, fourth, sixth, eighth and ninth.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The most notable is the open 6th District, where Republican Micah Quinney Jones will face Koh, who was backed by former President Joe Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, alongside several other alumni of the Biden administration. The support gave Koh a powerful establishment coalition in the crowded contest to succeed Moulton.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Following Koh's win, Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin congratulated the former Biden administration aide.

"From Boston City Hall and the U.S. Department of Labor to the White House, Dan Koh has dedicated his life to public service and ensuring government actually delivers for working families. He is a Massachusetts native who knows how to bring people together to solve problems and fight for our communities," Martin said in a statement. "In Congress, Dan will prioritize bringing down costs, protecting healthcare, making housing more affordable, strengthening workers’ rights, rooting out corruption, and holding Donald Trump accountable. The DNC is ready to work alongside him to make life more affordable for people throughout Massachusetts’ 6th Congressional District."

World.title: Inside the far-left's anti-data center push and what experts say is driving it: 'Playbook we've seen before'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As the development of data centers continues to grow into one of the top hot button political issues in the United States, some experts are sounding the alarm on the various left-wing groups and climate activists who are pouring money and resources into data center opposition campaigns.

"It's a playbook we've seen before," Larry Behrens, communications director at Power The Future, told Fox News Digital in an interview.

"I think Americans saw this with the Dakota Access Pipeline. They see this with oil or natural gas production within the United States. This seemingly grassroots organization pops up, but yet they're all wearing the same t-shirts. They're all singing the same playbook and they're only carrying the same signs and so when we see that, we see that that's not really a grassroots organization that money is coming from somewhere, and in this case, against data centers."

Several left-wing organizations backing data center opposition have benefited from major progressive funding networks, including Public Citizen, which has listed George Soros’ Open Society Foundations among foundations whose "generous support" makes its work possible, and the Sierra Club, which received $3.6 million from Arabella Advisors’ Sixteen Thirty Fund between 2014 and 2022.

TOP ENERGY GROUP WARNS WEALTHY FOREIGNERS ARE POTENTIALLY BANKROLLING ANTI-DATA CENTER CAMPAIGNS ACROSS US

CodePink, which has targeted data center projects, has received funding linked to socialist megadonor Neville Roy Singham, who has deep ties to the Chinese Communist Party. Fox News Digital previously reported that Singham funneled roughly $285 million into six activist nonprofits, as the U.S. and China battle for global AI dominance.

In Texas, viewed by many as the front line of the data center fight, opposition has been fueled by a network of left-wing groups, including Public Citizen, the Sierra Club and the Party for Socialism and Liberation. Public Citizen is a founding member of the Texas Data Center Rebellion, which brought activists from across the state together for a two-day convening in San Antonio, while the Sierra Club’s Austin chapter, PSL and Save Our Springs Alliance teamed up for a July "Defend Dog’s Head" forum opposing a massive Austin development that includes data centers.

Several of the groups actively involved in fueling anti-ICE protests and "No Kings" protests across the country are also involved in pushing back against data centers. Earlier this year, Fox News Digital reported that Power the Future, a pro-energy advocacy group, sent a letter asking Congress to take a closer look at opposition to data centers springing up across the country, pointing out the various left-wing groups that were backing those efforts.

"What they do is they send their money through a maze of organizations, deliberately trying to mask what it is being used for and seeing that the tentacles reach in from far and are made to look local," Behrens explained. "Now, to be clear, there is local opposition and there are legitimate questions to ask, but when the legislative language is the same, when the talking points are the same. And the lawyer's points are the same, then we start to see that this is not an organic local movement."

THE HIDDEN LEFT-WING NETWORK POWERING A ‘CONSERVATIVE’ REBELLION AGAINST A MAJOR TRUMP PRIORITY

The main driver of left-wing groups opposing data centers, in addition to ideological disdain toward President Donald Trump, who has been a staunch supporter of American AI dominance, is the opposition to fossil fuels, Behrens says.

"It's the same thing that they've always opposed, any real progress they're going to be against, anything that strengthens America, they're gonna be against, and when it comes to data centers, the reason they're against them is absolutely clear because it represents American jobs and it has to be supported by American energy," Behrens explained.

"And those are two things that the environmental left just absolutely cannot stand. And they're gonna use delay or distracting tactics. They're gonna use tactics like saying it's about the water, it about land use. But lo and behold, when it comes time to grow cannabis, they're more than happy with the water use. When it comes to time to plaster solar fields across farmland, they don't care about land use. When it comes time to put their solar fields across an endangered species area, they don't care about that endangered species. It's never what they say it's about, it's always against progress and production for American energy and American workers really."

Data centers have become one of the most talked about political issues of the midterm election season, particularly in states like Texas, Ohio, and Nevada, and Fox News polling this summer found voters overwhelmingly oppose building data centers in their own communities, with 70% opposed and 30% in favor.

AGITATORS UNITED BY CHINESE MONEY, HATE FOR AMERICA TARGET DATA CENTERS, EXPERTS WARN

Nearly 8 in 10 voters said construction should move more slowly to address environmental and local concerns, while just 20% favored building as quickly as possible to preserve the U.S. competitive edge over China and other countries. Opposition crossed generational lines, though MAGA Republicans and Republican men were the most supportive groups, at 46% and 45%, respectively.

In a recent Fox News Digital op-ed, Consumers’ Research Executive Director Will Hild made the case that data center developers ignoring the concerns of the consumers’ has been a problem that could cost the United States victory in the AI race.

"Climate radicals who spent decades trying to kill fracking, pipelines, and American energy dominance have found their next target," Hild told Fox News Digital. "They are hijacking legitimate consumer concerns to fuel a massive disinformation campaign aimed at frightening Americans into shutting down the technology infrastructure. The same activist machine that fought American oil and gas is now mobilizing against modern data centers, because its answer to American innovation is always to stop building begins."

Data center backlash is increasingly reshaping midterm races nationwide, with candidates in both parties facing pressure to distance themselves from data center development or demand tougher restrictions as voters raise concerns about electricity costs, water use and the impact on local communities.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The issue has emerged in major Senate and gubernatorial contests from Ohio and Michigan to Pennsylvania and Texas, with campaigns using data centers in attack ads and candidates who once touted the projects increasingly calling for new regulations, tax changes or construction pauses.

In Texas, the fight has also become part of Democrats’ broader midterm organizing effort in the state. Texas Together, a $30 million coordinated campaign backed by the Texas Democratic Party, Texas Majority PAC, Beto O’Rourke’s Powered by People and other Democratic groups, has hosted data center-focused town halls and press events featuring Democratic candidates, while the El Paso Young Democrats and El Paso County Democratic Party organized a protest against what they called "destructive AI Data Centers."

Behrens agreed with Hild’s call for different messaging and spoke to Fox News Digital about what data center companies need to do to shift the narrative.

"I think they need to discuss very specifically with local stakeholders, not the ones that are being astroturfed in, they need to talk about the benefits of it, they need to talk about exactly what the data center does because there are legitimate questions about it and Americans have a right to say, what is this going up in our area?"

Behrens added, "But I would also caution to say if you're not throwing up opposition to any other type of manufacturing, if you're not throwing up opposition to a large Buc-ees gas station then why the anger over data centers? Because those operations can use a lot of water, they can use a lot of land just like the data centers. So asking the questions is absolutely legitimate, but throwing up needless roadblocks because this is something that the environmental left has told you to dislike, we really need to watch out for that. And I think the bottom line would be if AOC, Bernie Sanders, and Kathy Hochul are your intellectual guiding stars for opposing data centers, then you need to really think about where you stand because they've been wrong on every major energy issue ever since they entered public office."

Fox News Digital reached out to CodePink, the Sierra Club, Open Society Foundations, and Public Citizen for comment.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a Sixteen Thirty Fund spokesperson pushed back saying the group "proudly supported the Sierra Club."

The spokesperson added: "Across the country, people have legitimate questions about how these projects could affect their communities. Dismissing those concerns as anti-American or anti-progress is absurd. Corporate interests should focus on addressing the potential impacts of data center development rather than attacking those who speak out."

World.title: Healthcare tops the Democrats’ to-do list if they win control of the House in 2026
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Vying to become House speaker in a few months, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries outlined four items on the agenda that he said would enjoy “uniform Democratic support” and advance the party’s goal of “making life more affordable.”

The first two were about healthcare, and all four set a direct contrast with President Donald Trump.

“We have to reverse the Medicaid cuts. We should extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits,” Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Monday in response to a question from NBC News. “We should restore congressional authority as it relates to tariffs, because the Trump tariffs are making life more expensive for the American people. And we should end, decisively, if it’s still going on, Donald Trump’s reckless and costly war of choice in the Middle East.”

Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., said there is consensus that Democrats’ first bill out of the gate, legislation that carries high symbolic weight known as H.R. 1, would need to focus on affordability.

But there’s not yet consensus on what the bill would look like, as voters cite the cost of living as a top concern heading into November’s elections.

Beyer argued that the best way to tackle the topic would be to restore hundreds of billions of dollars in Medicaid and the ACA subsidies that were cut in Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill.”

“In the affordability debate, nothing’s more central to it than healthcare,” Beyer said in an interview. “My expectation is that it’ll very much be about affordability one way or the other.”

Jeffries said there are “a whole host of things” still to work on, saying, “We’ve established five working groups on affordability” — on housing, healthcare, childcare, groceries and food, and gas and utilities.

He added that Democrats would also conduct aggressive oversight of the Trump administration and “certainly will fight to hold the crooks accountable.”

Jeffries’ agenda for a possible majority reflects an emerging consensus among many Democrats across the party spectrum, who said healthcare should top the party’s legislative to-do list in 2027. The lowest-hanging fruits are restoring Trump’s Medicaid cuts, which no Democrats voted for, and reviving the expired ACA, or “Obamacare,” tax credits, which every Democrat wanted to extend last year before Republicans blocked them, leading to coverage losses and substantially higher premiums for millions.

Still, many Democrats say reversing Trump on Medicaid and the ACA would be the bare minimum — and want the party to do much more on healthcare.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said it would “absolutely not” be enough to simply restore Medicaid and ACA funds.

“Of course, we need to take immediate action on those ACA subsidies and making sure that we lower those prices immediately. But it doesn’t fix the deeper systemic issue that has led healthcare to be one of the primary drivers of inflationary costs over the last decade, frankly,” she said in an interview.

“We need to be doing a lot more to take on corporate power, to break up a lot of these monopolies that are rolling up — Big Pharma, insurance, private equity entering the space of healthcare unchecked,” she added. “I think there’s a lot here for us to really dig in on, to work on.”

While there’s agreement on restoring the Medicaid and ACA funds that were undone by Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress, there are divisions inside the Democratic Party about what its own healthcare agenda should be.

A large and influential faction on the left wants to pursue a “Medicare for All” system that would diminish — if not abolish — private insurance and give the government power to negotiate prices of medication and services downward. Many moderate Democrats have rejected that idea in favor of less disruptive changes, although the center-left hasn’t coalesced around a preferred vision. One outside center-left group floated “free primary care for all” as a way to break the stalemate between supporters of a single-payer Medicare for All system and of focusing on building on the current ACA.

Part of what House Democrats would do next year depends on the size of their majority, should they win. If it’s a narrow majority of a handful of seats, as the House has operated in since 2021 under either party, they might be limited to the lowest common denominator and blocked from doing anything too aggressive on healthcare or any other major issues.

Jeffries, who is politically cautious by nature, is leery of getting ahead of his conference and overpromising without knowing what kind of majority he’d have.

A source familiar with Jeffries’ thinking said Democrats plan to take action in three tranches: the first 100 hours, when they would focus on urgent priorities with party consensus to provide relief for Americans; then the first 100 days, to build on that foundation with more aggressive efforts to lower costs alongside investigative moves; and then the first year.

Rep. Jared Moskowitz of Florida, a moderate Democrat in a competitive district, said the Medicaid and ACA plans may not be “a complete agenda” but backed those positions as a good place to start.

“Let’s talk about what we can get done quickly to provide the American people economic relief,” Moskowitz said. “You know we need 60 votes in the Senate for any piece of legislation, and then we need the president to sign it.”

Democrats have consistently enjoyed an issue advantage on healthcare since 2018, the last time they captured the House. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that Americans trust Democrats over Republicans to handle healthcare by 38% to 25%.

Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., who is poised to chair the Budget Committee if Democrats flip the House, also said he would be focused in the new year on “reversing the damage” to healthcare from Trump’s megabill.

“Keep in mind that when we take over in January, we will literally just be one month into the Medicaid cuts’ taking effect. That’s the biggest bulk by far of their healthcare cuts and where millions more people are going to lose their healthcare,” Boyle said in an interview. “So from the Budget Committee perspective, that’s what I’m focused on.”

Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-Texas, a member of the Appropriations and Budget committees, said she wants the party to take a much broader, more ambitious approach.

She said she is proud of the work House Democrats did on President Joe Biden’s Build Back Better agenda, which died in the Senate because of opposition from moderate Joe Manchin of West Virginia, who is no longer in office. Escobar said she would want to pursue much of that framework in Democrats’ first bill, including paid family and medical leave, universal prekindergarten, childcare subsidies and ACA subsidies, as well as student loan forgiveness.

“I would want to go big. My constituents and Americans all over the country are really hurting — it is so profound. And the increase in utility bills has been so overwhelming. I have constituents in my district who are paying more for their utility bills than their mortgage, and so people are really suffering right now. And my view is we have to offer the solutions that they deserve and they need, and we’ve done it before,” Escobar told NBC News.

“There is a way to message it. Obviously, the bigger it is, the more challenging that is,” she added.

But, she said, “there would be one central theme: bring down the costs that are making your life difficult.”

World.title: Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch defeats a younger challenger in Massachusetts primary
World.content:
Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch has defeated a younger, more progressive primary challenger, NBC News projects, in the highest-profile test remaining for House incumbents after a turbulent primary season.

Lynch, 71, won renomination over Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old former aide to former Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick. With his win, Lynch staved off an attempt to add him to the list of Democratic officeholders dethroned by rivals pushing for generational change.

Elsewhere in the state, fellow veteran Democratic Rep. Richard Neal also secured renomination, defeating teacher Jeromie Whalen in another Democratic primary.

Rep. Stephen Lynch in 2025. Michael Brochstein / Sipa USA via AP file

On the other side of Massachusetts, Roath outraised Lynch, outspent him significantly on the airwaves and scored The Boston Globe editorial board’s endorsement to go with backing from Patrick, progressive activist David Hogg’s group, Leaders We Deserve, and key teachers unions.

That support helped Roath press Lynch for months in one of the toughest fights of his political career. He highlighted Lynch’s various breaks with his party in the past, including votes against the Affordable Care Act and, more recently, for the Laken Riley Act. Roath also called for progressive measures like “Medicare for All,” abolishing ICE and restricting military aid to Israel.

But Lynch persevered, trumpeting work that he says held the Trump administration accountable and leaning on his decades of experience, including deep relationships with unions and other fixtures in the district.

“I got to know this district by living here and regularly attending hundreds of town meetings, not just to speak, but to listen and understand the needs and priorities of the people that I represent,” Lynch said at an August forum sponsored by the League of Women Voters Hingham and others.

Patrick Roath at a rally in Hingham, Mass. last year to protest President Donald Trump's policies. Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images file

He touted “tens of billions of dollars that I’ve been able to bring back to our district” and added that he “accomplished much of that as a member of the minority party in Congress. You can only imagine what we can do together if the situation changes.”

Lynch’s victory means he has avoided the fate of 11 of his House colleagues — including seven Democrats — who lost primary challenges this year as voters took some of their frustrations with Washington out on incumbent lawmakers. Another two senators, both Republicans whose primary opponents got Trump endorsements, also lost primaries this year.

Neal also avoided defeat in another primary marked by arguments over generational change and progressive policy proposals. Whalen, 39, a high school teacher, ran a campaign decrying the “old-school political entanglements that got us into this mess” and called to abolish ICE and cut off U.S. military aid to Israel.

Neal spent more than $1 million on campaign ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, about 10 times what Whalen spent.

Meanwhile, in the open 6th District, Dan Koh won the Democratic primary in the race to succeed Rep. Seth Moulton, who ran for the Senate but lost that primary to Sen. Ed Markey.

Koh was an aide to a variety of top Democrats, including former Boston Mayor Marty Walsh, and chief of staff of the U.S. Labor Department, and he was the top fundraiser in the race.

Both former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris have appeared in an ad for Koh, who has emphasized that he wants to take on Trump and his “corruption,” calling to abolish ICE and pass “Medicare for All.”

World.title: Alaska finalizes Senate race for November: 3 Republicans, 2 Dan Sullivans and 1 Democrat
World.content:
The Alaska Division of Elections on Tuesday named the four Senate candidates who will be on the ballot this fall in a closely watched race that will be decided by ranked-choice voting.

Voters will make their selections among two Republicans named Dan Sullivan, another named Gerald Heikes and Democrat Mary Peltola, who finished first during the all-party primary in which the top four advance to the general election.

Democrat David Leslie had finished fourth, but he withdrew from the race Monday. His withdrawal means fifth-place candidate Gerald Heikes, a Republican, will appear on the ballot.

Dan J. Sullivan and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, R-Alaska. AP; Getty Images

The race is considered one of the most competitive in the 2026 cycle and a potential pickup for Democrats, who are hoping to gain control of the Senate. It’s made headlines due to the novelty of having two candidates with the same first and last name.

Dan J. Sullivan, a former schoolteacher who came in third in the primary, is seeking to unseat Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. But his candidacy has faced legal challenges from the senator and other Republicans who allege he is working with Peltola, a former congresswoman, and entered the race as a potential spoiler. He and Peltola have denied any coordination with each other, as have their campaigns.

Although the Alaska Supreme Court allowed Sullivan to stay on the ballot after originally being disqualified by the Division of Elections, state and federal authorities are conducting their own investigation into his campaign.

The Division of Elections on Tuesday also named general election candidates for the governor’s contest, including Republicans Dave Bronson and Bernadette Wilson and Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the top finisher in the primary.

They are running to replace term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy.

Tom Begich, a Democrat who finished second in the primary, withdrew from the race before Tuesday.

World.title: Key Texas county votes to cut polling sites ahead of the midterms
World.content:
Officials in Texas’ third-largest county voted Tuesday to significantly reduce the number of polling sites for this fall’s midterm elections, drawing protests from Democrats and voting rights advocates.

Commissioners in Tarrant County, a fast-growing and politically competitive area that includes Fort Worth, approved a plan that results in 92 fewer Election Day polling locations compared with the 2022 midterms. The roughly 30% reduction leaves the county with 224 polling sites to serve 1.3 million voters. Voters in the county are able to cast ballots at any of those polling sites.

The three Republicans on the Tarrant County Commissioners Court voted for their plan, while the two Democrats voted against it.

Research has found that each additional minute of travel time to a polling location can affect voter participation. The NAACP, the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas and other groups said in a letter that the changes would hit voters of color hardest because many of the reductions are in majority-minority areas in Fort Worth and Arlington.

Supporters of the plan say that it will save money and that there are more than enough options for people to vote.

The move comes amid a critical Senate contest in Texas, with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico taking on state Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican.

Talarico urged the county to reject the plan ahead of Tuesday’s vote.

“The most powerful people in this county, the most powerful people in this country, don’t want us to be able to vote easily,” Talarico told reporters Sunday, according to The Associated Press.

Tarrant County has emerged as a key political battleground in Texas. President Donald Trump won it in the 2024 presidential race after Joe Biden flipped it four years prior. And Democrats Beto O’Rourke and Colin Allred narrowly carried the county in the 2018 and 2024 Senate races, respectively, even as they both went on to lose.

Texas law gives counties the power to decide how many polling sites they use. And some counties have begun using fewer sites as they have moved to countywide voting in recent years.

Dozens of voters urged the commissioners to vote against the cuts. Some criticized the elimination of specific polling places — like one at the University of Texas at Arlington — while others noted that the county has experienced significant population growth and voter participation in recent years.

“The right to vote is the bedrock of our democracy,” said a woman named Linda Northern. “This will make it harder for brown, Black and low-income voters to have the same right to vote as you do. This is wrong.”

Tarrant County Commissioner Roderick Miles Jr., a Democrat, added ahead of the vote, “This is about ensuring that the rights that people bled and died for are accessible to everybody.”

Tarrant County Judge Tim O’Hare, a Republican on the commissioner court, argued that Miles wanted more polling sites in his area.

“There’s no argument to that that you can come up with other than you want to be able to have more in your precinct,” O’Hare said.

A handful of speakers supported the plan, noting that some sites were used by few voters and required a significant number of poll workers and financial resources.

“I support the proposition that’s in front of us as far as reducing the number of voting sites. I’ve been a poll watcher, a poll worker, a precinct chair and all those things, and when you vote, when you go to a poll place that had 34 people all day long, you think this is kind of a waste of resources,” said one speaker, who did not identify herself.

World.title: No plans for ICE to be at polls for midterms, DHS says
World.content:
ICE officers have not received guidance telling them they need to do anything in addition to their regular duties on the day of November’s midterm elections, a senior Homeland Security official told NBC News.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a news conference Tuesday in New York that ICE officers will be at a polling place only if “there is a threat to that polling place” or if officers are serving a warrant on someone “that we have been actively tracking down.”

“ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places,” Mullin said.

Asked whether ICE officers would enter polling places, Mullin said they would if they had warrants.

“If we’re serving a warrant, we will be where we need to be,” Mullin said.

President Donald Trump and Mullin have claimed without offering any evidence that there are over 250,000 noncitizens on voter rolls across several states. Mullin recently threatened state election officials with possible prison time if they didn’t comply with the administration’s methods to determine whether noncitizens were on their voter rolls. Several state officials have pushed back against sharing private state voter roll data that includes personal information, such as Social Security numbers.

World.title: Thousands of U.S. service members arrive in Thailand after record stint at sea
World.content:
LAEM CHABANG, Thailand — The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier arrived Wednesday at a port in eastern Thailand, where thousands of U.S. sailors and Marines are disembarking for the first time in more than 280 days after a record-setting deployment in the Middle East.

The toll of the more than nine-month deployment, most of it spent supporting military operations in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, was visible on the carrier as it pulled into Laem Chabang Port in Chonburi province. Paint has worn off and the metal underneath is rusted on the 1,092-foot warship, which is one of the largest in the world.

The USS Abraham Lincoln approaching Laem Chabang Port near Pattaya, Thailand, on Wednesday. Mithil Aggarwal / NBC News

The Lincoln is in Thailand for a four-day “rest and relaxation” stop on its way home to San Diego after having spent weeks in the headlines as the lengthy deployment raised concerns about supply shortages and the effect on sailors’ mental health.

The U.S. Navy confirmed the ship’s arrival in a statement, saying the Lincoln strike group arrived in Laem Chabang while the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. docked in nearby Sriracha and the guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls went to Map Ta Phut in neighboring Rayong province.

The Navy said it was the Lincoln’s first full port stop after 286 days at sea since the deployment began in November.

This will be the first time on dry land for the sailors after a record-setting stint at sea. Anthony Wallace / AFP via Getty Images

“Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our sailors and Marines to rest and recharge,” said Rear Adm. Robert E. Loughran, commander of Carrier Strike Group 3. “It also underscores the strong and enduring partnership and alliance between the United States and Thailand.”

About 5,000 sailors and Marines are expected to hit the streets of Pattaya, a nearby coastal resort city that is one of the most popular tourist destinations in Thailand. Each service member will get three “liberty days” and one day of duty aboard the ship, a U.S. military official said.

Local businesses in Pattaya have welcomed the sailors with large banners outside restaurants and bars. Sakchai Lalit / AP

Upon the Lincoln’s arrival in the morning, service members could be seen working aboard the deck as loudspeakers played announcements about the process for disembarkation. A whistle could be heard ringing across the deck, a Navy tradition that signals coming ashore.

00:16 Thai police crackdown on sex workers 00:00 00:00

Around 1 p.m. local time (2 a.m. ET), service members began disembarking from the ship in civilian clothes, some carrying backpacks. One service member was carrying his golf clubs. Waiting for them across the way were dozens of Ford pickup trucks and buses lined up in columns to take them into town.

“Please be on your best behavior,” a commanding officer could be heard saying over loudspeaker.

Locals in tourism-dependent Pattaya have eagerly awaited the arrival of the Lincoln, which pulled into sight from the shore after sunrise before it made a wide turn and harbored itself at a major cargo terminal.

Officials in Pattaya, where international tourist arrivals have dropped because of travel disruptions and soaring fuel prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East, say the visit is expected to inject about $3 million into the local economy.

Authorities in Pattaya have stepped up security, with heightened police patrols and checks along the roads. Businesses here are also trying to woo the sailors, with some putting up banners to welcome them.

About 5,000 sailors and Marines are expected to hit the streets of Pattaya. Anthony Wallace / AFP via Getty Images

Wichai Yuankham, 35, a factory worker who came to watch the ships arrive, said the naval visit was a welcome boost to the local economy.

“I am just excited to see the destroyer docking,” he said. “This is my first time seeing the destroyer, and I feel good seeing it, and we can boast to our neighboring countries about this.”

World.title: U.S. strikes targets in Iran near Strait of Hormuz as Iran says it is retaliating
World.content:
U.S. strikes targets in Iran near Strait of Hormuz as Iran says it is retaliating

What the jury must consider while deciding Lindsay Clancy's fate
