World.title: Burnham promised hope. Reality is already getting in the way
World.content:
He pledged to shake up England’s privatized water sector as part of a “10-year plan” this fall. He promised to impose his predecessor Keir Starmer’s social media ban on under-16s “at pace.” He repeated his long-held vows to radically reform the social care system, move powers and officials out of Whitehall, release public land for a wave of house-building and “end” rough sleeping — while still bringing down the welfare bill. “Working together to build a new sense of optimism around the country, we can make this next decade better than the last,” he said.

The parliamentary chamber began to empty, MPs turning to other duties and their bladders, as the hardiest stayed behind in the hope they would extract yet another commitment from the prime minister.

As the session wore on, Burnham hinted he could one day scrap England’s system of local taxation, which is based on property valuations from 1991. In the third hour he even promised to save Jodrell Bank, a locally-beloved cluster of deep space radio telescopes near Manchester that has had its funding cut.

The new prime minister was not offering a free-for-all and, like any minister, swerved more invitations to commit policy than he accepted. He insisted he will make tough choices.

Yet he is also enjoying a practical by-effect of being a new leader: He hasn’t yet had to disappoint all the people he will eventually disappoint.

Rhetoric vs. reality

The 125 questions he took showed that the difficulties and trade-offs that come with power are already coming into view.

World.title: Spain calls for probe into reports government agency blamed Morocco for Ceuta migrant influx
World.content:
Spain's interior minister has asked police to check a report that a government agency blamed Moroccan security forces for July's mass entry of migrants to the enclave of Ceuta, ministry sources said on Wednesday.

 

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Monday that Morocco was not responsible, instead accusing Israel, Russia and the far right of spreading disinformation about the mass entry of around 70,000 migrants into Ceuta.

Sánchez told Cadena SER radio that "no intelligence service with which the Spanish government normally cooperates" had suggested "any involvement in one way or another of the Moroccan authorities."

But online newspaper El Español reported that Spain's National Centre for Immigration and Borders (CENIF) said the incident "was guided by Moroccan security forces...with an objective other than migration."

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska has written to police chief Francisco Pardo to check on the information, which CENIF reportedly sent to a judge collecting information on the incident, said ministry sources.

Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska talks to reporters during a press conference in Valletta, 4 March, 2023 AP Photo

"Any such information should have immediately been made available to the National Security Council...and to other bodies with powers in this field," the minister said in his letter.

More than 70,000 migrants entered the small Spanish territory in north Africa on 30-31 July, swimming or crossing on foot from neighbouring Morocco in an unprecedented rush that left scores dead.

Some analysts have suggested the crisis may have been a message sent to Spain by Morocco over the disputed Western Sahara after Sánchez visited Rabat's historic enemy Algeria in July.

The Western Sahara is a former Spanish colony largely controlled by Morocco but claimed by the Algerian-backed pro-independence Polisario Front.

Political flashpoint

The influx triggered fresh tensions within the European Union over the sensitive topic of immigration and dealt a blow to one of its main achievements, the Schengen free-travel zone.

Italy's right-wing government imposed border checks for one month on travellers from Spain after the crisis, with Madrid reciprocating a week later.

Both governments announced a 15-day extension of the controls on Monday.

Although the vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours, thousands remain in the tiny territory of 18 square kilometres and 84,000 inhabitants, many living rough on the streets.

Their fate has become a major political flashpoint, with the conservative and far-right opposition demanding that all those who entered Ceuta, including minors, be returned to Morocco.

Migrants try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, 30 July, 2026 AP Photo

Ceuta residents have held regular demonstrations over what they say are security and hygiene problems linked to the influx.

Sánchez said that 6,000 spaces at reception centres would soon be available in the territory for migrants, whose status must be verified by the Spanish authorities before any possible return to Morocco.

He also pledged an additional €168 million in aid for Ceuta to respond to the crisis.

At the end of August, Madrid asked the European Commission (EC) for the support from Frontex, Europol and the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) to assist with the screening and processing of migrants who are staying irregularly in Ceuta.

World.title: EU eyes additional sanctions on Ukrainian children deportation
World.content:
The EU's diplomatic service presented on Wednesday additional listings targeting 27 Russian individuals and entities involved in the forced deportation and indoctrination of Ukrainian children.

 

EU ambassadors reviewed the new blacklisting at their first meeting since the summer recess. It is expected to be adopted by the end of the month.

It is not the first time Brussels has targeted those responsible for Russia's illegal mass abduction, deportation and re-education of minors from Ukraine's occupied territories. Several individual listings have already featured in previous sanctions packages.

In May, EU countries blacklisted 16 individuals and seven entities to mark the high-level meeting of the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children. A follow-up conference is due to take place in Toronto, Canada, on 28-29 September.

Following Wednesday's presentation, further technical work is required to finalise the listing, as legal checks must ensure the sanctions are robust enough to withstand challenges in court.

The European External Action Service (EEAS) has also shared with member states a list of 1,600 individuals and entities directly contributing to Russia's war effort, part of a broader shift away from large, sector-focused sanctions packages.

Ukraine has verified the deportation of more than 20,500 children to Russia to date. Yale’s Humanitarian Research Lab estimates the number may be closer to 35,000, while Moscow has openly suggested it could be as high as 700,000.

The US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) think tank said that the true number of deported children is almost impossible to verify.

Euronews reported earlier that Russia-installed occupation authorities in Ukraine’s regions created an online “catalogue” of Ukrainian children, offering them for coerced “adoption” through the education department.

The minors are reportedly sorted and categorised so users can “filter” them by age, gender, and physical characteristics such as eye and hair colour. The children are also described in terms of personality traits, with some labelled as “obedient” or “calm.”

For Ukraine it can take years to return one child from Russia after abduction, from the beginning of the identification until the return takes place.

Almost every return so far has been mediated by a third state, notably Qatar, South Africa and the Vatican.

In March the United Nations said that the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia constitutes a crime against humanity and a war crime.

World.title: The World’s 50 Best Hotels 2026: 16 hotels in Europe feature on extended 50-100 list
World.content:
As the hospitality world counts down the days to see which properties make the cut for The World's 50 Best Hotels 2026 list, an extended ranking has revealed the hotels in 51st to 100th place.

 

Unveiled by 50 Best, the 51-100 list features hotels from 23 different territories and 40 cities, with 16 properties in Europe, including nine in Italy.

Determined by the votes of more than 800 anonymous experts, The World’s 50 Best Hotels ranking for 2026 will be unveiled in Paris on 15 September.

Asia leads the way, followed by Europe

In the 51-100 rundown, Asia tops the list with 20 hotels ranked. Japan alone has seven properties in the ranking, with Janu Tokyo at No.52, while other new entries in the capital include Park Hyatt Tokyo (No.53), The Okura (No.69) and Palace Hotel Tokyo (No.73).

Represented by 16 hotels, Europe’s entries on the extended list span both “newly opened properties and long-established favourites”, 50 Best said.

La Réserve Paris re-enters and tops the extended list at No.51, while France is home to three other properties, including new entries Ritz Paris at No.72 and Carlton Cannes (No.80).

The Maybourne Riviera, in Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, has also re-entered the list at No.93.

Il San Pietro di Positano was No.58 on the 51-100 list The World’s 50 Best Hotels

Of the European countries, Italy has the highest number of hotels included, with nine.

Il San Pietro di Positano (No.58) is Italy’s highest new entry, while Castiglion del Bosco in Montalcino (No.62), Orient Express La Minerva in Rome (No.66), Forestis Dolomites (No.68) in Brixen, and Villa Treville in Positano (No.91) all enter the list for the first time.

Splendido in Portofino comes in at No.60, followed by Borgo Santandrea in Amalfi at No.84 and Borgo Egnazia in Savelletri at No.88. Reschio in Lisciano Niccone was ranked at No.95.

Elsewhere in Europe, the UK has two hotels on the list: new entry Rosewood London (No.56) and Gleneagles (No.100) in Auchterarder, Scotland. In Türkiye, independently-owned Maçakızı in Bodrum was at No.76.

Meanwhile, North America had a total of nine hotels on the 51-100 ranking, while South America and Oceania had two each, and Africa one.

World.title: Europe vows to stay united as hybrid war activity surges
World.content:
European foreign ministers have said they're ready to stand firm against a surge of Russian hybrid war attacks across the continent, rallying behind Germany after its decision to formally hold Russia responsible for a drone incident at Leipzig airport last month.

 

The show of unity came at a summit of EU foreign affairs ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, also attended by ministers from Ukraine, Canada, Switzerland and the United Kingdom.

The Leipzig airport incident on 4 August saw German authorities intercept a drone carrying military-grade explosives. Berlin has been unequivocal in attributing the incursion to the Kremlin.

"The means used – such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems – are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia," German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Tuesday, framing the attack as part of a "long series of destabilisation operations" against Europe.

In remarks condemning Russia's activities, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband referred to his country's experience of Russian attacks in recent years, such as the attempted chemical assassination of former Russian KGB operative Sergei Skripal in Salisbury.

"We stand in full solidarity with Germany and Ukraine," Miliband told journalists. "We know from the past from Russian attacks on our soil these attempts to divide us will not work, but this is a dangerous sign of attempt by Russia to divide us and to think they can send a chilling effect on European countries when it comes to their invasion of Ukraine."

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys, meanwhile said Russia appears to be dialling up the volume of hybrid attacks it is launching.

"We see they are expanding and quadrupled attacks against us in the last year," he said. "Our goal is to show these activities won't intimidate us or stop us supporting Ukraine."

Also on the agenda at the informal so-called Gymnich meeting are proposals that the European Commission could reopen the question of using immobilised Russian sovereign assets to fund Ukraine, an idea being pushed by Sweden, Spain and Poland and the Netherlands.

Finnish Minister for Foreign Affairs Elina Valtonen said that "Europe needs to support Ukraine ahead of the winter".

"This is a good space and time to talk about the frozen assets," she said ahead of the summit. "We need to explore all options on the table."

World.title: Strictly successful: Greece's Naima Gerassopoulou claims world tango champion title
World.content:
Greece's Naima Gerasopoulou has been crowned world tango champion together with her Argentine partner, Lucas Gauto at the annual competition in Buenos Aires.

 

The duo lifted the trophy after stealing the judges hearts with an impressive dancing display that was watched by thousands of people around the world who followed the event online

As the bright lights shone on the dazzling couple as they completed their routine, they both shared their joy at winning the highly coveted crown.

For Gauto, winning the title was a long held dream come true: "It was a dream I had twenty years ago, when I first came to the World Championship. That day I said I wanted to become a world champion and hear my name announced. It was wonderful."

Naima Gerasopoulou of Greece and Lucas Gauto of Argentina dance after winning the salon category at the Tango World Championship in Buenos Aires, 1 Sep, 2026 AP Photo/Rodrigo Abd

For her part, Gerassopoulou recalled her first steps in the world of tango and the feeling that made her devote herself to the dance: "When I started in Greece, honestly, I didn't even know what tango was. I didn't even know it existed. And when I went, what I felt was a sincere embrace from someone I didn't know. And I wondered: how is it possible to be in such a close and genuine embrace with someone I had never met in my life? That was what, I don't know, bewitched me. It made me fall madly in love with tango."

The final featured dancers from several countries including Russia, Turkey, Japan, Indonesia and Kazakhstan, underlining tango's global and growing appeal.

It is an art form which, as the competitors themselves described, serves as a deeply personal means of expression, communication and connection between people beyond cultural and geographical borders.

World.title: Astrotourism: Two resorts in Saudi Arabia are the first to receive DarkSky certification
World.content:
Can’t wait until 2027’s “eclipse of the century” for your next celestial adventure? DarkSky International has given its seal of approval to two resorts in Saudi Arabia which offer guests the perfect vantage point to gaze into the night skies.

 

DarkSky, which champions efforts to tackle light pollution while promoting responsible outdoor lighting that is “beautiful, healthy and functional”, kickstarted its Approved Lodgings & Resorts certification programme in August.

Based on a set criteria, the certification process assessed factors, including whether a facility is located in a region with an exceptional dark sky resource, as well as understood sensitive nighttime resources and means to reduce the impact of light.

Two resorts in Saudi Arabia are among the first to receive the accolade, including Nujuma, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve and the expansive 30,000 square-metre Desert Rock Resort.

Nujuma, encircled by the isles of Saudi’s turquoise Red Sea, takes its name from the Arabic word for “stars” and offers guests a beachfront escape, private villas with wall-to-wall windows with panoramic views of the starlit-filled sky come sundown.

The hotel has its very own resident astronomy expert who leads guests on guided stargazing tours, inviting them to look up and learn about the local significance of the stars.

Meanwhile, recognised for the quality of its night sky, outdoor lighting practices and providing educational outreach, Desert Rock’s 54 villas and 10 suites are embedded within the mountains or suspended from rocky pinnacles in the heart of the Kingdom’s Hijaz Mountains, where, according to the resort, “the landscape continues long after sunset”.

A 20-minute drive away from Red Sea International Airport, the resort’s residences each feature their own private pool alongside sweeping views of the valley.

At sundown, the Astronomy Centre allows guests to observe planets, constellations, meteor showers and other celestial wonders visible from the resort’s vantage point, using powerful telescopes.

The hour-long Arabian Astronomy Observation experience blends science and Saudi culture to explore the dark skies.

Desert Rock also encourages guests to venture out on night hikes, including via its Luna Trail, which offers an ideal route for stargazing in the desert landscape.

The Al’Ayali Albeidh Lunar Nights experience is led by an astronomy expert, where the moon and stars are the focal point of discussions about their cultural significance as well as historic role in navigation and calendaring.

All these efforts are made as part of prioritising protecting the night sky. Desert Rock limits its use of unnecessary artificial light, helping to create optimal stargazing conditions, while maintaining the natural light-dark cycle for local wildlife.

World.title: Weight-loss pill "Wegovy" available in German pharmacies from 1 September
World.content:
As of today, the Wegovy weight-loss pill from Danish manufacturer Novo Nordisk will be available in German pharmacies from 1 September. Following EU approval in July, Germany is the first country in which Wegovy is being sold. Novo Nordisk described the authorisation as a "milestone".

 

The prescription-only medicine is intended as an alternative to the weight-loss injection already on the market and works with the same active ingredient: semaglutide. It mimics a gut hormone that is responsible for the feeling of fullness. As a spokesperson for the manufacturer explained, the retail pharmacy price of the weight-loss pill is expected to be between 170 and 280 euros. While the injectable version of Wegovy has already been approved for children aged 12 and over, the tablet form is only approved for adults.

When taking semaglutide tablets, adults with overweight reduced their body weight by an average of around 13.6 percent, according to the OASIS-4 study (source in German), which essentially formed the basis for EU approval. It was carried out by an international team of researchers.

In the trial, 205 participants took the drug. A further 102 participants received a placebo. With the injection, the average weight loss was higher, at 19 percent. However, the treatment period in that study was 72 weeks, two months longer than for the tablet (64 weeks).

As with the injection, the oral version also comes with side effects: many patients who use the medicine experience gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea and diarrhoea. It can also lead to inflammation of the pancreas.

Compared with the injection, the tablet has to be taken every day. For the injection, administering it once a week is sufficient. For both products, however, what matters alongside regular use is diet and exercise, said Julia Szendrödi, president of the German Diabetes Association.

100 billion dollar market

"Whether injection or tablet: medicines against obesity are not miracle cures for optimising weight, but components of a therapy for a chronic disease," said Szendrödi. The use of products such as Wegovy is always part of a broader treatment concept. These drugs do not replace prevention, Szendrödi added. There is a need for better nutrition labelling, quality standards for school meals and restrictions on advertising unhealthy foods to children.

Globally, the market for weight-loss medicines is fiercely contested. According to analysts, by 2030 it could be bringing in 100 billion dollars a year for pharmaceutical companies, business daily Handelsblatt reports. Various products are now available. In the United Kingdom, for instance, the pill "Foundayo" from US manufacturer Eli Lilly will be on sale from the end of August.

These weight-loss medicines are intended for people with obesity, with a body mass index (BMI) above 30. In cases of conditions such as type 2 diabetes or sleep apnoea that are linked to excess weight, they can also be used below a BMI of 30.

World.title: What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey
World.content:
Nearly a week after the Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to dissolve, the consequences are beginning to take shape for Syria's Kurds and neighbouring Turkey. As the former US-backed force is absorbed into the Syrian state, questions remain over what the country's Kurds have secured in return – from language and political rights to protections for women – and what the end of more than a decade of Kurdish-led autonomy means for Turkey's own conflict with Kurdish militants.

Advertising

SDF leader Mazloum Abdi announced the force's dissolution last Tuesday, saying its fighters would be integrated into the Syrian army.

At its height, the predominantly Kurdish force numbered around 100,000 fighters and controlled nearly a fifth of Syrian territory in the northeast, including major oil fields and fertile land. Under SDF rule, Kurds gained cultural and political rights denied to them under previous governments in Damascus.

“It means the end of Kurdish autonomy. After more than one decade of freedom, now they are under the control of Damascus,” said Syria expert Fabrice Balanche of Lyon University, who frequently visited the region.

Kurdish rights

“There are no guarantees for the Kurdish language because it's just a presidential decree: ‘let the Kurds use their language and teach Kurdish in schools,’ but there is nothing in the constitution,” Balanche said.

The decree, issued by President Ahmed al-Sharaa in January, recognised Kurdish as a national language and allowed it to be taught in schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations.

It also restored citizenship to Kurds who had been left stateless under measures stemming from a controversial 1962 census and made Nowruz, the Kurdish New Year festival, an official national holiday.

The Education Ministry followed up on 27 August with rules providing for three Kurdish-language classes a week in public and private schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations, with marks counting towards pupils' final grades.

‘Words and promises not enough’ as Syria’s Kurds face uncertain future

Abdi was also appointed as an adviser to al-Sharaa on Friday, days after announcing the SDF's dissolution. It remains unclear whether the role will be more than ceremonial.

But questions remain over what the end of the Kurdish-led administration will mean for women. The SDF and affiliated institutions used a system in which governing bodies were jointly headed by a man and a woman.

“During these 10 years of autonomy, men and women were equal,” Balanche said. “In the region’s administration. It was always a co-presidency. In Raqqah, for example, the mayor was Leyla Mustafa, a woman, and the co-president was a man. Now that is no longer the case.”

Balanche also said the change could threaten restrictions on polygamy introduced under the Kurdish-led administration. Another unresolved question is what will happen to female SDF fighters as the force is absorbed into Syria's armed forces, which currently have no female troops.

Shifting alliances

For years, the SDF was Washington's main partner on the ground in Syria in the fight against the Islamic State group. But its position weakened as the United States built closer relations with Syria's new rulers.

A Syrian government offensive in January seized large areas held by the SDF and pushed the Kurdish-led force back into negotiations over integration with Damascus.

Washington, meanwhile, has increasingly embraced al-Sharaa's government, dismantling broad sanctions against Syria in 2025 and last week removing the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

Turkey has emerged as one of al-Sharaa's main foreign allies and has long pressed for the SDF to disarm and integrate into the Syrian state.

Ankara considers the SDF a terrorist organisation linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which launched an insurgency against the Turkish state in 1984. The SDF has rejected Turkey's claim that it is an extension of the PKK.

A year after Assad's fall, Syrian hopes for transitional justice are fading

The United States and European Union designate the PKK as a terrorist organisation, but not the SDF.

Turkey has carried out several cross-border military operations against the SDF in northern Syria since 2016 and still has thousands of troops stationed in the country. Ankara says those forces will remain until the security threats it faces have been eliminated.

The SDF's dissolution therefore achieves a longstanding Turkish objective in Syria. Turkey's ruling AK Party welcomed the move last week as an important step towards strengthening Syria's unity.

“Stability in Syria means Turkey perhaps being able to divert some of the resources it's been spending on counterterrorism into other areas of its defense that are absolutely necessary at a time like this, a time of regional turmoil,” said Turkey expert Asli Aydintasbas of the Washington-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey's Kurdish conflict

The SDF's dissolution could also remove an obstacle to the fragile peace process between Ankara and the PKK.

The process is intended to end the PKK's decades-long armed campaign against the Turkish state through the group's disarmament and dissolution.

Jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to disarm and disband in February 2025, and the PKK announced three months later that it would do so. A group of militants symbolically burned their weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq in July 2025.

Turkey's parliament passed a law in August establishing a legal framework for the PKK's disbandment. Kurdish politicians have said broader democratic and legal reforms will also be needed for lasting peace.

Macron to become first Western European leader to visit post-Assad Syria

For Ankara, however, the process does not stop at Turkey's borders. It has repeatedly insisted that the SDF must also dissolve, because it regards the Syrian force as part of the same militant movement as the PKK.

The SDF has disputed that characterisation, with Abdi saying in 2025 that the PKK's decision to disarm did not apply to his forces in Syria.

The dismantling of groups Ankara regards as PKK affiliates across the region is essential to the process, said Middle East expert Serhan Afacan of Istanbul's Marmara University.

“The PKK should not exist anywhere in the region. This is what Ankara has been saying for more than a year,” Afacan said.

“If there is going to be any kind of peace process or reconciliation, the PKK is not supposed to exist anywhere in this region, in Turkey, in Iran, in Iraq, Syria.”

World.title: EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack
World.content:
The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the attempted attack had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." She said the EU was summoning a Russian envoy, with France announcing a similar step.

The European Unions's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that she summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels over the alleged attempted hybrid attack involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.

Germany's foreign and interior ministers said in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the government in Berlin had concluded that Russia was responsible for the failed attack, reinforcing suspicions that arose as soon as the news broke in August.

Kallas says incident has 'all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism'

"We are discussing the Leipzig attacks, and also it is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," Kallas said ahead of an informal gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.

"The question is, what do we do about this? We have already summoned the Russian ambassador," she said.

The former Estonian prime minister also said that the EU was continuing its work on its next package of some 1,600 sanctions listings related to Russia's war in Ukraine and said "maybe there is more to be added."

France takes similar step, summoning charge d'affaires

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also told reporters in Dublin that Paris was summoning a Russian ambassador in response.

"I have summoned the Russian charge d'affaires in Paris to protest, Barrot said, adding that sanctions should be taken at a European level, notably against Russia's so-called shadow fleet of ships.

Non-EU foreign ministers from Ukraine, the UK, Canada, Norway, Iceland and Switzerland also traveled to Ireland to attend Wednesday's informal talks.

Germany's Wadephul says 'pressure on Russia is being stepped up'

German Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul told reporters that the EU would continue to work on additional sanctions "in the coming weeks."

"Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Urkaine also remains at a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at this time," he said.

The Christian Democrat politician said that Russia had chosen to escalate, and "must now live with these consequences."

He also defended Tuesday's announcement in Berlin, calling the government's response a "necessary and proportionate" one based on a "well-founded opinion and verdict."

What did Germany say about its investigations?

Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the federal government in Berlin held Russia responsible for the failed attack.

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," Dobrindt said on Tuesday, without going into specifics.

Wadephul said that the "means used — drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine."

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, have rejected the allegations and accused Germany of fabricating its version of events.

Leipzig/Halle Airport is a key freight hub. Ukrainian airline and aircraft manufacturer Antonov uses the airport as a base of operations, frequently transiting material to Ukraine via the the eastern German city.

World.title: What really helps Europe deal with drought
World.content:
Fix leaks, or ban pools? As European countries prepare for hotter, drier years to come, here's what the data says about how to really save water

Europe is in drought. As the burning of fossil fuels pushes up temperatures that are making summers hotter and drier , the continent's soils, lakes and rivers are struggling to recover. Southern and Western European countries are particularly affected. But they're not the only ones.

"We've seen drought risks expanding northward during the last decade", says Gisela Elsner, Climate and Sustainability Policy Officer at the German Konrad Adenauer Foundation, who has followed EU water management efforts for years.

"Central and Western Europe, but also southeastern European countries, are increasingly vulnerable due to climate change."

For the month of August this year, satellite data shows areas as far north as Denmark and Sweden experiencing extremely dry conditions more often seen in regions such as the Sub-Saharan Sahel.

The impact is palpable. Some of the continent's longest rivers like the Rhine or the Danube have reached historic lows, disrupting inland shipping routes. Farmers from Germany to Ukraine are reporting below-average harvests, and areas from the United Kingdom to Switzerland to Germany have announced restrictions on household water use.

German municipalities impose water restrictions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To make matters worse, this year's El Niño event — a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures — is set to be one of the strongest on record. Experts predict that 2027 will be even hotter and drier as a result.

Europe will have to adapt to this reality, says Gisela Elsner. "It is not yet a matter of not having water in our taps anymore. But we need to prioritize and use our water resources efficiently."

So, how can countries across the continent set about doing this? DW analyzed water usage in European nations and reviewed the evidence to find out which measures have the most impact.

Which European countries use the most water?

Private households in Europe account for a relatively small share of water usage. Depending on the country, they consume a daily per capita average of between 50 and 300 liters, which equates to less than 20% of all use.

Two thirds of water withdrawn continent-wide is for agriculture — mostly for irrigation — as well as electricity cooling for nuclear and fossil fuel power plants.

In already drought-prone countries like Greece, Turkey and Spain, agriculture accounts for most of the near 2000 liters of water withdrawn per person each day.

Electricity cooling is the biggest factor in Eastern European countries like Bulgaria or Hungary, but also in the Netherlands or Estonia, which use between 1000 and 2000 liters per capita daily in total.

Where Europe can save the most water

"There is no single solution that is sufficient to solve this challenge," says Gisela Elsner. "It has to be a combined bundle of measures."

And they exist. A recent report published by the European Environmental Agency (EEA) found that EU countries could save between 10 and 40% of water annually by implementing targeted strategies.

For states in Western and Eastern Europe, shifting to clean energy would make a big difference. While nuclear, and planet-heating oil, gas and coal need huge amounts of water for cooling, wind and solar do not.

Electricity cooling: renewables to the rescue

So besides becoming the cheapest forms of energy, the renewables that are increasingly replacing fossil fuels are also helping countries to save water. Over the past two decades, Europe has reduced its water usage by around a quarter — mostly because of more efficient electrical cooling.

Even with nuclear plants still requiring water in countries like France, Spain or Sweden, the potential savings are massive. The EEA estimates that EU countries could make significant further savings of between 45 and 95% — equal to hundreds of liters per person each day — by expanding renewables and improving cooling systems.

Better irrigation can help in agriculture

In Southern Europe, agriculture is the big-ticket item. The EEA report recommends, for instance, replacing open water transport channels with closed pipes to avoid evaporation during heatwaves, switching from surface irrigation to sprinklers or drip irrigation, and opting for less water-intensive crops whereever possible.

Public water supply: leaky pipes lose lots of water

In EU countries, around one in four liters of drinkable water from the public supply is lost to leaky pipes and evaporation before it ever reaches its destination — according to estimates by the European association of water providers EurEau.

In Romania and Italy, the share is more than 40%. According to the EEA report, avoiding these losses would account for most of the potential savings in the EU's public water supply.

Once drinking water reaches households and businesses, individual behavior has an impact as well. The EEA report lists extensive recommendations for savings in daily life, from low-flow toilets and efficient washing machines and dishwashers, to harvesting rainwater. Yet even if every citizen in Europe did all they could, it would only reduce the daily per person household water use by between 10 and 40%.

Citizens could also contribute through more responsible consumer decisions, such as considering the water footprint of the products they buy or support, says Alexander Psomas, water resources expert at the Greek consultancy Brilliant Solutions, who co-authored the EEA report.

"Citizens can also push our governments to be more accountable on their energy policy and the impact it has on water."

What Europe can learn

Drought and heat waves are not just a European problem. Many parts in the world are even more severely affected by the climate crisis. And data from the United Nations shows regions in Northern Africa, the Middle East and Asia have been dealing with much higher levels of water stress for a long time.

This also means that Europe can collaborate with, and learn from, the rest of the world on how to adapt to water scarcity. "The UN World Food Program and the FAO are all working on similar questions in the Global South," said Giriraj Armanath, Research Group Leader at the International Water Management Institute.

What one of the world's driest cities teaches us about water To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gisela Elsner recounts, for instance, chip manufacturers in the German state of Saxony recently looking to expertise from Singapore on how to reuse wastewater to cool their factories.

"We can definitely learn from those countries which already have all the knowledge and the technologies that can be used in our context as well," she said.

Public and politics are paying more attention to water use

Both Gisela Elsner and Alexander Psomas say they have noticed both politics and the public becoming more aware in recent years.

"The water scarcity and droughts topic did not have a relevant EU working group until 2022", Psomas told DW. "Today, it's one of the working groups with the highest participation. There is a growing interest and concern on this issue."

What he would like to see more of, he says, is public debates about water strategies, especially during election periods.

"If a country runs low on water, it affects everyone," he says. "I would like to see politicians discuss what kind of solutions they're offering for making their countries more water resilient in 10, 20 years from now."

Edited by Tamsin Walker and Gianna Grün

World.title: Charlie Kirk murder suspect to face potential death penalty
World.content:
Tyler R., accused of fatally shooting Charlie Kirk, will stand trial on aggravated murder charges after a Utah judge ruled prosecutors had enough evidence to seek the death penalty.

The murder case against Tyler R., the man accused of fatally shooting conservative activist Charlie Kirk last September, is headed to trial, and he could face the death penalty if convicted, under a new ruling.

Utah District Judge Tony Graf ruled late on Tuesday that prosecutors had presented sufficient evidence to proceed, ordering that the defendant be set for trial.

The 23-year-old suspect pleaded not guilty to all seven charges, including aggravated murder, following the ruling. A hearing to schedule the trial date is set for October 23.

What did the prosecutors say?

Prosecutors say Tyler R. fired a single shot from a rooftop more than 400 feet (~122 meters) away, striking 31-year-old Kirk in the neck as he addressed a crowd of more than 3,000 people at Utah Valley University.

A strong supporter of President Donald Trump, Kirk has been credited with motivating young voters to turn out for him in the 2024 US presidential election.

Charlie Kirk was often referred to as the 'youth whisperer' of Trump's MAGA movement Image: DW

Utah County prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court the defendant "lay down in a prone position, and he would have seen this mass of people, of 3,000-plus people there for the event, took aim, put his crosshairs on Charlie Kirk and fired."

McBride argued the shooting "created a great risk of death that anyone would know about."

Prosecutors also pointed to the rifle's additional unfired rounds as evidence that the suspect "came prepared to shoot again," and presented DNA evidence they say ties him to the weapon and to a tool allegedly used to engrave one of the cartridges with the words "Hey Fascist! CATCH!"

What did the defense say?

The defendant's attorneys have argued the case does not meet Utah's legal threshold for aggravated murder, which requires showing that others faced a high probability, not just a possibility, of harm.

Defense attorney Staci Visser told the court, "There is one act. There is one shot. There is one bullet. There is one victim," adding that there was "zero evidence that there was any action taken towards other people."

The defense also challenged the reliability of the prosecution's DNA testing.

Court hears argument for political motive

Prosecutors say the defendant targeted Kirk over his political views, citing a text message in which he allegedly wrote to his roommate, "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out."

A handwritten note he reportedly wrote the roommate, who he was romantically involved with, read: "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it."

However, defense attorney Richard Novak countered that Kirk had spoken "hatefully" about LGBTQ people and that the wording of the message didn't necessarily indicate a political motive.

Charlie Kirk shooting deepens divide in US politics To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kirk family welcomes 'important step' for justice

Kirk's parents and widow, Erika Kirk, who now leads his organization Turning Point USA, attended the hearing. In a statement, the Kirk family said the ruling "marks an important step in our family's pursuit of justice for him."

"Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father," read the statement posted by Erika Kirk on social media.

Legal analyst Seth Zuckerman told Reuters he expects the case to go to trial rather than end in a plea deal, saying prosecutors "may not be willing to take the death penalty off the table, and that would probably require a trial."

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: Women's football: Anyomi, London City and the German exodus
World.content:
Nicole Anyomi has joined Alexia Putellas and other star names in signing for the ambitious English club London City Lionesses. The Germany winger told DW England is a better place to develop her game than back home.

The London City Lionesses have existed for less than a decade, have played in England's top flight for just one season and can't play in the Champions League. Yet, having broken the women's transfer record last year, the Lionesses have signed some of the game's biggest stars for the coming season as their ambition becomes ever more apparent.

As well as two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas and her Spanish teammate Mapi Leon, England's Euro 2022 winning goalkeeper Mary Earps and French star Kadidiatou Diani, Germany winger Nicole Anyomi is among the new arrivals.

Anyomi left Eintracht Frankfurt, where she'd scored 50 goals in 101 Bundesliga games over five years, for what she considers a greater challenge in England.

The 'perfect step'

"The next step was to go to the league to compete every single weekend and this is what I see here in this league," she told DW.

"I have some friends who already played in the WSL (Women's Super League) and they told me about the league so I think this will be the perfect step for me."

Anyomi is one of several players to leave Germany's Women's Bundesliga for England this summer. Among them are Anyomi's international teammates Vivien Endemann (Wolfsburg to Liverpool), Selina Cerci (Hoffenheim to Arsenal), Carlotta Wamser (Bayer Leverkusen to Manchester City) and England's Georgia Stanway (Bayern Munich to Arsenal).

Anyomi pointed to the increasing gap in infrastructure, finances and coaching as the primary reasons for the exodus.

"In Germany you have two, three teams who are competing at the top but here in England there are five, six, seven, eight teams.

"Also, the facilities and the staff members. We have 30-plus staff members here whereas in Frankfurt we had like seven or eight. You can learn from each person and there is something new to learn every day. I think that's how you develop as a player faster."

Germany falling further behind?

With England's national team having won the last two Euros, a competition once dominated by Germany, and no German side having won the Champions League since 2015, there is a concern that Germany rested on its laurels for too long.

In an effort to address this issue, last December, the Frauen-Bundesliga FBL e.V. (Women's Bundesliga Association) was formed. Similar to the DFL, which operates the men's Bundesliga, the FBL is designed to improve the league's marketing and increase revenue. It is to take over operation of the league next July 1.

"They have to bring something, not new, but something different into the league so maybe the players would stay," Anyomi said.

"I think it's an investment thing, but I think now they are building something new, to do different things. I'm going to see this season of course and watch the Bundesliga. I hope they are going to invest more, do more for the league so players also from abroad can come to Germany."

Bayern Munich have won the last three Bundesliga titles and no side but them or Wolfsburg has won since 2012 Image: O. Behrendt/Contrast/IMAGO

Her new club are the foremost example of the changing face of women's football. London City did not exist until 2019 when, effectively, they took over the license of another team, Milwall. Their progress has recently been accelerated by Michelle Kang.

The Korean-American businesswoman is a serial investor in women's football and added London City to an ownership portfolio that includes serial Champions League winners OL Lyonnes and US side Washington Spirit in December 2023. Kang's deep pockets and ambition mean London City are on track to compete at the top end of the WSL within the next few years.

Kang ownership presents possibility and prohibition

But her ownership of OL Lyonnes prohibits London City from playing in the Champions League. UEFA, who organize the tournament, have enshrined laws that mean clubs that are in multi-ownership structures cannot both be in the same competition in the same season. Last season, in the men's game, this led to English side Crystal Palace being demoted from the Europa League to the Europa Conference league.

Nicole Anyomi believes moving to England was a smart move despite a lack of Champions League football – for now Image: London City Lionesses

"Why would we want to preserve the sporting integrity of men's football, but not of women's football? It's out of the question," said UEFA's head of women's football and former Germany international, Nadine Kessler earlier this year.

"In any sport you want to preserve sporting integrity, that's the most important thing."

Anyomi, who must recover from a hamstring injury before she can make her debut, said she trusts the club, who have so far "done everything they promised" to find a solution.

But the lack of continental football means fewer chances to make her mark alongside the other new arrivals. Given that the World Cup in Brazil is at the end of the coming season, the move could be seen by some as a risk.

"I did think about that because I know I have to play at the club level, otherwise I won't be selected," she said. "I wanted to go abroad two years ago and I didn't in the end, so I decided to go this summer. I had the feeling this is the right step."

Whether it's to London City, or to the WSL more broadly, she's not the only Bundesliga player to feel that way.

World.title: Cargo ship with 10 crew sinks off Turkey coast — authorities
World.content:
Coast guard vessels and a helicopter are searching for 10 missing crew members off the coast of Istanbul. Authorities say they lost contact after the bulk carrier crashed into a chemical tanker off the coast of Istanbul.

Turkish authorities are searching for 10 people aboard a cargo ship that sank after a collision with another vessel in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul early Wednesday.

"We believe, and have more or less confirmed, that the Tugberk Imamoglu has sunk," Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu told reporters in Istanbul.

Uraloglu said all 10 crew members aboard the vessel were Turkish nationals and that attempts to reach them by mobile phone had been unsuccessful.

"We can say that the sinking occurred rapidly in 11 minutes. No one has been found alive," he added.

The bulk carrier Tugberk Imamoglu and the chemical tanker Alsu collided at around 3 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) off the city's western Silivri district, the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement.

Two helicopters and 12 search and rescue vessels are scouring the area.

The Transport Ministry's maritime directorate said that life-saving equipment, including a lifeboat belonging to the Tugberk Imamoglu, had been found floating on the surface.

"Unfortunately, the crew members were not inside," it added.

The 90-meter (295-foot) cargo ship Tugberk Imamoglu, built in 1990, was traveling from Turkey’s Iskenderun to Eregli in the Black Sea Image: DHA

What else do we know about the missing ship?

The 90-meter (295-foot) Turkish-flagged bulk carrier was en route to the Black Sea ​port ‌of Eregli from Iskenderun when the collision happened.

According to the maritime directorate, it was carrying 4,200 tons of rolled steel.

Authorities believe it sank in waters around 900 meters deep.

The 91-meter Turkish-flagged Alsu, was sailing from Kocaeli, east of Istanbul, to the Aegean port of Aliaga. It was empty at the time of the collision and did not appear to have suffered any damage, the governor's office said.

The Sea of Marmara forms part of one of the world's busiest shipping corridors, linking the Mediterranean to the Black Sea via the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits.

World.title: Germany news: Terror probe opened in power station attack
World.content:
09/02/2026 September 2, 2026 Police open terrorism investigation after Brandenburg grid sabotage

The area around the substation has been sealed off while police investigate Image: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

Police in the eastern German state of Brandenburg on Wednesday said they were investigating the possible formation of a terrorist organization in connection with an attack on a power plant and substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg.

According to officials, on Tuesday morning, a projectile managed to carry a cable into the extra-high-voltage power line at a substation near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant, creating a conductive connection to the ground that caused a brief outage.

On Wednesday, Brandenburg's state Interior Minister Jan Redmann said "we were damn lucky" that only one of more than a dozen "rocket-like objects equipped with a propellant charge" reached its target.

He added the suspects had positioned the projectiles directly beneath the power lines near the Turnow-Preilack substation on the border with the state of Saxony.

Police continued investigating around the Turnow-Preilack power station on Wednesday Image: Frank Hammerschmidt/dpa/picture alliance

The search for suspects continues, and an investigation is looking into all possibilities.

Brandenburg police said their investigation also includes disruption of public services, the causing of an explosion and the destruction of important equipment.

"At this point, we must assume that the perpetrators had been on the scene for several days beforehand and had installed the necessary equipment," Redmann said.

The construction and installation of the devices required a considerable amount of "technical expertise," he added.

World.title: Tunisia's human rights defenders decry civil society crackdown
World.content:
Five years into the authoritarian rule of Tunisian President Kais Saied, Human Rights Watch and other activists warn that Tunisia's once vibrant civil society is in danger of being completely stifled.

"Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities."

Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues.

"What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention, the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said.

Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report , published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely.

"It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights.

"The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW.

He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said.

Young Tunisians are increasingly unhappy with the government, while older Tunisians are more satisfied that a decade ago, according to one survey Image: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS

Saied was elected president democratically in 2019. But in July 2021, he dissolved parliament and launched a power grab. Since then, he has dismantled most democratic bodies, repressed political dissent and arrested opposition figures.

For Anthony Dworkin, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations who focuses on human rights and democracy, Saied's goals remain unchanged. "They have been the same for the last five years, namely to consolidate power and remove potential checks on and critics of his rule," he told DW.

Saied has rejected accusations that he is an authoritarian ruler and argued that his measures are necessary to tackle corruption and uphold democracy. He has accused critics of receiving foreign funding to stir unrest and undermine Tunisia's national interests. DW reached out to the Tunisian presidency for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.

Growing discontent prompts calls for Saied's resignation

Despite the widespread crackdown on dissent, some people still dare criticize the government. On July 25, the fifth anniversary of the president's power grab, thousands took to the streets of the capital, Tunis, to protest worsening living conditions, democratic backsliding and the government's handling of basic services.

The demonstrations came amid widespread water and electricity outages, which Saied has described as "premeditated acts aimed at inflaming the situation by all means and spreading lies and rumors to sow confusion."

In late August, protesters once again called on the president to step down by chanting "The people want the fall of the regime," a popular slogan from the 2010-2011 Arab Spring uprising.

The demonstration was initiated by Nafas, a new citizen-led umbrella initiative that was launched in May. Mohamed Hawel, a university teacher and member of the Nafas collective, told the news agency AP that Nafas was created to unite people around basic necessities, including water, electricity and food.

Growing gap between older, younger Tunisians

Despite some unity at these protests, according to an Arab Barometer survey there is an emerging generational divide in Tunisia. A report published in July on the basis of a survey conducted in the fall of 2025 found that older and less educated people had vastly different views on the country's economic and political conditions from younger, better educated people.

The survey showed that the older generation saw the current political and economic situation in the most positive light since the Arab Spring and had more trust in the government than over the past decade.

In comparison, younger Tunisians were more pessimistic about the country's economic and political development. They also remained more skeptical of state institutions while maintaining a high trust in civil society organizations: 49% of people between the ages of 18-39 expressed trust in these, compared with only 32% of those aged 40 and older.

"What really stands out in Tunisia is that the recent decline in trust in civil society is almost entirely a story about older Tunisians. Two years prior, there was almost no generational gap between citizens," Michael Robbins, the director of Arab Barometer, told DW. "Since then, trust in civil society among Tunisians 40 and older has fallen quite sharply, while it has not changed meaningfully among those who are aged 18-39."

Tunisia has a population of approximately 12 million people. People aged 18–39 account for roughly 30% of the population, while those aged 40 and older account for approximately 43%.



"I think the notion of a divided society is overstated," said Dworkin. "Moreover, the recent demonstrations are not large enough to pose a serious threat to Kais Saied," he added, while admitting that Saied had lost considerable public support over his failure to improve the country's economy. "But there are no attractive political alternatives and people are also tired of political upheaval."

In his view, many Tunisians are just trying to get by with daily life, while many others are looking to emigrate.

DW's Tarek Guizani in Tunis contributed to this report.

World.title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to collusion
World.content:
The prominent activist pleaded guilty to colluding with foreign entities. He faces a lengthy prison sentence.

Pro-democracy Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong on Wednesday pleaded guilty to a charge of colluding with foreign entities.

Wong, who is already serving a nearly five-year prison sentence for subversion, was due to be released next year and could face up to life in prison.

What was Wong accused of?

Wong was accused of conspiring with fellow activist Nathan Law and others to ask foreign countries, or institutions, organizations, or individuals to impose sanctions or engage in other hostile actions against Hong Kong or China between July and November, 2020.

It's the second prosecution of Joshua Wong under the national security law introduced in Hong Kong in 2020 Image: Chan Long Hei/AP Photo/picture alliance

Wong sat in the courtroom dock as the charges were read out, before confirming his guilty plea, AFP journalists reported from inside the court.

He smiled and nodded after someone in the public gallery shouted "hang in there!"

Among those attending proceedings were several Western diplomats.

Who is Joshua Wong?

Wong first became widely known in Hong Kong as a teenager in 2012 when he led protests against national education being introduced in the city's schools.

In 2014, he rose to fame as one of the student leaders in the city's Occupy Movement, during which demonstrators occupied streets for 79 days while calling for direct elections for Hong Kong's leader.

However, Wong's efforts to garner overseas support for protests angered Beijing, which labelled him an advocate of Hong Kong independence who had "begged for interference" from foreign forces.

The political party he co-founded, Demosisto, was disbanded after the security law was enacted on June 30, 2020.

Joshua Wong speaks to DW To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 29-year-old was among dozens of activists arrested in 2021 for taking part in an unofficial poll to select candidates for a 2020 legislative council election.

His protest efforts have effectively been outlawed by Beijing's sweeping national security law.

Critics say Wong’s case illustrates the lengths to which authorities are willing to go to silence prominent dissidents.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Marlaska exige al director de la Policía que aclare si el cuerpo tiene información de que Marruecos estuvo tras el asalto masivo a Ceuta
World.content:
El titular de Interior asegura en una carta a Pardo Piqueras que desconoce la información entregada a la Audiencia Nacional sobre la implicación de gendarmes marroquíes en los hechos del 30 de julio

El ministro de Interior de España, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, ha exigido en una carta en la madrugada de este miércoles al director general de la Policía, Francisco Pardo Piqueras, que, “de ser cierto”, ponga en su conocimiento desde cuándo disponía el cuerpo policial de información que apunta a que agentes marroquíes dirigieron la entrada masiva de personas a Ceuta con un objetivo distinto al migratorio. El titular de Interior da este paso después de que la unidad de inmigración de la Comisaría de Extranjería haya remitido un informe a la Audiencia Nacional comunicando que la entrada de unas 70.000 personas el pasado 30 y 31 de julio pudo estar planificada para colapsar el acceso fronterizo.

El contenido de dicho informe que se ha entregado ante la magistrada María Tardón, adelantado por El Español, expone que gendarmes marroquíes a las órdenes de agentes de paisano guiaron a los migrantes con el fin de colapsar el sistema fronterizo. Según confirman también fuentes policiales a este periódico, dicho documento analiza con detalle todas las imágenes y vídeos que se han visto sobre el terreno. Una información que el ministro Grande-Marlaska desconocía, de acuerdo con el oficio dirigido al director de la Policía.

En esta carta, a la que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS, Grande-Marlaska insiste en que necesita “saber desde cuándo disponía la Policía Nacional de esa información, absolutamente esencial” para que, más allá de las actuaciones judiciales, él, como ministro del Interior, dice, “pueda ejercer mi responsabilidad y, en definitiva, el Gobierno pueda adoptar las decisiones oportunas en relación con la crisis migratoria de Ceuta”. El titular de la cartera recuerda que es a él a quien corresponde adoptar decisiones en materia de “defensa del Estado” y evidencia así que ignoraba lo redactado por el Centro Nacional de Inmigración y Fronteras (CENIF), remitido este lunes a la Audiencia Nacional.

El oficio añade que se trata de una información que, “habiéndose declarado la situación de interés para la seguridad del nacional prevista en la Ley 36/2015, de Seguridad Nacional, debe ponerse inmediatamente a disposición de los miembros del Consejo de Seguridad Nacional, de la autoridad funcional designada por real decreto del Presidente del Gobierno y de los demás órganos con competencias en este ámbito”. Todo ello, dice Marlaska, “al margen de las actuaciones judiciales que puedan realizarse, que, de momento, se encuentran en un estadio incipiente”, y que no puede ser obstáculo para que las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad del Estado le detallen a él estas cuestiones. “Te agradeceré que me informes a la mayor brevedad sobre la veracidad de lo publicado”, remata.

La cuestión de si Marruecos estuvo o no tras lo ocurrido a finales de julio es nuclear en esta crisis, puesto que el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha defendido públicamente que no existe ningún indicio que haga sospechar que Rabat pudo organizar a los migrantes. Sánchez, en una entrevista en la Cadena SER este mismo lunes, señaló que el país vecino ofreció una “cooperación instantánea, inmediata” y aseguró que se estaba colaborando de forma estrecha para las devoluciones. El líder del PSOE insistió en que tras lo sucedido podían estar mafias, pero siguió la línea marcada antes por Marlaska, que aseguraba que nunca existió información suficiente de que un número tan elevado de personas fuera a cruzar la frontera.

Lo cierto es que María Tardón tiene en su mesa este documento policial que trasladó este martes a la Fiscalía para que se pronuncie. La magistrada decidió el pasado 3 de agosto dar un primer paso para iniciar una investigación después de que el partido Iustitia Europa denunciara la entrada masiva de personas a la ciudad autónoma. Antes de abrir una causa, la instructora pidió distintos informes policiales tanto a la Policía como a la Guardia Civil para aclarar si lo ocurrido se trató de “una acción concertada o dirigida” por algún “grupo criminal” o cualquier otro actor y si, en su caso, el Gobierno manejaba cualquier tipo de información previa.

Una vez la Unidad de Extranjería contestó, la jueza ha remitido la información a la Fiscalía para que esta aclare si el asunto es competencia de la Audiencia Nacional, según informan fuentes judiciales. Está previsto que, tras la contestación del ministerio público, la magistrada dicte un auto que decida si efectivamente hay material suficiente para iniciar una investigación y si esta debe quedarse en ese órgano judicial porque afecta a la seguridad del Estado o trasladarse a un juzgado ordinario de Ceuta.

En la denuncia de Iustitia Europa se planteaba que la “movilización” de personas migrantes de Marruecos a Ceuta no podía “ser calificada como un fenómeno migratorio ordinario o espontáneo” por la “dimensión temporal y la concentración de miles de individuos lanzándose simultáneamente al mar desde las costas marroquíes”. “Nos encontramos ante una instrumentalización de flujos migratorios que, por su volumen y forma de ejecución, supone un desbordamiento de las capacidades de las fuerzas y cuerpos de seguridad del Estado y de los servicios de acogida, comprometiendo la integridad territorial y la seguridad pública en una frontera exterior de la Unión Europea”, exponía.

World.title: Última hora de la entrada de inmigrantes a Ceuta, en directo | El director de la Policía se reúne con el jefe de los agentes que elaboraron el informe sobre Marruecos
World.content:
Bolaños pide “cautela” ante el informe policial que señala a Marruecos: “Es el momento de analizarlo en profundidad”

El ministro Félix Bolaños ha respondido tras ser preguntado por si da credibilidad al informe policial conocido esta mañana según el cual la policía marroquí habría instigado o estado detrás de la organización de la entrada masiva en Ceuta, que “en estos momentos” se está trabajando en analizar los detalles de ese informe, del que se tuvo noticia a través de una información de El Español. “Por tanto, es el momento de la cautela, de analizar en profundidad ese informe, esa información, y de conocer todos los detalles que se mencionan en esa pieza periodística y que se refieren a un informe”, ha señalado, insistiendo en que hasta no conocerlo y estudiarlo “en detalle y en profundidad” pide “máxima cautela”. Bolaños ha asegurado que el Gobierno es “el primer interesado” en conocer con exactitud qué ocurrió los días 30 y 31 de julio en Ceuta y en la frontera terrestre, y en que las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad del Estado avancen en la investigación.

Preguntado directamente por si el Gobierno ha ocultado información sobre la implicación de Marruecos, Bolaños lo ha negado “en absoluto”: “El Gobierno de España tiene que trabajar con información fiable, objetiva, acreditada”, ha dicho, remitiendo de nuevo a que ayer por la noche tuvieron noticia de la información periodística y ahora están analizándola. Sobre si el Ejecutivo depurará responsabilidades dentro de la Policía o pedirá explicaciones a Marruecos, incluso convocando de urgencia a su embajadora, como reclama Sumar, Bolaños ha vuelto a remitirse a la cautela, señalando que corresponde esperar la respuesta a la carta que el ministro del Interior envió anoche al director general de la Policía.

Y sobre las concentraciones convocadas para esta tarde, ha reiterado que el Gobierno “está absolutamente volcado en que Ceuta recupere la normalidad cuanto antes”, citando como ejemplo el refuerzo de las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad del Estado y de las Fuerzas Armadas, la mejora de las instalaciones para los migrantes y el decreto ley de 309 millones de euros para la ciudad, “más del 15% del producto interior bruto” de Ceuta. Bolaños ha acusado a quienes “instigan” las concentraciones de actuar “desde el partidismo”, señalando en particular al PP y a Vox por haber votado en contra de los 25 millones aprobados para atender a los menores en Ceuta.

La UE ha identificado intentos por parte de Rusia de sacar partido de la entrada de migrantes, aunque no disponen de pruebas que demuestren que esas campañas provocasen cruces masivos

World.title: Salir de Ceuta por su propio pie: “No puedo más, me voy. Aún no sé para qué vine”
World.content:
Tarek y su hermana Salma llegan mirando al suelo y arrastrando los pies. Vinieron a Ceuta sin nada y se van sin nada por la frontera. Ni una lágrima ni una mirada atrás cuando salen de Ceuta. Ambos describen el último mes como “el peor” de sus vidas. Sin embargo, ampliando la mirada, su aventura ha roto una ciudad, se enmarca en una crisis con ramificaciones internacionales, con Rusia, Israel e Italia en el punto de mira, y ha puesto al Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez frente a su mayor emergencia migratoria. “No puedo más, me voy. Aún no sé para qué vine”, dice Tarek, de 20 años, antes de abandonar Ceuta hacia Marruecos por un camino de tierra —el único habilitado para quienes entraron de forma ilegal y deciden regresar— a un costado del control de pasaportes. “Quiero volver al instituto”, añade su hermana Salma, de 17 años, que decidió unirse a la caravana para entrar en España sin saber muy bien por qué. Tarek y Salma han pasado un mes juntos protegiéndose mutuamente y emprenden este lunes su regreso a Oued Laou, a dos horas en coche de Ceuta y a cinco de Melilla por la costa.

Media hora después, aparece Karim Molahid. Tiene 20 años, va solo y cojea al andar. Alguien le golpeó por la noche con un palo y lleva el tobillo hinchado. “Esto no es vida. Llevo un mes viviendo como una rata. Durmiendo en la calle, comiendo lo que puedo o lo que me dan. Me duele el cuerpo y me han roto el móvil”, dice mostrando un teléfono con la pantalla cuarteada. “Mi madre se ha puesto enferma y quiero volver”, dice llorando antes de emprender el camino a su pueblo, cerca de Casablanca.

No es difícil detectar a quienes salen de Ceuta. Bañador, chanclas, la derrota en la cara después de 30 días durmiendo al raso. Unos más y otros menos, pero la mayoría llevan algún golpe: una herida en el lomo, un moratón en la pierna, tres puntos en la cabeza. Unos se los hicieron tratando de llegar a Ceuta el día que murieron más de un centenar de personas y otros se los han hecho durante la noche. “Por aquí”, le dice un guardia civil a Karim para que sepa que debe salir por el camino de tierra y no por la garita oficial con escáner y control de pasaportes.

Karim Molahid sale de Ceuta hacia Marruecos este lunes por la frontera del Tarajal. Ariadna Roig Ripoll

Según la Delegación del Gobierno y fuentes del mando único, unas 162 personas salen voluntariamente de Ceuta cada día. Las cifras recogidas sin mayor rigurosidad científica que la observación diaria, los datos del periódico El Faro y la mirada del agente que vigila bajo el sol la extraña frontera, son muy inferiores. El martes 25 de agosto, hace una semana, salieron 60 personas por el día y 30 por la noche. El pasado jueves fueron 60 adolescentes y el viernes 50 chicos por el día y 10 por la noche salieron voluntariamente de Ceuta. Si los datos oficiales fueran precisos, de las casi 8.000 personas que hay en Ceuta, descontando unos 2.000 menores, en cinco semanas se habría terminado sola la crisis.

“Se terminarán marchando todos”, dice Abdl Kazar, de 32 años, antes de dar la espalda a Ceuta y emprender el camino de vuelta a Jadiada, un pueblo cerca de Rabat. Kazar llegó nadando, pero lleva colgada del hombro una bolsa de piel con ropa. “La ropa me la trajo un familiar de Holanda”, explica. “Mi tío regresaba desde Marruecos después del verano, así que aprovechó para venir a Ceuta con su pasaporte europeo y me dio ropa para estos días y después se marchó”, detalla. “Pero no aguanto más”, dice antes de ponerse a caminar hacia Marruecos.

Cada día hay un goteo de adolescentes que regresan a casa, lo que contrasta con escenas paradójicas. El domingo, un niño de no más de 11 años llegó caminando a la frontera para volverse a su pueblo “porque no quería que le siguieran pegando otros chicos”, dice afectado el agente de la frontera. Sin embargo, no le dejó salir. El protocolo obliga a que, en caso de ser menor, venga la Policía Nacional, le tome los datos y lo envíe a un centro de menores.

El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, atribuyó la entrada masiva de casi 80.000 personas en Ceuta a que se difundieron “rumores y desinformación desde redes sociales vinculadas tanto a Rusia como a Israel y a una internacional ultraderechista”, dijo en la Cadena SER. Cuando los adolescentes explican las razones por las que se animaron a venir, se parecen bastante a esto. Todos coinciden en que se animaron a venir un día cualquiera y sin mayor preparación que una mochila, un par de camisetas y el móvil. “Me llamó mi madre y me dijo que había oído en la radio que la frontera de Ceuta estaba abierta”, dice Tarek. “Lo leí en Facebook”, explica Karim. “Escuché a una gente de mi pueblo hablar de esto y me animé”, recuerda Abdl.

Karim Molahid se despide de su amigo en la frontera antes de salir voluntariamente este lunes de Ceuta a Marruecos por Tarajal Ariadna Roig Ripoll

Cuando explican por qué el resto de marroquíes no sale de Ceuta, Abdl dice que prefieren “aguantar ahí a volverse derrotados a su pueblo después de pisar España”. Otros, sin embargo, dicen que no entienden que, si van a ser expulsados, hayan montado tiendas tan grandes y haya tantos vehículos de la Cruz Roja atendiéndolos. “Tal vez se está preparando llevarnos a Madrid”, dice.

“¿Entiendes el enfado de la gente de Ceuta?”. “Sí, ellos tienen razón”, dice Tarek. “Yo solo venía a trabajar, pero no es esto lo que creía. La culpa es del rey de Marruecos”, dice resignado.

La frontera del Tarajal es uno de los lugares donde mejor les va a algunos de los chicos. Por aquí entran marroquíes con pasaporte español que se apiadan de ellos y les regalan un pan, unas monedas o algo de ropa. Otros resisten del lado español agolpados junto a la valla que separa ambos países porque es el único punto donde pueden captar la señal de telefonía marroquí. Es lo único que les interesa del país que dejaron.

World.title: “La reacción de las autoridades marroquíes sobre Ceuta me parece vil”
World.content:
Para Fouad Abdelmoumni, economista y activista marroquí, la crisis migratoria actual muestra que la frustración de sus compatriotas está mucho más extendida de lo que pensábamos

Fouad Abdelmoumni, ex director en Marruecos de Transparencia Internacional, en 2021 en Rabat.

La crisis migratoria de Ceuta también suscita muchas preguntas también al otro lado de la frontera. Muchos marroquíes echan de menos que sus autoridades expliquen cómo decenas de miles de personas pudieron entrar en España en tan poco tiempo.

Hablamos con Fouad Abdelmoumni, economista y activista veterano de derechos humanos, desde Suiza, donde vive desde hace dos años después de sufrir, según denuncia, un chantaje sexual del aparato de seguridad marroquí. Ha sido, además, condenado en primera instancia a seis meses de prisión por afirmar que Marruecos utilizó Pegasus y asegura que su entorno le aconseja no regresar a su país.

Abdelmoumni cree que la reacción de las autoridades marroquíes ante lo ocurrido en Ceuta ha sido insuficiente y le parece inverosímil que algo así pudiera pasar inadvertido para un Estado con un aparato policial y de inteligencia tan fuerte, aunque reconoce que no hay fuentes suficientemente sólidas que demuestren que hubiera un plan organizado.

El que fue director de la ONG anticorrupción Transparencia Marruecos y miembro del partido Alianza de la Federación de la Izquierda, señala que el descontento profundo no solo afecta a los jóvenes marroquíes en paro: también hay trabajadores que consideran indignas sus condiciones y muchas mujeres jóvenes dispuestas a arriesgar su vida para optar a algo mejor. Las oportunidades, denuncia, las acapara una élite vinculada al poder, y este dedica gran parte de los recursos a proyectos como el Mundial de fútbol, en lugar de apostar por la educación, sanidad y el empleo estables.
