World.title: Kallas califica el ataque fallido con drones en Leipzig de “terrorismo patrocinado por un Estado”
World.content:
Un artificiero trabaja en los restos del dron, en el aeropuerto del aeropuerto de Leipzig, en Alemania, el pasado 5 de agosto.

La jefa de la diplomacia de la UE prevé nuevas sanciones contra Moscú. Alemania y otros países europeos convocan a los embajadores rusos

El frustrado ataque con drones cargados con explosivos contra el aeropuerto de la ciudad alemana de Leipzig tenía “todas las características del terrorismo patrocinado por un Estado”, ha afirmado este miércoles la responsable de la Política Exterior de la Unión Europea, Kaja Kallas, quien ha reiterado que Europa debe coordinarse para ver “qué más se puede hacer” ante la escalada de los ataques de Rusia contra Ucrania.

El martes, el Gobierno alemán señaló formalmente a Rusia como responsable de este ataque, perpetrado el 4 de agosto y que tenía como objetivo aviones de carga ucranios. Tras estas acusaciones, la UE y varios países europeos como Francia, Países Bajos, Bélgica— y la propia Alemania— han convocado a los embajadores rusos.

Kallas, que participa este miércoles en una reunión informal de ministros de Asuntos Exteriores europeos en Irlanda, ha recalcado que en este encuentro se debatirá sobre nuevas sanciones contra personas y entidades rusas. En la misma línea, el ministro de Exteriores alemán, Johann Wadephul, ha confirmado que la Unión Europea se plantea nuevas medidas punitivas contra ciudadanos rusos en las próximas semanas.

“La UE ha impuesto sanciones de gran alcance a Rusia, pero sin duda seguiremos trabajando para imponer sanciones a personas concretas en las próximas semanas”, ha dicho desde Irlanda, en declaraciones reproducidas por la agencia Reuters. “Se está intensificando la presión sobre Rusia y el apoyo a Ucrania también se mantiene en un nivel elevado. Esa es la unidad que estamos demostrando en estos momentos”, ha agregado Wadephul.

World.title: La batalla de los mapas: Google y Apple cambian el lago Ontario por el lago América y se dispara la ‘app’ de su competidor
World.content:
Apple también ha cambiado la denominación lago Ontario por lago América en su servicio de mapas. La plataforma sigue la decisión de Google de acatar la orden ejecutiva de Donald Trump de cambiar el nombre oficial del lago entre Estados Unidos y Canadá. El presidente estadounidense tomó la decisión como represalia por la guerra comercial que enfrenta a los dos vecinos, tradicionales aliados hasta la llegada del republicano a la Casa Blanca.

El cambio de momento solo se muestra a los residentes en EE UU. En el resto del mundo, Apple Maps sigue dando “lago Ontario” como único resultado y Google Maps devuelve ambos nombres: “Lago Ontario (Lago America)”. Google ha dicho que su decisión se debe a que sigue la denominación oficial del Gobierno de EE UU. En Canadá han mantenido el nombre oficial de toda la vida: lago Ontario.

Esta polémica ha servido para que un pequeño competidor, MapQuest, haya escalado hasta el puesto 1 en descargas en la App Store de Estados Unidos, una señal de protesta contra las grandes tecnológicas por doblegarse ante los caprichos de Trump. La app fue pionera en los mapas online, pero hace años que perdió popularidad y tiene un uso menos generalizado entre el gran público.

“Hemos adoptado el mismo enfoque que con el golfo de México: participar en la conversación y ofrecer a la gente una aplicación que conserva los nombres que les resultan familiares”, ha dicho Doug Berger, director ejecutivo de MapQuest. “Cientos de miles de personas nos han indicado que acertamos y han descargado nuestra aplicación”, añade.

Como menciona Berger, no es la primera vez que ocurre una polémica similar. En febrero de 2025, Trump ordenó el cambio de nombre del golfo de México por golfo de América. Google Maps sigue dando hoy ambos nombres para los usuarios globales.

World.title: Nelio Biedermann, el escritor de 23 años que narró un siglo entero: “Olvidar es una forma comprensible de sobrellevar la Historia”
World.content:
Es uno de esos fenómenos que se producen, a lo sumo, una o dos veces por década: una novela salida de la nada convierte a un veinteañero desconocido en estrella literaria. Así empieza la historia de Nelio Biedermann, autor suizo nacido en 2003 al que Lázár, una saga histórica escrita con el aliento propio de un discípulo de Thomas Mann, ha catapultado a la fama. Publicada en los países de lengua alemana en septiembre de 2025, la novela superó los 200.000 ejemplares y vendió sus derechos de traducción a una treintena de territorios. Patti Smith la elogió en público y Dua Lipa la recomendó a sus seguidores, mientras que Tom Tykwer, director de Corre, Lola, corre y de la serie Babylon Berlin, ya prepara su adaptación al cine. El libro llega este jueves a las librerías españolas, editado por Salamandra.

No está mal para un autor que todavía estudia literatura y cine en la Universidad de Zúrich, y sigue compartiendo piso con su hermana y un amigo en Seefeld, elegante barrio a la orilla del lago que preside la ciudad, donde nos citó a finales de julio. Su padre regenta la agencia de viajes situada en la planta baja del edificio. “Perdón por no hacerte subir, pero mi hermana está enferma”, dice al llamar al timbre. Unos minutos después, aparece un joven de bigote fino, atuendo informal y una cadena al cuello, algo perplejo y sobrepasado por todo lo sucedido. “Han pasado tantas cosas que parece que el libro lleve tres años publicado, pero ni siquiera ha pasado uno. Aunque, en realidad, mi vida personal no ha cambiado tanto”, asegura en la terraza soleada del café de la esquina.

En realidad, Biedermann no era un novato. En 2023 ya publicó una primera novela, se formó leyendo con entrega a los clásicos y encontró la inspiración para Lázár en una materia que conocía desde niño: la memoria húngara de la rama paterna de su familia. Sus mayores solían llevarlo de vacaciones a Hungría para mostrarle los castillos que les habían pertenecido. Esas visitas dejaron huella: un orgullo familiar herido, pero también el silencio sobre los episodios más oscuros del siglo XX —la pregunta inevitable en ese rincón de Europa: qué hicieron tus abuelos durante la guerra— y la impresión de que un trauma se transmitía de una generación a la siguiente. “Hay historias concretas de mi familia en la novela, pero al terminar me costaba saber dónde terminaban esos relatos reales y dónde empezaban los inventados. Partí de recuerdos y relatos familiares, pero al convertirlos en ficción surgió algo que tenía vida propia. Las historias de mi abuela y las del libro se parecen, pero no son exactamente lo mismo”, asegura.

“Los libros de historia son esenciales, pero no bastan. Entendemos que sucedió algo terrible sin llegar a sentirlo. La novela puede crear empatía por las vidas concretas”

La novela acompaña durante casi 300 páginas a los Lázár, una estirpe noble que atraviesa la disolución del Imperio austrohúngaro, las dos guerras mundiales, la ocupación nazi y el estalinismo, hasta plantearse el exilio en los años cincuenta. Como en Los Buddenbrook, la monumental saga de Mann, la historia con mayúscula se confunde con la familiar, aunque aquí aparezca atravesada por una veta gótica y otra que parece emparentada con el realismo mágico. Lajos nace el día de Reyes con una piel casi transparente, bajo la que se distinguen sus órganos. Es un niño de ojos azul aguamarina, hijo de la baronesa Mária y, aunque nunca llegará a saberlo, de uno de sus criados. El secreto queda encerrado en un castillo situado junto a un bosque que enloquece a quienes se adentran en él. Sus hijos, Pista y Eva, heredarán su apellido, pero también los silencios, la violencia y las pérdidas de la familia. Tras el fracaso del levantamiento húngaro contra el dominio soviético, deberán decidir si permanecen en Budapest o escapan por Yugoslavia para tratar de llegar a Suiza.

La pregunta es si una saga histórica de estas características, artefacto muy poco habitual entre los escritores de su generación, fue concebida contra ciertas modas literarias, en un momento muy dominado por la autoficción y otras formas del testimonio. Biedermann asegura que no escribió contra ninguna corriente. Todo nació de una lista de lecturas que un profesor le impuso durante sus estudios: más de un centenar de títulos que iban de Goethe y Schiller a Peter Handke o Patrick Süskind. “Quería entender por qué muchos de aquellos libros seguían teniendo tanta influencia, por qué continuaban vivos y qué podían decirnos todavía hoy”, afirma.

A partir de esas lecturas parió una novela desbordante y algo desigual, cuyo relato avanza a trompicones y tiende a la saturación de desgracias, como ha señalado parte de la crítica. Biedermann se permite incluso abandonar durante unas páginas a los Lázár para narrar las últimas horas de Stalin, que agoniza con un libro de Gógol a su lado. Aunque esos altibajos no ocultan la ambición mayúscula del proyecto, su talento para la imagen literaria y una sensibilidad poco común. El autor admite que temió cargar el libro de sufrimiento, pero acabó rechazando la idea de ahorrar incomodidades al lector: “Esas generaciones tuvieron que vivirlo. Nosotros solo tenemos que leerlo”.

El autor suizo Nelio Biedermann, en Zúrich, en una imagen cedida por la editorial Salamandra. Ruben Hollinger (Editorial Salamandra)

En su propia familia, los relatos llegaban con fragmentos silenciados: su abuela solía omitir todos los episodios traumáticos. Mucho más tarde descubrió rincones oscuros y supo que su abuelo, a quien no conoció, había sufrido una depresión grave. “En medio de ese silencio se transmitían el orgullo y el sentimiento de pertenencia, pero también el miedo y las maneras de hacer daño”, afirma. Escribir no garantiza que el ciclo se interrumpa, pero obliga a observar lo que antes quedaba fuera de campo. “No sé si escribir basta; no tengo tanta fe en la literatura”, bromea Biedermann. “Pero sí sirve para tomar conciencia de lo que ha salido mal, y eso ya es algo”. La ficción, añade el escritor, puede conseguir algo que no logra por sí solo un ensayo firmado por un especialista: “Los libros de historia son esenciales, pero no bastan. Entendemos intelectualmente que sucedió algo terrible sin llegar a sentirlo. La novela puede crear empatía por las vidas concretas”.

A lo largo del libro, los Lázár se debaten entre dos formas de supervivencia: la locura y el olvido. Imre, tío abuelo de Pista y Eva, pasa buena parte de su vida recluido en un sanatorio: enloquecer parece la respuesta lógica a un mundo que ha perdido la razón. Mientras tanto, Lajos, su sobrino y cabeza de familia, conserva la cordura, pero solo a base de autoengaño. “Me pregunto cómo pudieron seguir cuerdos quienes atravesaron esa parte del siglo XX. Aunque el ser humano tiene una extraordinaria capacidad de adaptación: puede suceder algo intolerable que, con el tiempo, se convierte en la nueva normalidad. Olvidar es una forma comprensible de sobrellevar la Historia”, opina el autor.

Una de las mayores virtudes de Lázár consiste en negarse a convertir a sus protagonistas en víctimas. La familia padece la guerra, la ocupación y la represión comunista, pero llega a ese derrumbe desde una posición de riqueza y privilegio sostenida por el trabajo de otros, algo que Biedermann nunca pierde de vista. Lajos, además, no es un simple testigo de su época: en 1944 participará en la organización de la persecución y deportación de judíos. “En todas las familias se tiende a contar la parte buena, la leyenda familiar. Yo sabía que tenía que mostrar la otra cara”, responde el autor. Con todo, evita dictar sentencia: “Prefiero dejar el juicio en manos del lector. Los personajes ambiguos son más interesantes. Y, sobre todo, reflejan mejor nuestra realidad”.

De su próximo libro solo da una pista: transcurrirá en la actualidad. No dirá más. Biedermann ha dedicado esta novela a reconstruir todo lo que su familia trajo consigo hasta esta orilla del lago. Tal vez el siguiente paso consista en averiguar qué queda de su historia en el turbio presente.

World.title: Dutch woman living in Nepal found alive after surviving floods
World.content:
The Dutch foreign office has made contact with a woman living in Nepal who had been reported missing in the wake of last week’s devastating floods, which have killed more than 1,100 people.

Foreign affairs minister Tom Berendsen said there had been “good news” as he spoke to reporters during a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.

The woman is one of three Dutch nationals who were known to be in Nepal when a glacier in the Himalaya region collapsed last Wednesday, causing water and mud to surge down the Bhote Koshi river and wipe out villages in the Rawusa border region with Tibet.

She was in the Himalaya region when the disaster struck, but has reached the Nepalese capital Kathmandu, where she contacted the foreign ministry.

A spokesman said the government was still “very concerned about the fate of the two other Dutch nationals”, 29-year-old Christiaan Berghuis from Nijkerk and 51-year-old Maaike Moolhuijsen from Haarlem.

They were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred Tibetan mountain, when the floods hit. The group of 80 pilgrims were believed to be in an immigration office that was in the path of the floodwaters.

World.title: Cheap Chinese parcels to the Netherlands fall 46% after EU levy
World.content:
The number of small parcels arriving in the Netherlands from outside the EU fell by 46% in July and August compared with the previous six months, according to customs figures presented to parliament. It is the first clear sign that a new €3 import charge is changing the flow of cheap goods from China.

The drop was revealed by Eelco Eerenberg, the junior finance minister responsible for customs, during a debate in parliament on Tuesday.

Around one million such parcels were arriving in the Netherlands each day before the change, 80% to 90% of them from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress.

Since July 1, a new EU-wide charge of €3 has applied to parcels worth up to €150 sent from outside the bloc, which were previously exempt from import duties. The fee is levied per type of product rather than per parcel, so an order containing several different items can be charged more than once.

Customs officials say online retailers are already changing how they operate, moving away from sending millions of individual packages and instead importing goods in bulk to store in warehouses inside the EU before shipping them on to shoppers. The same shift has been seen in France and Belgium.

“The figures give a first indication that fewer loose parcels are going straight to the consumer,” Nanette van Schelven, director-general of the Dutch customs service, told broadcaster NOS, “which makes it easier for us to check whether products are safe.”

A single large shipment is easier to screen for unsafe or banned goods, she said, than a constant stream of separate parcels.

The Dutch share

The charge raised about €134 million in import duties in July alone, of which roughly a quarter went to the Dutch treasury. Customs duties are collected as an EU revenue source: member states keep a share to cover the cost of collection and pass the rest to Brussels.

The Netherlands had drawn up plans for a national surcharge of its own on cheap parcels but dropped them in January, choosing to rely on the EU charge after France and Belgium shelved similar schemes and Brussels brought its levy forward.

World.title: Riot police break up protest against refugee shelter in Zeeland
World.content:

Riot police had to disperse a crowd of around 300 people who staged a protest against plans to set up an emergency shelter for 150 asylum seekers.

Councillors were trapped inside the town hall in Tholen, Zeeland, after demonstrators gathered outside with banners during a meeting to discuss the proposed site.

Police said riot squad officers were sent in “to restore public order as quickly as possible” after some of the protesters were accused of inciting violence.

The council wants to accommodate 150 refugees in a building on Postweg for a maximum of two and a half years to meet its obligations under the so-called “spreading law” (spreidingswet), which requires all municipalities to share the responsibility of housing asylum seekers.

Mayor Marleen Sijbers told councillors not to leave the building until they were given the all-clear by police.

Police dogs and a helicopter were also used to clear the crowd outside the town hall by 11pm. Police have not said if any arrests were made.

World.title: Justice minister warns of “unprecedented” violence after attack
World.content:
Justice minister David van Weel has called the violence in the Gelderland village of Overasselt “unprecedented” for the Netherlands, after dozens of armed men shot a man dead and opened fire on police in the early hours of Tuesday.

Dozens of young men moving through a village armed and immediately shooting at police was, he said, something the country had never seen before. Van Weel said it was probably international gangs settling scores – “drug cartels, mafia” that operate across borders.

Both Het Parool and De Telegraaf have cited sources reporting that the attack grew out of a dispute over a large shipment of cocaine tied to the organisation of Jos “Bolle Jos” Leijdekkers, the fugitive regarded as the Netherlands’ most wanted drug lord.

According to Het Parool, figures in the criminal world believe the group came to recover part of a missing cocaine shipment, which would explain the number of men involved.

Residents of Overasselt, who had been told to stay indoors during a day-long manhunt, were allowed back out on Tuesday evening. Police said there was no sign that any suspects were still in or around the village, though extra patrols were deployed overnight and the investigation is ongoing.

Officers confirmed that a 51-year-old man from nearby Wijchen was shot dead – reportedly a security guard hired by the household that was targeted. Two police officers were seriously injured, one of them at one point in a life-threatening condition, though both are now out of danger.

A total of 34 people were arrested at various locations around the country, among them nationals of Belgium, France and Algeria as well as the Netherlands.

Van Weel would not say who was behind the attack, and the public prosecution department has declined to comment on any potential links while the investigation continues.

The targeted property has a long history of drug-related incidents. A drug lab was found there after a fire in 2019, and the same address was shot at with an AK-47 last year. One of its residents is appealing a four-year sentence for drug trafficking, according to broadcaster NOS.

Van Weel rejected the suggestion that the Netherlands had become a “narco-state”, where drugs gangs have free rein, but acknowledged that criminal networks such as those of Leijdekkers and the convicted crime boss Ridouan Taghi had taken root in the country and are benefiting from Dutch financial and logistical facilities.

World.title: Minister sent death threats over plans to shoot “problem wolves”
World.content:
Junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens says he has has received death threats after bringing new rules making it easier for provincial and local governments to shoot wolves that pose a danger to people.

Erkens told MPs that local authorities needed more powers to drive away wolves that had lost their fear of humans, with shooting a last resort to deal with so-called “problem wolves”.

He faced criticism in parliament on Tuesday for announcing the measures in July before they could be debated, as well as for his comments in an interview about the shooting of a wolf known as Bram in December 2025.

“The world is on fire, all sorts of things are going on and at the same time people in our country are organising funerals for Bram the wolf. Totally out of touch with the world,” Erkens told the Telegraaf.

Bram, officially designated wolf GW3237m, became a cause célèbre for animal welfare campaigners after Utrecht province gave a local hunting organisation a licence to kill him last July.

It followed a number of incidents in which the wolf had approached humans, including an attack on a child. Bram was shot dead last December after campaigners lost a court battle to have the permit revoked.

14 packs

Erkens also criticised a report by scientists at Wageningen University, who said the Netherlands’ wolf population should be allowed to grow both for legal reasons and to benefit the ecosystem.

He said there was “not a single realistic scenario in which you’d want 56 wolf packs”. Currently there are 14 packs established in the country, with more than 100 wolves altogether.

The return of the animals to the Netherlands a decade ago has sharply divided opinions, with right-wing and rural parties calling for stronger measures to cull their numbers while progressive parties have said they should be protected.

Under Erkens’ rules, a wolf becomes a “problem wolf” if they attack people, react aggressively rather than running away, or attack horses or cattle more than once in a two-week period.

Local authorities then have a range of options to drive off the wolf, including shooting them with paintball guns, with killing them as a last resort. “I would hope that all of us would draw a red line if a child is attacked by a wolf,” he said.

World.title: “Grey divorce” on the rise among the Dutch over-60s
World.content:
The number of couples divorcing in the Netherlands is still falling, but a growing share of those who do split are over 60 – a trend sometimes called “grey divorce”.

Some 24,555 marriages ended in divorce in 2025, according to national statistics office CBS, down from 30,729 in 2018. The decline has been going for more than a decade. Fewer people are marrying in the first place, and those who do tend to stay together longer.

Older couples are the exception. Divorces among the under-60s have dropped since 2014, but among people over 60 they have gone up, and their share of all divorces has climbed from around 8% a decade ago to about 13% last year.

Hundreds of couples now divorce after 40 years or more together, including some who separate after a 50-year anniversary, which was almost unheard of at the turn of the century.

Relationship therapists link the shift to changing attitudes, with divorce more widely accepted than it was a generation ago, and to the moment when children leave home or retirement approaches and long-married partners find they have little left in common.

There is a knock-on effect on housing. Many older people who split up choose to live apart together rather than move in with a new partner, keeping two homes between them and freeing up fewer properties on an already tight market.

World.title: Cabinet to scrap welfare cuts in revised budget deal – RTL
World.content:
The Dutch government has scrapped most of its planned cuts to social security as it tries to attract opposition support for next year’s budget, RTL Nieuws has reported.

The cabinet will also delay raising the excess charge for health insurance by a year and invest €1.5 billion in mitigating the impact of inflation, particularly rising energy prices, on spending power.

The deal was the outcome of protracted negotiations between the three coalition partners, D66, VVD, and CDA, which ran through the weekend and most of Monday as the party leaders stretched the deadline to send the draft budget to the Council of State.

RTL Nieuws said it had seen leaked details of the budget proposals, which will not be formally announced for another two weeks when finance minister Eelco Heinen presents it to parliament.

The U-turn on welfare spending is a blow for the right-wing VVD, which had earlier said it would not compromise on the €6.5 billion worth of cuts to incapacity benefit, unemployment payments and substitute pay for new mothers on maternity leave.

Another plan in the coalition agreement to save €2.8 billion by increasing the retirement age in step with life expectancy, rather than by eight months for every extra year, has also been cancelled, as announced earlier by social security minister Hans Vijlbrief.

Heinen and prime minister Rob Jetten had spent the last two weeks trying to do a deal with opposition parties in advance to get their support for the budget, as the coalition is 10 seats short of a majority in the lower house and 16 seats short in the Senate.

But those talks ended without agreement as the three coalition parties struggled to agree among themselves about what concessions they should make to opposition groups on the left and right. Ministers will now have to find the votes when the budget plans go through parliament during the autumn.

Jetten’s D66 party and the Christian Democrats (CDA) reportedly wanted to scale back welfare cuts to appeal to the largest opposition party, the left-wing Progressief Nederland (Pro), while the VVD preferred a package that addressed the demands of right-wing parties such as JA21, with more tax cuts and less welfare spending.

World.title: Far-right TV show editor Niemöller leaves after Hitler remarks
World.content:
Joost Niemöller is stepping down as editor-in-chief of far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON), weeks after he said on air that Adolf Hitler had put certain things “very well”.

The broadcaster said the immediate reason was a “difference of view about the editorial direction and recent programming”, according to director-general Peter Vlemmix. Its statement, reported by NOS, runs to two sentences and does not mention the item that set off weeks of criticism.

In the late-July broadcast, Niemöller said there were “certain things of Hitler’s” he agreed with, aside from the Nazi leader’s antisemitism.

Co-presenter Raisa Blommestijn also backed a statement, put to the pair after a clip of a Hitler speech referring to Jewish people, that a cosmopolitan elite was inherently hostile to ordinary people. Both said they did not share all of Hitler’s ideology.

Media minister Rianne Letschert called the broadcast “terrible, distasteful, hurtful and unnecessary”, and the ombudsman for the public broadcasters logged dozens of complaints. The cabinet is examining whether ON can be forced out of the public broadcasting system, and Letschert has said a decision will come “very soon”.

Ongehoord Nederland joined the public broadcasting system in 2022 and has been reprimanded and sanctioned several times for breaching journalistic rules. Niemöller became editor-in-chief about 18 months ago.

World.title: Poland grants Ukraine permission to search for remains of Ukrainians massacred by Polish partisans

Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. The decision marks the latest step towards reconciliation between the two countries over their difficult shared history. Following a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv has also granted Poland permission to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists. On Tuesday, Ukrainian deputy culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi announced that the Polish authorities had granted a permit for a Ukrainian group to conduct exploratory work in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine. The search aims to uncover the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by the Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), a major underground resistance movement that emerged in Poland during the German occupation of World War Two. Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population, was attacked by a Peasant Battalion unit on 10 March 1944, with some estimates suggesting around 300 civilians were killed. Among those who died was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk. On the same day, members of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa), Poland’s largest armed resistance movement, also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń. According to estimates, they killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there. Dariusz Kopciowski, the conservator of monuments in the Lublin province where Łasków is located, confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that a permit for exploration work in Łasków had been granted. The issue had recently begun to cause tension, with Ukrainian media reporting last week that Ukraine has been waiting over a year for permission to carry out searches in Łasków. By contrast, Kyiv has granted permission for Poland to conduct such searches on its territory. Those Polish efforts are focused in particular on finding and exhuming the remains of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards those massacres as a genocide. However, Ukraine strongly rejects that label and also points to the fact that Polish partisan units killed Ukrainian civilians during the war. Poland, in turn, argues that many such incidents were acts of reprisal for the massacres carried out by Ukrainians. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine introduced a moratorium on search and exhumation work on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument in Poland dedicated to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). The UPA led the Volhynia massacres but is still celebrated by many in Ukraine for its role in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Last year, following negotiations with Poland, Ukraine lifted that moratorium and again began issuing permits for searches and exhumations of Polish victims on its territory, a number of which have already taken place. Last Sunday, Verbytskyi attended a funeral ceremony for 55 Polish massacre victims, around half of them children, whose remains were recently found and exhumed in a former Polish village located in what is now Ukraine. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 However, as well as those moves towards reconciliation, there have also been regular clashes between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, in particular following President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision in May this year to name a military unit after the UPA. That triggered strong protests from Poland, whose president, Karol Nawrocki, stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. Poland has also expressed concern over a new national pantheon being established by Ukraine. It has warned that, if figures associated with the massacre of Poles are included, that could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. World.title: Poles eating more meat but drinking less alcohol
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, the latest data from Statistics Poland (GUS) show. The average person in Poland ate 82 kilograms of meat in 2025, which was 7.5% more than a year earlier. It also marks an increase of 15.7% since 2015 and 22.7% since 2005. Likewise, consumption of eggs rose 8.5% in 2025 to an average of 218 per person. The increases have come amid rapidly rising incomes, which make such products more affordable. A separate GUS study earlier this year showed that the proportion of Poles who cannot afford to eat meat at least every other day fell from 8.2% in 2015 to 3% in 2025. By contrast, vegetable consumption has changed little, with the average Pole eating 108 kg in 2025, compared with 107 kg a year earlier and 110 kg in 2005. However, consumption of potatoes, a starchy staple of the Polish diet presented by GUS separately from other vegetables, has fallen sharply over the longer term, despite a slight increase last year. The average Pole ate 96.5 kg of potatoes in 2025, down 23.4% since 2005. Meanwhile, alcohol consumption last year continued its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. In 2025, the amount of wine drunk per person, at 4.9 litres, fell even more, by 9.3% year-on-year. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. A 2023 study by ProVeg, an NGO, conducted in partnership with the University of Copenhagen and Ghent University, found that Poles were the most carnivorous among ten European countries surveyed. Three quarters of Poles (74%) said they ate meat frequently, compared to an average of 62% across all countries. Italians and Spaniards (both 69%) were the next biggest meat eaters, while Germans (45%), Austrians (48%) and the Dutch (53%) were the least likely to eat meat frequently. Meanwhile, 7% of people in Poland said they were either vegan (2%), meaning consuming no animal products at all, or vegetarian (5%), meaning they do not eat meat or fish. That was just below the European average of 8%. In terms of what kinds of meat are favoured by Poles, GUS’s most recent such breakdown, from 2017, showed that pork was most popular, with the average Pole consuming 39.8 kg that year, followed by poultry (26.kg) and beef (2.3 kg). Poland's first company to produce cultured meat – which is grown in a lab from animal cells without the need to raise and kill livestock – has received a state grant to support its work. LabFarm this year presented a prototype of its chicken meatball https://t.co/pezABciGU6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2024 Earlier this year, Poland’s current government, a coalition ranging from left to centre right, announced new rules intended to improve the quality and variety of school meals, including offering less meat. From the start of the new school year, which began today, school canteens are expected to serve meat no more than twice a week, offer fish at least once per week, and offer a plant-based option at every meal. They should also limit fried food to no more than twice a week, use seasonal and locally sourced products, and include fruit and vegetables with meals. However, an attempt by the government to further raise taxes on alcoholic, sugary and sweet drinks was vetoed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last December. After a fire at a facility belonging to WB Electronics, the EU’s largest drone maker, Polish prosecutors have launched an investigation into suspicions that the incident was a “crime of a terrorist nature” committed with the “participation of foreign intelligence”. Prokurator z Małopolskiego Wydziału Zamiejscowego Departamentu do Spraw Przestępczości Zorganizowanej i Korupcji @PK_GOV_PL w Krakowie wszczął dziś śledztwo w sprawie brania udziału w działalności obcego wywiadu przeciwko Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej i dopuszczenia się przestępstwa… https://t.co/h6k4Fvv3CK — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026 Shortly after midnight, a fire broke out in storage facilities at WB Electronics’ plant in the city of Skarżysko-Kamienna. The site is used to produce components for drones that are supplied to the Polish and Ukrainian armed forces, among others. The fire was soon extinguished with no injuries reported. Speculation immediately emerged that the blaze could have been caused deliberately. Poland has been the primary target in Europe of sabotage activities carried out by operatives working on behalf of Russia. While the Polish authorities initially refused to speculate on the cause of the fire, the provincial police headquarters in nearby Kielce confirmed that a burglar alarm had been triggered in the area around midnight. When the emergency services arrived, they confirmed that a fire had broken out. Shortly before 5 p.m. local time on Monday afternoon, prosecutors announced that they had launched an investigation into the potential involvement of foreign intelligence and the committing of a terrorist offence. “The offence consisted of intentionally starting a fire on the premises of WB Electronics in Skarżysko-Kamienna on 31 August 2026 by planting a charge containing flammable materials,” they wrote. The resultant fire destroyed the warehouse facilities, causing at least 15 million zloty (€3.46m) of damage. Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for Poland’s security services, revealed that the Internal Security Agency (ABW) was conducting the investigation in cooperation with prosecutors. 🔴 Pożar w Skarżysku-Kamiennej. W zakładzie dronowej firmy doszło do podpalenia. ✒️ @jodynaa… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) August 31, 2026 The incident in Skarżysko-Kamienna came shortly after a separate fire on Sunday at a warehouse in another Polish city, Lublin, that belonged to a company that also supplies components for drones used in Ukraine, according to news website Wirtualna Polska. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka refused to confirm to Wirtualna Polska whether the authorities are treating the two fires as related, but said that “every aspect will be thoroughly investigated”. Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism on Moscow’s growing campaign of sabotage in Europe found that Poland is the “primary focus of Russian activity”. Last year, Poland confirmed that Russia was behind the fire that in 2024 destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre. It is also seeking to detain two men believed to have sabotaged a rail line in Poland last year on Russian orders. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. World.title: Fundraiser for baby orphaned by speeding driver in Polish city reaches 1 million zloty
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A fundraiser for an eight-month-old baby who survived an accident in the Polish city of Kraków in which his parents were killed by a speeding driver has reached more than 1 million zloty (€231,000). The tragedy has prompted widespread anger, with calls from residents and local politicians for the authorities to take action to deal with dangerous driving in the city. To będzie jedna z najtrudniejszych zbiórek, jakie wspólnie przeprowadzimy.💔Proszę o RT🙏 Kilka dni temu rozpędzony kierowca w Krakowie wjechał w młode małżeństwo. Mateusz i Klaudia zginęli. Ich kilkumiesięczny synek, Oliwier, trafił do szpitala. Mam dla Was dobrą wiadomość.… pic.twitter.com/R8L1xgEBPn — Damian Żurawski (@damian_zurawski) August 26, 2026 On 22 August, a married couple, Mateusz and Klaudia, both 32, were walking with their baby on Solna Street, close to the southern bank of the Vistula river, when a car driven by 26-year-old Hubert B., whose surname is masked under Polish privacy law, mounted the pavement, killing both parents. The child, eight-month-old Oliwier, survived the accident but was hospitalised. His condition is continuing to improve, reports broadcaster TVP Kraków. According to prosecutors, the car was travelling around 40 km/h (25mph) faster than the speed limit in the area. Hubert B. has been charged with unintentionally causing a fatal accident, for which he could face up to eight years in prison. “The suspect pleaded not guilty to the offence he was charged with, explaining, among other things, that the car skidded due to the uneven road surface,” prosecutors said, adding that the suspect has been placed in pretrial detention. An online fundraiser set up last week to provide Oliwier “with financial security for years to come” shared the news that the baby’s condition is now stable, although “his arm and leg are in plaster”. “We can’t give Oliwier back his mum and dad,” reads the fundraiser’s description. “However, we can do everything we can to ensure he has the resources for his education and a peaceful start to adult life.” At the time of writing, the fundraiser has reached more than 1.05 million zloty, over double its initial target. There have been more than 23,300 donations so far. Meanwhile, Oliwier’s grandfather, Andrzej, told newspaper Fakt that the family had given its consent for the fundraiser and was very grateful for those who had donated. A court in Kraków has granted Mateusz’s brother custody of the child. As well as sympathy for the victims, the accident aroused anger from residents. Several hundred people attended a protest at the site, holding signs reading “How many more people must die for something to change?” and “Stop road killers”. They installed their own mock-up pedestrian crossing and speed bumps. “Such tragedies are not isolated incidents,” said the organisers, quoted by news website Interia. They cited police figures showing that Kraków had the most road accidents of all Poland’s provincial capitals in 2025. Its figure of 941 was over 100 more than in Łódź and over 250 more than in Warsaw. Local councillor Rafał Zawiślak told news website Onet that he was filing a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, saying the city authorities had been negligent, failing to respond to warnings from 2024 that the site of the accident was dangerous. Godzina ciszy w Krakowie. Mieszkańcy upamiętniają parę, która zginęła w sobotniej tragedii przy ulicy Solnej. Na miejsce przybyły tłumy. „Nie chcemy bać się chodzić po chodnikach” – apelują.@RadioKrakow pic.twitter.com/DlOn5GvyL5 — Elżbieta Raczyńska (@_eraczynska) August 25, 2026 Acting mayor Stanisław Kracik said that an inspection of the street carried out after the accident had not shown any problems with the existing signage or need for traffic-calming measures. He added, however, that the city would be installing a speed bump. “I believe that this is simply what we should do…as a kind of expression of solidarity with the victims of this tragedy,” he said, quoted by broadcaster TVN. City police said they had been monitoring and taking action about road safety issues in the district for years, but that the street in question had not previously been reported as a particularly dangerous place, with just one incident causing one injury in the five years before the fatal accident. MPs from The Left have called for tougher rules on illegal street racing, saying police currently do not have sufficient legal tools. It comes after a crash on Saturday in which four men died after their car was filmed driving at dangerously high speeds https://t.co/OSRvyPAtVA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2023 The police also claimed that Kraków is “one of the safest cities” in Poland, with 768 road accidents per 100,000 residents this year, compared to over 1,000 in some other cities. However, TVN points out that the same statistics show that, this year, Kraków has had 71 accidents per 100,000 inhabitants in which someone was injured or killed, compared to 28 in Katowice and 27 in Warsaw. Road safety in Poland has improved dramatically, with the country recording the EU’s largest decline in road deaths between 2019 and 2024. However, its overall number of road deaths in relation to population is still above the EU average. Road deaths have fallen by 35% in Poland since 2019, which is the largest decline in the EU. World.title: Polish student accused of planning Islamist terrorist attack on Christmas market to stand trial
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish student is to stand trial accused of planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market in Poland as an act of support for Islamic State. On Monday, prosecutors announced that they have filed an indictment against the 20-year-old suspect, a student at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) who can be named only as Mateusz W. under Polish privacy law. Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesman for Poland’s security services, confirmed that Mateusz W. had been “preparing a mass attack at a Christmas market, which he planned to carry out using explosive materials”. Wracamy do sprawy 20-letniego Mateusza W. – studenta Katolickiego Uniwersytetu Lubelskiego podejrzewanego o przygotowywanie masowego zamachu na jednym z jarmarków świątecznych, którego planował dokonać z wykorzystaniem materiałów wybuchowych. Do Sądu Okręgowego w Koszalinie… https://t.co/6vGPcjiDnc pic.twitter.com/seFGV8nHMz — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026 The suspect was detained late last year, when details of his alleged plot and plans to establish contact with Islamic State were first revealed. He has remained in custody since then. Though the authorities have confirmed that Mateusz W. was a first-year student at KUL, a leading Catholic university that counts the late Pope John Paul II among its former students and lecturers, and that they have also searched premises in the province of Łódź, they have not revealed where his alleged attack was planned. However, prosecutors reported today that the suspect had established contacts through which he could gain access to explosive materials and devices, had looked for bomb-making instructions, and had tried to recruit others to his terrorist cause. “Mateusz W.’s actions were intended to further the policies of the terrorist organisation known as Islamic State and to seriously intimidate people with views contrary to the ideology espoused by the suspect,” wrote Katarzyna Calów-Jaszewska, a spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office. In a separate statement, the Internal Security Agency (ABW) revealed that the suspect had “intended to join a terrorist organisation affiliated with the so-called Islamic State and sought people who could help him carry out this plan”. Neither the security services nor prosecutors have indicated whether Mateusz W. denied or admitted to his alleged crimes or has offered any explanation for his actions. If convicted of preparing a mass attack, he could face up to ten years in prison. Last year, after Mateusz W. was detained, Dobrzyński said that he came from a devoutly Catholic family but had become “deeply infatuated with Islam” and had “fallen in love with terrorism”. In an appeal to parents, Dobrzyński said that, “if you see your children interested in Islam, communism, or fascism, and collecting all sorts of information and items on the subject, that’s the first sign. Take care of your own children, because things can only get worse from there”. Poland has detained a man who was allegedly planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market as an act of support for Islamic State. The suspect, a 19-year-old Pole, had become "infatuated with Islam", say the security services https://t.co/N4WDVZdlai — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 After news of Mateusz W.’s detention emerged, KUL suspended his student status. The university’s spokesman, Wojciech Andrusiewicz, said that neither fellow students nor lecturers had noticed any unusual behaviour by the suspect. World.title: Polish WWII massacre victims reburied in Ukraine at ceremony attended by officials from both countries
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of 55 Poles – around half of them children – massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, many of whose bones show signs of brutal deaths, were exhumed this summer after Ukraine recently ended a moratorium on searches for tens of thousands of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres who are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. “This is an important moment for [the victims’] families, but also the Polish state, because this funeral follows decades of waiting,” said Polish culture minister Marta Cienkowska at the ceremony in Ostrówki (Ostrovky in Ukrainian), a depopulated former village that, before the war, was part of Poland and now lies in Ukraine. “Poland has the right and obligation to speak about the crimes committed against its citizens. It has the obligation to commemorate the victims, search for their remains, and provide them with a dignified burial…We will continue this work…everywhere that the graves of the victims of the Volhynian crimes still remain.” Pogrzeb ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej Na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach na terytorium Ukrainy odbyła się uroczystość pogrzebowa 55 ofiar zbrodni dokonanej 30 sierpnia 1943 roku. W uroczystości, zorganizowanej w 83. rocznicę tragicznych wydarzeń,… pic.twitter.com/4dXPOj4m7y — Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) August 30, 2026 Others to attend the reburial included deputy Ukrainian culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi; Vitaly Skomarovsky, the bishop of Lutsk and president of Ukraine’s Roman Catholic episcopate; Piotr Zgorzelski, the deputy speaker of the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament; and former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. Karol Polejowski, the deputy head of Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which led the exhumation work, said that the presence of Ukrainian representatives “fills me with optimism for the future”. While Polish President Karol Nawrocki did not attend, one of his advisors, Jakub Banaszek, read a letter on his behalf, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will never forget those who died in agony simply because they were Poles,” wrote Nawrocki. “We will not cease our efforts to ensure that all our compatriots murdered by members of the OUN-UPA are properly buried and commemorated.” ✝️ W 8⃣3⃣. rocznicę zbrodni dokonanej przez ukraińskich szowinistów, na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach pochowaliśmy ofiary ludobójstwa na Wołyniu. 🔻🔻🔻 pic.twitter.com/5oh3uiCKX4 — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 30, 2026 The Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Poles were killed, were led by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was a partisan group founded by a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) faithful to nationalist leader Stepan Bandera. They sought to ethnically cleanse areas that they saw as Ukrainian territory by wiping out other ethnic groups, in particular the large Polish population. Massacres took place in dozens of villages, including Ostrówki and the neighbouring Wola Ostrowiecka (Volya Ostrovetska in Ukrainian), where on 30 August 1943 the UPA killed over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Exhumations previously took place on the site of the two villages in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Earlier this month, the IPN announced the results of that work. They uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres by Ukrainian nationalists during WWII have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools https://t.co/LbLPzJcG1b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 8, 2026 The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit. Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where Zelensky’s counterpart Karol Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest honour. In his letter read at Sunday’s ceremony, Nawrocki warned those who “continue the tradition of Banderite ideology” that they “place themselves outside the community of citizens of the free, civilised world” and are sending “a clear sign of hostility towards Poland and Poles”. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Since the crisis broke out in May, there have been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Earlier this month, Zelensky signed a law establishing a new national pantheon of Ukrainian heroes. Poland has warned that the inclusion of figures associated with the massacres could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. A survey conducted this month by Rating Group, a Ukrainian research agency, which asked Ukrainians to name their country’s greatest hero found that Bandera was the fourth most popular choice, having been chosen by 11% of respondents. World.title: Poland is terrible at promoting itself – but has never had better press
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Two incidents this month have highlighted how state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad often disappoint. Yet, at the same time, the country has never had better international press. Politicians should let Poland’s successes speak for themselves, and support those already telling its story. Poles care a lot about what the world thinks of their country. Major Polish media outlets regularly devote entire articles to what Western journalists, commentators and influencers are saying about Poland. “A German showed what he saw on the streets of Poland,” read one typical recent headline by Onet, Poland’s biggest news website, which devoted an entire report to one video by a German-speaking TikToker with around 7,000 followers. One rarely sees such reports in more self-confident Western countries. Given Poland’s history, such sensitivity regarding the country’s status is not surprising. Poland was, up until the 18th century, a major European country. But, for most of the last 250 years, it has been under foreign subjugation. Only since 1989 has it been able to develop independently, and Poles are understandably keen for the world to take note of their return to the top table. Poland has emerged as Europe’s undisputed growth champion over the past 35 years. In the first part of a new series of articles and podcasts, @AlicjaPtak4 explores the reasons behind Poland's rapid economic development, and the dangers that may lie ahead https://t.co/bW3bnV7Ozn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2025 Polish politicians are also inevitably eager to capitalise on such sentiment by showing voters that they are making an effort to promote Poland abroad. The problem is that such efforts are often poorly conceived and executed – as two examples this month have shown. In mid-August, the sport and tourism ministry launched a new advertising campaign intended to attract visitors from western Europe and the United States. However, the first advert – featuring Polish football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, and actor Nikodem Rozbicki playing Fryderyk Chopin – was widely panned in Poland. Res Futura, an organisation that monitors social media sentiment, found that 85% of comments about the advert were negative. The campaign’s slogan – “Poland. More than you expected” – is negative and lacking confidence. The Polish Tourism Organisation says it is based on research showing that visitors to Poland are often positively surprised by how nice it is. Yet, while that is undoubtedly true, it does not mean it is a good idea to try to attract potential tourists by focusing on their low expectations. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The video also has no narrative, with the creators seeming to think that showing famous faces will be enough. Rubik does not speak a single word, while Eisenberg says only “Poland” and Lewandowski “More than you expected”. The film itself does nothing to show that Poland is more than anyone expects. In fact, its depressingly colourless palette and focus on Warsaw’s Stalinist Palace of Science and Culture actually reinforce (false) stereotypes of Poland as grey, dull and post-communist. The country has so many interesting and colourful places that could have been showcased instead. The advert is also a wasted opportunity to tell a story about the film’s stars, especially Eisenberg, who has reconnected with his family’s Polish roots, produced a critically acclaimed movie set in Poland, and last year obtained citizenship. Instead, Chopin dominates the film, but his dialogue is incoherent. When he says, “Warsaw is where my heart is”, almost no potential visitors would understand that this is a reference to the real Chopin’s heart being transported from Paris, where he died, to Warsaw, where it is now entombed in a church. Not long after that advert launched, another controversy emerged around a state official, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, who had been appointed only weeks earlier by the government to lead the promotion of Poland. It quickly transpired that a report she had authored last year on creating a national brand – and which appeared to have played a big part in her getting the new job – contained significant errors, questionable methodology, and bizarre language. Many parts showed signs of being AI-generated. Mróz-Gorgoń, who has now resigned, insists that the report was the genuine product of work by her and her team at Marka Polska (Brand Poland), a think tank she leads. However, that is not particularly reassuring given the report’s content. Many parts are simply obvious: at the end of the 26-page text, the three recommendations for the government are to “develop a coherent, long-term national branding strategy”, “invest in promotional campaigns in key markets”, and “coordinate between ministries and other entities”. Other sections are very strange, such as noting that “Germany does not build its brand on the Holocaust”. But perhaps the most telling aspect is that, although the introduction claims it is “a comprehensive report on building…a coherent, long-term branding strategy in the international arena”, the document focuses entirely on how Poles themselves view their own country (its title is even A Self-Portrait of the Poles). It includes no research into what foreigners know or think about Poland and what could interest or attract them. While any national branding exercise should of course take account of the views of the native population, it is clearly incomplete without research into the target of such a campaign, the outside world. Yet that is sadly typical of many state-led efforts to promote Poland, which focus more on pleasing a domestic audience – the voters that politicians want to keep happy – than on being truly outward looking. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland's brand abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing major errors, bizarre language, and signs of being generated by AI https://t.co/9fpfzFCFuI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 It should be noted that such failings are nothing new. Successive governments have been responsible for botched efforts to promote Poland. The uninspiring slogan “Poland. More than you expected” has been used since 2021. A previous one, “Polska. Spring Into”, launched in 2014, was simply bizarre and quickly disappeared. In 2016, the former Law and Justice (PiS) government established the Polish National Foundation (PFN), which was pumped full of money from state-owned companies and tasked with promoting Poland abroad. Instead, it focused much of its efforts on domestic activity, often intended to support PiS’s political agenda. The work it did do internationally was often of questionable efficacy, such as spending millions on buying a yacht, naming it “I Love Poland”, then attempting to sail it around the world (before it ended up breaking down and getting stuck in port). A senior official under the former PiS government has been charged over alleged misspending of funds. The case relates to a campaign in 2017 that used money meant for promoting Poland abroad to instead advertise PiS's judicial reforms domestically https://t.co/tH64Bekhec — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 15, 2026 Yet, despite woeful state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad, the country has in recent times been enjoying a soaring international reputation. Western media have been full of articles about the country’s economic success; about how not only are Polish emigrants returning from the UK, but many Brits are moving to Poland too; about how Poles are becoming major buyers of property in Spain; about how companies with roots in Poland, such as InPost and ElevenLabs, are pioneering their industries. Social media feeds are full of influencers extolling Polish cities, with their safe, clean streets; the beauty of Polish nature, with its mountains, lakes and beaches; and the sense of dynamic development that you can feel as soon as you set foot in the country. Last weekend,@thetimes reported on how Brits are moving to Poland. This weekend, on how Poles are replacing Brits as property owners in Spain. pic.twitter.com/IDDdDlluTE — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) June 21, 2026 This positive publicity is largely organic – it is the product of Poland’s own actual successes, not of artificial efforts to create an image of success. It is generated from the bottom up, not from the top down. While the state can play a role – for example, by arranging visits for foreign journalists and influencers and supporting media and institutions that are already telling Poland’s story – it would be better for politicians to focus on creating the conditions for those successes, rather than concocting cockeyed schemes to promote them. World.title: Polish government sets out draft 2027 budget with deficit remaining at 7.1% of GDP
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence, healthcare and the energy transition among its spending priorities, while projecting another year of heavy borrowing. The deficit is forecast at 7.1% of GDP, unchanged from 2026 but well above the level of 3.7% the government had committed to reach by 2027 after Poland was placed under the European Union’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024. Rada Ministrów przyjęła projekt ustawy budżetowej na 2027 rok. Projekt odpowiedzialnie łączy finansowanie bieżących potrzeb państwa i przedsięwzięć wzmacniających jego bezpieczeństwo oraz potencjał rozwojowy.#BudżetPolaków 🔗 https://t.co/SjWyBUwi8U pic.twitter.com/X9ue6cw5ns — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 28, 2026 The budget – which must still be consulted with business and trade union representatives before being approved by parliament and then signed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki – sets total expenditure at 977.6 billion zloty (€225.4 billion), 58 billion zloty more than this year. Revenues are projected to rise by 68.4 billion zloty to 695 billion zloty, leaving a nominal budget deficit of 282.6 billion zloty, the highest on record and 10 billion zloty more than this year. Defence spending will remain high, at 198.1 billion zloty, equivalent to 4.5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in NATO. The healthcare budget will reach 274.1 billion zloty, up 26.3 billion zloty from 2026. Spending on energy security and transformation will rise 8.3% year-on-year to reach 19.7 billion zloty. The government expects GDP growth to remain strong, at 3% in 2027, while average inflation is forecast at 2.8%, within the central bank’s target of 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Average wages are expected to rise by 5.9% next year in nominal terms, slightly slower than the 6.4% forecast for this year. The government expects that unemployment, measured according to the national methodology, will stand at 6% at the end of 2027, broadly unchanged from its current level. Poland’s gross borrowing needs are projected at 565 billion zloty in 2027, below the 688 billion zloty budgeted for this year. Debt-servicing costs, however, are expected to rise to 107 billion zloty, up 17 billion zloty from this year. Finance minister Andrzej Domański said that the rise in debt-servicing costs is driven by an increase in the overall volume of debt and the need to refinance bonds issued in 2020 and 2021 at very low interest rates. Poland's debt has been growing at the second-fastest rate in the EU this year, and is set to continue rising. What is behind this trend – and should we be worried – asks Alicja Ptak in the latest of her series of articles and podcasts on Poland’s economy https://t.co/1pvnb2ZxoY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2025 The projected deficit leaves Poland under continued pressure to bring its public finances into line with EU fiscal rules. In 2024, the country was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure after its deficit exceeded the bloc’s limit of 3%. Warsaw pledged at the time to bring the deficit below 3% by 2028. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. “The 2027 budget represents a continuation of expansionary fiscal policy, and Poland is making no progress in correcting its excessive deficit and is taking no action to bring it below 3% of GDP,” wrote analysts at ING Bank Śląski today. “The result is a further increase in public debt.” Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Efforts to reduce the deficit have also been complicated by political stalemate between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed several fiscal measures, including tax increases. Nawrocki did, however, approve a new levy on banks that came into force this year. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. However, speaking today, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the 2027 budget reflects Poland’s position at a time when war is being waged across its eastern border and other conflicts are weighing on the country’s finances. Meanwhile, 2027 will also see pivotal parliamentary elections, at which Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, will seek a second term while the right-wing opposition, supported by Nawrocki, will attempt to win power. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
