“As we speak, before I finish answering, [..] in the next three minutes, at least 14 children will have died across the world from causes related to maternal and child malnutrition,” Thom said, adding that such deaths were preventable and “we cannot afford not to take action”.

She also noted that Pakistan was suffering an annual economic loss of $17bn due to stunting and malnutrition.

Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation speaks at the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

1:34pm - WFP official says malnutrition not just driven by poverty

Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that malnutrition was not just driven by poverty.

“It is also directly influenced and fed by poor access to services … health services and water and sanitation services,” he said.

1:15pm - Expert calls for focusing on adolescent nutrition

Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab, raised the alarm at the “missing adolescent middle” during conversations about malnutrition.

She said that nutrition discourse had been focused on the first 1,000 days of a child, but she stressed, “we are really missing the middle, which is between childhood and motherhood”.

“Focusing on adolescent nutrition is not to prepare them for motherhood, but it is also a window where the investment really returns in the form of human capital development,” she said.

She explained that during adolescent years, young girls were vulnerable to anaemia and iron deficiencies due to “rapid growth, hormonal changes and menstruation”.

“If she is not empowered, she cannot participate in education, and she has less cognitive capabilities,” Dr Wahab said.

Food security adviser on nutrition and social protection at GIZ Pakistan, Dr Faiza Wahab speaks at the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

1:10pm - WHO official stresses need for integrating social protection programmes with health services

Ellen Thom, the deputy representative for the World Health Organisation Pakistan, said integrating social protection with existing health and nutrition services is important.

She said that evidence showed that doing so and strengthening integrated primary healthcare was an effective way of reaching vulnerable families and delivering high-impact nutrition interventions.

1:02pm - WFP official says nutrition is not just about food

Thomas Conan, the deputy country director for the World Food Programme, said that nutrition was not only about food.

“It’s not only about access to food. It is about a healthy diet, the capacity to ensure multi-sectoral intervention and collaboration among us,” he said.

He said that it was also necessary to ensure access to a more healthy diet and the design of the social protection was nutrition-sensitive,” he said.

Thomas Conan. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

12:50pm - BISP official talks about Nashonuma programme

BISP Director General Dr Asim Ijaz spoke about the Benazir Nashonuma Programme (BNP), which he said had added a “nutritional and health layer” to the existing BISP registry.

He stressed that there exists a 1,000-day window for a child’s development, during which “irreversible damage can occur”.

“This is why BISP changed its thinking in 2019,” he said. He said that the recognition was then realised in the Nashonuma pilot launch in 2020, which was then phased out country-wide in 2021.

“Nashonuma itself is not a separate bureaucracy but layered onto existing platforms,” he said, explaining that BISP’s registry was now carrying a nutritional and health layer.

“So the idea was to have one beneficiary record with multiple beneficial layers,” he said.

12:42pm - ‘We can no longer afford to look away,’ BISP chairperson says

Senator Rubina Khalid, the chairperson of Benazir Income Support Programme, said in her keynote address that the responsibility lay not just with providing financial assistance, but with also helping families move from vulnerability towards dignity.

“We have gathered here today … because we can no longer afford to look away,” she said. She said that more than 40pc of children under five in Pakistan were stunted, while malnutrition placed a huge burden on the economy.

“Stunting is not only a health issue. It is a human capital issue, an economic issue and a challenge to Pakistan’s future,” she said. She said that the country lacked integration of the programmes it had to address these issues.

At the end of her address, she said: “We must work together so that every child in Pakistan has the opportunity to grow, learn and reach their full potential. Because every child we protect from malnutrition is not simply a life protected, it is the future protected, a family strengthened and a stronger Pakistan secured.”

Benazir Income Support Programme Chairperson Senator Rubina Khalid delivers the keynote address. — DawnNewsTV

12:40pm: Session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins

A session on integrating nutrition into social protection systems begins.

12:30pm - Sri Lankan doctor calls for understanding child growth trajectory in South Asia

Dr Rannan-Eliya, in answer to a question, pointed out that the child growth trajectory in South Asia was not the same as the rest of the world.

“We have sort of misunderstood the problem,” he remarked, adding: “There is no uniformity in child growth, and because we use a single growth standard, we partly misdiagnose what is going on”.

“In my sense, Sri Lankan kids need to be better nourished but there is a limit to what we can do and we need to understand that,” he said. He noted that a similar understanding was also being realised in India.

“So we need to do more as South and South East Asian countries, and it’s something that needs better investigation, and it is leading to a misunderstanding of what the problem is.”

12:13pm - Expert says nutrition an issue of human capital, economic growth

Dr Irshad Danish, the co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group, said that from his experience, Pakistan had low allocation, fragmented spending and implementation challenges.

“If we need $10 to feed malnourished children, we are spending only $2,” he said. He added that Pakistan was losing $17bn annually due to malnutrition.

He said that this also resulted in poor education outcomes, children with cognitive issues and lower workforce productivity.

“So, nutrition is not just a health issue. It is an issue of human capital and economic growth,” he said. He said that the cost of malnutrition was far greater than the cost of prevention.

“We need to move from fragmented spending towards strategic investment, and from hidden allocations to transparent budgets,” he said.

Dr Irshad Danish. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

12:00pm - Doctor stresses importance of lady health workers

Co-chair of the Global Nutrition Report Stakeholder Group Dr Irshad Danish stressed the significance of the lady health workers programme.

“It was one of the strongest community based health workers model and its coverage was around 60pc, with over 100,000 lady health workers,” he said, adding that the workers enjoyed community ownership.

“These workers were often the first link of access for healthcare [..] many independent evaluation where these health workers were available, there was better health knowledge and better access to essential services.”

11:46am - Sri Lankan official explains how country scaled health systems

Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya, the executive director of Sri Lanka’s Institute of Health Policy, said that 100 years ago, the South Asian country had worse health outcomes than the rest of the region.

“We were the sick man of South Asia, but now we have the best health plan. How did that happen? One simple reason I always tell people was the ballot box … the British decided to give self-rule,” he said.

He said that as a consequence, there was a pressure to give free education and to expand health services. He said that voters prioritised access to care over all other things.

Dr Ravi Rannan-Eliya. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzed

11:42am - Session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities

The session on South and South-East Asia’s current realities has now begun.

11:30am- Scaling Up Nutrition movement official highlights its progress

Asia Regional Representative of the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement Dr Srikanth Eadara spoke about the objectives of the movement, which he said was comprised of 67 countries and was a country-led global nutrition advocacy platform.

“It unites different stakeholders coming from civil society, private sector, donors, UN, agencies and other entities as well as youth to end malnutrition,” he said, adding that it was launched in 2013 to “ ensure a coordinated multisectoral and multi-stakeholder action to address malnutrition in all its forms”.

“We are currently in the fourth phase of the SUN Movement, and it is based on the current challenges and current context of nutrition, which shows that, yes, there is progress; however, the progress is slow and uneven,” he noted.

Dr Eadara also spoke of the issues surrounding nutrition finance, highlighting that the cost of malnutrition was “estimated to be around 5 to 11pc of the total GDPs of Asia and Africa”.

He warned that recent funding cuts, particularly in the World Health Organisation have “threatened to reverse progress” made on nutrition.

“The reduction will also result in increased hardships and deaths, with a lot of implications for public health and economic growth and stability,” he said.

11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’

Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow.

“Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said.

11:20am - Social protection can address malnutrition, says WFP official

The WFP official spoke of one of the three priorities the organisation held for its work in South Asia was advocacy for policy engagement.

She explained, “this is a continuous effort to work with governments from South Asia to highlight how social protection can be more than a safety net and more than a poverty reduction instrument”.

Hobbs said that with the right intentions, social protection held promise to improve nutrition, diets and address malnutrition.

“This is because social protection already reaches the families that are the most vulnerable and those are the families that face the highest challenges,” she added.

Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

11:12am: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries

Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs, in her address, spoke of the geographical realities of stunting, stating that the majority of children affected by stunting are from middle-income countries.

“Over 80pc of the world’s stunted children are in middle-income countries,” she said.

The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.”

She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”.

11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone.

“Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said.

“Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said.

11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition.

“Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty … are affecting food and health systems,” he said.

He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience.

“Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems.

10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins

The session on global and regional realities has now begun.

10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting.

“Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said.

She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes.

“Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said.

ernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, addresses the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”.

“When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. We are talking about whether a child reaches their full potential. We are talking about the strength of Pakistan’s capital. Nutrition is not only a health issue, it’s a development issue, an economic issue and an issue of equity and opportunity,” she said.

She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases.

10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations

Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations.

“When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required.

10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food.

“It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said.

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus’ video message plays during the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity.

“Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action.

10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today.

“It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said.

“We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action.

“Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said.

10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity

“Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. There can be no knowledge economy without developing the capacity of the human brain. There can be no productivity revolution without healthy and capable workers. There can be no genuine equality if inequality begins before a child is even born,” said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal.

“Therefore, investment in nutrition is not charity, it is economic policy,” he said.

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal addresses the conference as the guest speaker. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. He appreciated the initiative by DawnMedia Group to address the nutrition crisis and called on civil society to take up social issues.

“90 per cent of a children’s brain develops by the age of five .. so the first five years in the life of a child are the most critical,” he said.

“If we fail to develop that human infrastructure during the earliest years of life, we weaken every other investment we subsequently make,” he said.

“That is why stunting cannot remain merely a statistic. For the planning minister, it is a national development challenge,” he said.

9:57am - Planning minister says quality of human resource critical for countries

In his remarks, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, the chief guest, conveyed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s firm commitment to addressing malnutrition and stunting as a national development priority.

He said that as the planning minister, he spent much of his time dealing with the architecture of Pakistan’s development.

“We discuss motorways, energy, dams and digital networks. All of these are essential, but there is one investment more fundamental than all others: the investment in human development,” he said.

“Ultimately it is humans and people who build nations. Therefore, the quality of human resource is critical for any country,” he said.

9:55am - Dawn CEO says nutrition crisis does not ‘look the same’ across the country

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said the nutrition crisis did not “look the same in Tharparkar as it does in Chitral or in southern Punjab”, adding that the response could not be the same either.

“You will hear the economics of financing nutrition, the science of why children fail to grow even when food is technically available, and, I hope, the voices of the women and the mothers who carry the heaviest share of this burden and are so rarely asked to speak about it,” she said.

“With all those who have a role to play gathered around the same table, we have an opportunity to move from recognition of the scale of the problem towards urgent, coordinated and measurable action — action that can improve maternal and child nutrition, strengthen Pakistan’s human capital, and give future generations the opportunity to grow, learn and thrive,” she said.

“That is what this conference ultimately aims to achieve: to build a shared understanding of what needs to be done, and to begin charting a clear and practical roadmap for how we get there,” she added.

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani addresses the conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad

9:53am - Dawn CEO says nutrition not a problem for health ministry to solve alone

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that Pakistan loses close to $17 billion a year to the consequences of malnutrition, “more than what we typically borrow from the International Monetary Fund in any given year”.

“We spend enormous energy negotiating that borrowing. We spend comparatively little energy addressing a loss nearly as large, happening quietly, inside our own households,” she said.

“So this conference starts from a simple premise: nutrition is not a problem for a health ministry to solve alone. It sits at the intersection of health, agriculture, water, education, social protection, our economy and ultimately, our national security,” she added.

She said that countries such as Bangladesh, Peru, and Rwanda had demonstrated that stunting can be dramatically reduced within a generation, but “only when a nation decides, at the highest levels, that the future of its children is important enough to make it a collective priority”.

9:52am - Dawn CEO calls stunting crisis ‘a national emergency’

In her welcome remarks, Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that four out of every ten children under the age of five in Pakistan were stunted.

“These are children whose physical growth and cognitive development may be permanently compromised – often before they have spoken their first words, entered a classroom or had the slightest chance to even dream of their own future,” she said.

“And when this is the reality for four out of every ten children in our country, we cannot merely call it a health problem. It is a national emergency – and a profound failure of our collective priorities,” she said.

9:45am - Conference begins

The conference has begun with the playing of the national anthem and the recitation of the Holy Quran.

World.title: Pakistan 'hopeful' despite US-Iran escalation, will continue to strive for dialogue and diplomacy: FO
World.content:
Foreign Office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said on Wednesday that Pakistan remained “hopeful” despite recent escalations between the US and Iran and would continue to strive for dialogue and diplomacy.

Pakistan has been spearheading efforts for an end to the ongoing war that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February.

Besides signing the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding as the mediator in June, Islamabad had also brokered a ceasefire between the US and Iran in April. The April ceasefire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks, mainly around the Strait of Hormuz, have dimmed the prospects of a final peace agreement.

Recapping Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts in this connection over the week, the FO spokesperson recalled that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of an SCO summit earlier this week and discussed the evolving regional situation.

“The prime minister had reiterated Pakistan’s commitment to peace through restraint, dialogue and diplomacy, while stressing that the Islamabad MoU offered the most viable pathway to lasting peace and stability in the region,” he said.

He said Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also interacted with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the SCO summit, while Pakistan and Iran’s leadership had earlier discussed the Middle East and Gulf situation in Istanbul on the sidelines of the Makkah defence pact meeting.

Andrabi added that Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) Field Marshal Asim Munir had also visited Tehran last week as part of Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to facilitate an end to the US-Iran conflict, particularly reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital passageway for the world’s fuel supply.

“Regional de-escalation, breaking the military stalemate and exploring a negotiated settlement to restore regional peace and stability were the main topics discussed” during the meeting, he said.

The visit, he said, “underscored Islamabad’s sincere and constructive role in bridging differences between Washington and Tehran”. It generated momentum, as evident by the subsequent visits of Oman and Qatar’s leadership to Iran, he added.

Pakistan welcomes Hague court ruling on IWT

During the briefing, the FO also spoke about the Permanent Court of Arbitration’s (PCA) decision on Monday, under which it directed India to uphold the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) with Pakistan and suspend work on a hydro project in occupied Kashmir.

He said the PCA had reaffirmed that the IWT remained fully enforced and binding, rejecting India’s unilateral attempt to place the treaty in a so-called “abeyance”.

“The unanimous award of the Court of Arbitration constitutes an important reaffirmation of the sanctity of the IWT and the rule of international law,” he said.

Water and the IWT remain a contentious issue between India and Pakistan, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year — a move that was followed by a brief military conflict between the two sides in May 2025.

Following India’s move, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

In its order, the PCA backed Pakistan’s stance, declaring that the IWT between the two countries remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement.

The FO spokesperson said, “The court had confirmed that India’s purported decision to place the treaty in abeyance does not relieve it of its obligations under the treaty and the treaty’s dispute settlement mechanism remained operative.”

Moreover, he continued, the court’s interim measure concerning the Ratle hydroelectric power project further affirmed that rights and obligations under the treaty could not be altered or displaced through unilateral action, he added.

“Pakistan welcomes this clear and authoritative announcement, which validates our consistent position that differences concerning the Indus Waters Treaty must be strictly addressed within the framework of the treaty and in accordance with international law,” he said.

Concluding his opening statement, he introduced Ambassador Sajjad Haider Khan to his audience and said the latter would replace him as the FO spokesperson after the briefing.

World.title: Pakistan, Kyrgyzstan agree to boost bilateral trade to $200m in two years
World.content:
Pakistan and Kyrgyzstan signed an agreement on Wednesday to boost their bilateral trade to $200 million in two years.

The agreement was signed in Bishkek before Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and his delegation wound up their three-day visit to Kyrgyzstan.

Addressing the signing ceremony, PM Shehbaz said the two sides had initially signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to expand their bilateral trade to $200m.

But, he continued, “I suggested that an agreement should be signed instead of an MoU as it would be a concrete step to achieve [the target of] $200m trade.”

The prime minister said he requested Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov to consider this possibility and he agreed. Subsequently, an agreement was signed at the airport, he added.

Earlier in the day, the PM addressed a joint briefing alongside the Kyrgyz president, where he had announced the plan to expand bilateral trade between the two countries.

“To this end, we will be working on a comprehensive plan of practical measures aimed at gradually increasing bilateral trade to $200 million, improving trade mechanisms, promoting joint investment projects, strengthening industrial cooperation and expanding direct business-to-business contacts,” he said after the two countries signed multiple memoranda (MoU) of understanding.

He said he had noted during their meeting prior to the briefing that currently, bilateral trade between Pakistan and Kyrgyzstan stood at around $16 million, which, he said, was “not a patch on our friendship and our very strong relations.”

He recalled that during his talks with President Zhaparov, he had noted that “our present-day bilateral trade stands at around $16m, which is not a patch on our friendship and our very strong relations”.

“Today, we should have signed not an MoU but an agreement to make sure that in the next two years we increase our bilateral trade from $16m to $200m per annum. And this is not a very difficult task. Let us convert this MoU straight away into an agreement, if you kindly agree, after this meeting,” he added.

He said the two had held talks focused on economic cooperation and agreed that “our economic partnership must now move to a more practical and result-oriented stage”.

The prime minister further stated, “We welcome greater engagement between Pakistani businesses and financial institutions and their Kyrgyz counterparts to carry forward our shared vision of enhancing our bilateral economic cooperation.”

PM Shehbaz said connectivity remained central to the two countries’ shared vision of closer economic integration between South and Central Asia.

“We welcome the signing of the agreement on transit trade, which will help facilitate trade, improve logistics and create new opportunities for regional connectivity,” he added.

He said the two sides had also reaffirmed the importance of effectively implementing the quadrilateral agreement on traffic and transit and agreed to work towards simplifying transport, customs and administrative procedures.

“Energy cooperation is another very important pillar of our partnership,” he said, adding that the two sides had reaffirmed the importance of timely implementation of the Casa-1000 project and welcomed the establishment of a joint working group on energy to develop practical cooperation in the areas of electricity, hydropower, renewable energy, energy infrastructure and modern technologies.

“I am pleased that our two sides have expanded cooperation in education, science and technology, health, culture and tourism,” he further stated.

“We warmly welcomed the establishment of sister-city ties between Osh and Lahore,” he said, describing them as two ancient cities whose iconic landmarks reflected their rich history and cultural heritage.

PM Shehbaz said security and defence cooperation had also featured prominently in their discussions. The two sides reaffirmed their resolve to strengthen cooperation in the fight against terrorism, extremism and other contemporary threats, he added.

The two leaders also discussed regional and international issues of mutual concern, in addition to bilateral matters, PM Shehbaz said.

The prime minister said the two sides had agreed to deepen cooperation on environmental issues and concurred that effective multilateralism was key to resolving the priority issues of the day and achieving global peace and security.

“We remain committed to working together at the UN and other multilateral fora,” he said. “Pakistan regards the Kyrgyz Republic as its most important and valued partner in Central Asia, and we mean it.”

He told President Zhaparov he hoped that his visit marked the beginning of many more such interactions between the two countries. PM Shehbaz also invited President Zhaparov to visit Pakistan at a mutually convenient time.

Earlier in his address, he thanked the Kyrgyz president and the government and people of Kyrgyzstan for a “warm welcome and generous hospitality extended to me and my delegation”.

He further congratulated the people of Kyrgyzstan on behalf of the people of Pakistan on their independence day.

PM Shehbaz also extended felicitations to Kyrgyzstan for hosting the sixth World Nomad Games, on its election as a non-permanent of the United Nations Security Council for 2027-28 and on its successful chairmanship of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in 2025–2026.

“We are also very happy that Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar and his team worked tirelessly for your election as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council,” he said, adding that it was “heartening to witness Kyrgyzstan’s remarkable progress and development under your (President Zhaparov) energetic leadership”.

He added that Kyrgyzstan had also made “impressive economic gains and taken meaningful steps to translate this progress into an improved quality of life through expanded public services and targeted support for vulnerable communities”,

“I fully share your commitment to deepening cooperation between our two countries and strengthening the bonds between our two peoples in pursuit of our shared interests and broader goals of peace and cooperation among nations.

“And in this regard, I commend the positive and constructive spirit of our discussions held today, which culminated in the signing of several MoUs aimed at expanding bilateral cooperation and economic exchanges for the mutual benefit of our countries and our peoples,” he said.

The Kyrgyz president also spoke alongside PM Shehbaz at a ceremony, delivering his remarks in Kyrgyz. According to a translation carried by state-run Radio Pakistan, he said that “at a time when international tensions are increasing, strengthening friendship, deepening mutual understanding and developing cooperation are more important than ever”.

He said the joint statement signed after their talks reflected a shared vision for further strengthening Kyrgyz-Pakistani relations and identified key areas of cooperation.

Zhaparov said the economy should be “one of the main pillars” of the bilateral partnership and that the two countries had agreed to take steps to boost bilateral trade, expand the range of traded goods and attract investment.

The Kyrgyz president further stated that the two sides were ready to undertake joint projects in pharmaceuticals, agriculture, energy, light industry, tourism, the digital economy, virtual assets and other fields.

Zhaparov said Pakistan’s seaports offered Kyrgyzstan a natural route to South Asian markets and global trade routes.

He said the two countries had traditionally maintained close cooperation at the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the Economic Cooperation Organisation.

He also congratulated Pakistan on assuming the chairmanship of the SCO. Both leaders signed a joint statement encompassing the discussions and goals of Prime Minister Shehbaz’s visit to Bishkek.

The Foreign Office (FO) later issued a joint statement by the two countries, which added that the two leaders also condemned terrorist attacks in the region and beyond and “stressed the significance of stability, safety and security in Afghanistan as an important condition for realising the vision of seamless connectivity between South Asia and Central Asia”.

“In this regard, both leaders reiterated that Afghan territory should not be used for activities that pose threats to the security of other countries, in accordance with its international obligations,” it added.

The two sides agreed that a secure and conducive environment was necessary to realise the enormous potential for cooperation and connectivity between South Asia and Central Asia.

The statement further said the Pakistani side “reaffirmed its support for international initiatives of the Kyrgyz Republic aimed at advancing the global mountain agenda, sustainable development of mountain regions and adaptation to climate change, including the holding of the Second Mountain Summit Bishkek +25 in 2027”.

MoUs signed

Earlier, PM Shehbaz and President Zhaparov witnessed the ceremony where the representatives from both sides exchanged the pre-signed documents.

The two sides signed a diplomatic Programme of Cooperation between their foreign ministries for 2026-27 besides an MoU between the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad and the National Institute for Strategic Initiatives of the Kyrgyz Republic to strengthen research collaboration.

Both countries also finalised agreements on transit trade to facilitate bilateral commercial movement and promote science and technological cooperation, besides signing a treaty on extradition, the APP report said.

The governments of both countries formulated a draft agreement on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters, and an MoU was signed between the interior ministries of Pakistan and Kyrgyz Republic to combat the illicit trafficking of narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances, precursor chemicals, and related issues.

The Kyrgyz health ministry and Pakistan Medical and Dental Council signed an MoU focused on cooperation in medical education while another MoU was signed between the education ministries of both countries to promote cooperation in the field of education.

The Kyrgyz Ministry of Natural Resources, Ecology and Technical Supervision and Pakistan’s Ministry of Climate Change and Environmental Coordination signed an MoU to strengthen cooperation in the field of environment and climate change.

Moreover, Pakistan, National Defence University and the National Institute for Strategic Initiatives of the Kyrgyz Republic signed an MoU for academic research and cooperative activities.

The National Agency for Virtual Assets and Blockchain Technologies under the Kyrgyz President and the Pakistan Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority signed an MoU for cooperation in virtual assets.

Pakistan and Kyrgyzstan also signed an agreement on the establishment of a sister city relationship between Lahore and Osh city of Kyrgyzstan.

Furthermore, OJSC Kyrgyz Post and Pakistan Post reached a bilateral agreement for mutually beneficial cooperation in postal services and e-commerce while another agreement was signed between the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of the Kyrgyz Republic and the Federation of Pakistan Chamber of Commerce and Industry on cooperation to boost bilateral business ties.

Pakistan and the Kyrgyz Republic also signed multiple bilateral accords to enhance cooperation in security, education, environment and technology sectors.

PM’s arrival at presidential palace

PM Shehbaz had reached Bishkek on Monday, primarily to attend a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit that concluded on Tuesday.

He visited the presidential palace, Yntymak Ordo, today for his engagement with the Kyrgyz president and was given red-carpet welcome and a guard of honour upon his arrival, a statement by Pakistan’s government said.

“He was warmly received by President Zhaparov [and] the national anthems of Pakistan and Kyrgyzstan were played as the two leaders stood at the salute dais.

“The smartly-turned out contingents of the Kyrgyz armed forces presented the guard of honour,” the statement detailed.

Both leaders introduced their respective delegations to each other before proceeding for their meeting, it added.

According to the statement, PM Shehbaz later visited the Ata Beyit Memorial Complex in Bishkek, where he was received by Kyrgyzstan’s First Deputy Prime Minister Daniar Amangeldiev and Minister of Culture, Information and Youth Mirbek Mambetaliyev.

The prime minister laid a wreath at the grave of renowned Kyrgyz writer Chingiz Aitmatov and offered Fateha, it added.

Later, the prime minister also visited Ala Archa National Park in Bishkek, accompanied by President Zhaparo, the statement said.

During the visit, a demonstration of Kyrgyz culture and traditional activities, including cultural dances and other traditional arts, was presented to the prime minister, it added.

Describing Kyrgyzstan’s cultural traditions as admirable, PM Shehbaz emphasised the importance of further strengthening the historical, cultural and fraternal ties between the peoples of the two countries, according to the statement.

World.title: Uzma files another contempt plea in SC, this time over 'failure' to facilitate meetings between Imran and his family
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Dr. Uzma Khan, the sister of incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan, filed a contempt plea in the Supreme Court (SC) on Wednesday against government functionaries, including Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, accusing them of violating the court’s earlier directives to arrange the PTI founder’s meetings with his family and phone calls with his sons.

The interim order was issued on August 18, when the SC had directed the relevant authorities to move Imran to Shifa International Hospital for a medical check-up, as well as facilitate meetings between Imran and his family members once a week and phone calls with his sons twice a week.

Uzma filed a second contempt plea in connection with the order on Wednesday, earlier having approached the court on August 22 for contempt proceedings against those responsible for taking Imran to the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) instead of Shifa International Hospital.

Filed through Advocate Uzair Karamat Bhandari, the plea requested the court to treat the contents of the first petition as an integral part of the second one.

As in the first petition, Islamabad Chief Commissioner (retired) Lieutenant Sohail Ashraf, Interior Secretary Ahmed Raza Sarwar, Punjab Inspector General Prisons Mian Salik Jalal, Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif have been named as respondents in the second plea as well.

The plea explained the nomination of PM Shehbaz, saying that he was the chief executive of the federation. It then referred to the 2012 case of the appointment of Adnan Khawaja as the managing director of the Oil and Gas Development Company Limited (OGDCL), in which it was held that: “[In the] brazen and blatant failure or refusal of the federal government to obey and execute the relevant judgement and directions of the Supreme Court, the buck stops at the office of the chief executive of the federation i.e. the prime minister.”

The decision led to the conviction of then-prime minister Yousaf Raza Gilani, through a judgement following contempt proceedings, the plea recalled.

The petition argued that the same principle should be applied to the present case, leading to the same result.

“Whereas the rest of the respondents were primarily responsible for implementing the order, they have failed to discharge that responsibility. As such, each of the respondents is liable for being proceeded for contempt of this court,” the petition contended.

The plea said that as per the SC’s Aug 10 order, the respondents were required to arrange weekly meetings between Imran and his family members, including the petitioner, as well as phone calls with his sons twice a week.

However, these directives had been “blatantly violated” by the respondents, the petition alleged, adding that during the last 14 days, since the issuance of the order, the respondents had only allowed Imran two meetings with one of his sisters, Noreen Niazi — first on Aug 18 and then on Aug 25.

None of the other family members, including Uzma, had been allowed to meet him since the passing of the Aug 18 order, the petition said.

Similarly, the respondents “have failed to arrange phone calls between Imran Khan and his sons, who have not been allowed to speak to him since March”, it added.

The petition highlighted that the directives in the Aug 18 order were “clear, unambiguous, unequivocal and fully capable of implementation”. They were issued in the presence of the Islamabad advocate general and the additional attorney general of Pakistan. “No portion thereof requires any further interpretation, clarification or modification,” the petition stated.

Consequently, the respondents being the officials responsible for putting the directions into effect, were “under an absolute legal obligation to comply with the order in letter and spirit”, the petition argued.

It contended that the refusal on part of the respondents to arrange and facilitate such meetings and phone calls “leaves no manner of doubt that they have consciously chosen to disregard and violate the Aug 18 order”.

“This is a case of deliberate and wilful disobedience and violation of the order, interference with the process of law and obstruction of the judicial process. The respondents’ conduct has the effect of undermining and lowering the authority of this court and of bringing it into disrespect, ridicule and contempt.

“Such conduct warrants cognisance of the matter by the Supreme Court,” the petition said.

Imran has been imprisoned since Aug 5, 2023, for concealing details of Toshakhana gifts. He is serving a 14-year sentence at Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail in a £190 million corruption case, also known as the Al-Qadir Trust case .

Despite an order by the Islamabad High Court (IHC) allowing him twice-a-week meetings on Tuesdays and Thursdays with his family, lawyers and other associates, Imran was restricted from meeting visitors for several months before the passing of the new SC order.

The PTI founder’s sisters were once again denied a meeting with him on Tuesday, although Noreen Niazi had been allowed to meet him twice in August. Before last month’s order and subsequent meetings between Noreen and Imran, the last confirmed meeting of the PTI founder was with Uzma on Dec 2, 2025, and he had also previously met with Noreen on Nov 4 last year.

Last week, the SC registrar’s office had turned down Uzma’s first request for an early hearing of the contempt petition and turned down another request on Tuesday. The petition has been fixed before a three-member SC bench, comprising Justice Shahid Waheed, Justice Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Justice Ishtiaq Ibrahim, for Sept 16.

World.title: Iran targets American assets in Middle East after vowing 'severe' consequences for fresh wave of US strikes
World.content:
Iran pushed ahead with strikes targeting American interests around the Middle East on Wednesday after vowing “severe” consequences to a fresh wave of US attacks.

The latest flare-up is part of a cycle of retaliation that followed US strikes on Iran, with fighting over the Hormuz strait expanding to Washington’s Gulf allies, military bases and commercial shipping.

Tehran said it launched ballistic missile attacks on two US bases in Jordan, according to Iranian media.

Washington did not immediately comment on the reports, although US President Donald Trump had warned earlier of “much harder and higher” attacks if Iran retaliated to US strikes.

The Jordanian army said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired from Iran, and did not confirm any injuries or hits. Three other missiles landed in remote areas, it said.

Missile and drone attacks were also reported in Kuwait, where the army said they were responding to Iranian hostilities, and AFP reporters in Bahrain heard alert sirens for airborne attacks ring out early on Wednesday.

Iran’s army said it launched drone attacks targeting US forces at an air base in Bahrain, a key Washington ally in the Gulf.

In Iraq’s autonomous Kurdistan region, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday that they struck US bases with missiles and drones, destroying a maintenance centre, warehouses and equipment, state-run IRNA reported.

The latest round of conflict began when Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday, the first known strikes in several weeks, after which Tehran’s forces targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks.

More US strikes came on Tuesday, with Iranian state television reporting explosions in the country’s south along the Hormuz strait and on an island in the Gulf, and that US forces hit an airport in the southern province of Kerman.

The Iranian Red Crescent said shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a home where a wedding celebration was taking place in the city of Kuhestak, killing four people, including a child, and wounding more than 50.

Later, Iranian state media reported that seven people died and eight were injured in an attack in the southwestern province of Khuzestan.

IRNA also reported that “four projectiles hit areas within the counties of Chabahar and Konarak”, without specifying whether there was any damage.

Trump said the “large and powerful” strikes were “in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait” and “the Iranians shooting eight missiles, all successfully knocked down, at our Military Base in Jordan”.

He later said on Truth Social that he was “not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table” and asked: “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”

Earlier, Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi warned that Washington “will regret its new attacks”, saying that “severe punishment awaits the aggressors”.

And Ebrahim Zolfaghari, the spokesperson for Iran’s Khatam-al Anbiya central military command, warned on Wednesday that “any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army will face more severe, more widespread and destructive responses”.

The US military said Tuesday’s strikes followed “attempted attacks by (the Revolutionary Guards) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region”, the US Central Command (Centcom) wrote on X.

Asked if the US military had received any credible reports of civilian casualties in the attacks, Centcom spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins said “the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC”.

Tanker attacks

After six months of war, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed and the United States persisting with a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

Washington said its forces attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak on Sunday to prevent Tehran from planting mines in the strait’s key shipping lanes.

The Middle East war began in late February with US-Israeli attacks on Iran that assassinated its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

A fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran collapsed after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies flowed before the war.

Greek maritime risk management firm Marisks said on Tuesday that two crude tankers were hit by “unknown projectiles” late the previous day.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency registered one of the incidents earlier, adding that no casualties or environmental effects had been reported.

Despite the diplomatic deadlock, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian vowed on Tuesday to match any US move to return to a deal aimed at ending the war.

He also warned that a return by the United States to “a policy of pressure and threats could derail the path of diplomacy”.

World.title: PIA to increase weekly flights to London from four to seven from Oct 27
World.content:
Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) on Wednesday said that it would be increasing its weekly flights to London from four to seven starting October 27.

Under the new schedule, five flights would depart from Islamabad while two would operate on the Lahore-London route, the airline said in a statement.

“The increase in the number of flights reflects passenger confidence and rising demand,” the statement added.

Pakistani flights had been banned from flying to the European Union, the United Kingdom and the US in June 2020, after one of its aircraft crashed in Karachi, killing nearly 100 people on board.

The European Union Air Safety Agency had barred PIA from operating in EU countries over safety concerns, and the ban on flights followed then-aviation minister Ghulam Sarwar Khan’s statement on the floor of parliament, where he termed pilots’ licences “dubious”.

The European agency lifted the ban after more than four years on Nov 28, 2024. In July 2025, the UK also removed Pakistan from its Air Safety List, allowing Pakistani airlines to apply to operate flights in Britain.

In September 2025, PIA received approval to resume direct flights to the UK after a gap of nearly five years. The airline subsequently restarted operations, with Manchester becoming the first destination .

In March, PIA also resumed direct flights to London.

World.title: 'We had to do this to set his soul free': Families hold symbolic funerals in Nepal for missing flood victims
World.content:
Nepali families held symbolic funerals on Wednesday to “liberate the souls” of relatives missing since deadly flash floods swept away their villages and homes in the Himalayan region a week ago.

Emergency teams have recovered more than 1,100 bodies, and nearly 4,500 people are missing after the gigantic wave of freezing water, rocks and debris triggered by a high-altitude glacial collapse roared down the China-Nepal border on August 26.

After days of searching shelters and mortuaries, relatives of some of the missing lost hope and began conducting last rites, burning straw effigies in Hindu rituals.

“We had to do this to set his soul free, so that he is at peace and happy wherever he is,” said Dolma Newar Tamang, flanked by her sobbing son, at a funeral for her husband.

He had been en route to China when the disaster struck.

“I saw the news and called him,” she told AFP.

“I called repeatedly, but he never picked up.”

Relatives mourn during symbolic funerals held for flood victims still reported missing as they cremate Kush grass effigies in accordance with Nepali Hindu rites at Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu on September 2, 2026. — AFP

A week on from the colossal disaster, Nepali rescuers are still seeking survivors, including by digging through packed sludge that has entombed multiple tunnels of hydropower plants.

So far, rescuers have recovered only bodies from tunnels, but teams were still digging, drilling and blasting through debris.

Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said he still hoped some missing could be alive.

“Miracles do happen,” he told AFP.

“At this point, I do not want to completely give up hope.”

Global responsibility

There is growing anger at the scale of destruction to hit Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people.

The country has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming, but is among those suffering its consequences.

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah warned the catastrophe was “a serious indication” of the risks the Himalayan nation faces.

Scientists say the Himalayas, the world’s highest mountain range, are warming rapidly as global temperatures rise, accelerating glacier melt.

Glaciers in the wider Himalayan and Hindu Kush ranges are a crucial water source for around 240m people in the mountainous regions, as well as for another 1.65 billion people in the South Asian and Southeast Asian river valleys below.

“Climate change is a global contribution, and disaster response is also a global responsibility,” Shah said in a social media post.

Kathmandu has warned reconstruction could cost billions of dollars.

Nepal, which marks a year this month since deadly mass protests over rampant corruption and a woeful economy overthrew the then government, has limited resources to respond to a disaster of this scale.

In an illustration of the scale of destruction, Chinese state media said road access to hard-hit Gyirong Port in Tibet had finally been restored on Wednesday after “days of round-the-clock repair work”.

Mass burials

With mortuaries overflowing in Nepal, authorities have had to bury hundreds of unidentified bodies after DNA sampling.

Nepal said 1,114 bodies had been recovered by Wednesday, while 3,916 people remained missing.

China’s state media reported 16 dead and 546 missing.

That takes the overall number of reported dead to 1,130, and 4,462 missing.

Security personnel stand next to unidentified bodies of flood victims kept for mass burial at the Gokarna forest reserve in Kathmandu on September 1, 2026. — AFP

More than 800 foreigners from over 30 nations are among the missing: 583 in Nepal and 261 in China.

They include tourists who came to trek in the Himalayas, as well as Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash.

At least 17 bodies have also been pulled from rivers downstream in India.

In China, foreign journalists are restricted from reporting in Tibet, and Chinese authorities have a tight grip on information sources in the region.

Tibetan advocacy groups in exile have questioned China’s account of the disaster, but Beijing insists that the “release of information has been open, transparent and timely”.

World.title: Pakistan launches dual-tranche Eurobond offering
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan on Tuesday launched the process for a US dollar-denominated benchmark dual-tranche Eurobond offering with five-year and 10-year tenors, as the government seeks to deepen its return to international capital markets following recent sovereign rating upgrades.

Adviser to the Finance Minister Khurram Schehzad said in a post on X that the proposed transaction was subject to market conditions and represented another step in Pakistan’s renewed access to international capital markets.

The size of the proposed issuance, pricing and final yields are yet to be announced and will depend on investor demand and prevailing market conditions. Mr Schehzad said the transaction followed improvements in Pakistan’s sovereign credit ratings and macroeconomic indicators and reflected the country’s growing engagement with international investors.

The latest move comes less than five months after Pakistan returned to the international bond market following a four-year absence.

Minister’s aide calls it another step in country’s renewed access to global capital markets

In April, the government initially raised $500 million through a three-year Eurobond under its Global Medium-Term Note (GMTN) Programme at a coupon of 6.975pc. The issue was subsequently increased to $750m through a $250m green-shoe option after stronger-than-expected investor demand. The bond matures in April 2029.

Pakistan has also repaid a $1.4 billion Eurobond that matured in April, allowing the government to re-establish a pricing benchmark in international debt markets after several years of relying heavily on multilateral, bilateral and commercial financing.

On Tuesday, S&P also assigned a ‘B’ rating to Pakistan’s GMTN programme and the proposed benchmark US dollar notes, in line with the sovereign rating.

Fitch Ratings also assigned the GMTN programme a ‘B-’ rating with a Recovery Rating of ‘RR4’, in line with the country’s long-term sovereign rating.

The latest offering extends the maturity profile beyond the three-year tenor used in April, with the proposed five- and 10-year tranches providing a test of investors’ willingness to hold Pakistani sovereign debt for longer periods.

Published in Dawn, September 2nd, 2026

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets."
