Sure, fix the roads. Then what? Stop building the SRL? Then what? If the LNP wants Victorians to back them for more than one term, they’ll need to do more heavy lifting than they’re offering.

Frank Flynn, Cape Paterson Seen in contempt

Another day, another damning article, (″⁣Another Victorian era is set to crash″⁣, 2/8). I was a Labor supporter for most of my adult life because I was attracted to the values the party purportedly stood for. But no longer. For all the reasons Shaun Carney outlines and more, I am now firmly one of the 75 per cent of voters who hold this government in contempt.

Ivan Glynn, Vermont PM, turn off the taps

Of course Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ducked a question on whether the world shared collective responsibility for the climate change-driven disaster in the Himalayas (“Nepalese know only too well the devastating dangers of climate change as reality hits”, 2/9). He knows Australia is failing its climate commitments. Despite promising action and progressing well with the renewable energy roll-out, the Albanese government continues to enable and promote the coal, oil and gas that drives climate change and all the disasters it is bringing.

Nowhere is immune. Even my home state of Tasmania has had its warmest winter on record and is at higher risk of bushfires this spring (“Melbourne records its warmest winter on record”, 2/9). If Albanese wants credibility on climate, he needs to back our Pacific neighbours and start to turn off the coal and gas tap.

Sharee McCammon, Pelverata, Tas Energy policy folly

On Monday, after celebrating its win in the Secret Harbour electorate in WA, One Nation announced its energy plans for Victoria outside the Loy Yang A power station in Gippsland. These plans would be a disaster for Victorians. One Nation plans to keep Loy Yang A station running, which is owned by AGL and planned for closure in 2035 due to its age and being no longer able to compete against the cheap renewable electricity now available from wind and solar. The station is 50-years-old and has enormous maintenance costs. One Nation says it will shut down the planned expansion of wind farms and hopes to introduce nuclear power as the main form of baseload electricity. The CSIRO and energy experts have all warned this would be far too costly and take too long, not to mention the problem of storing the radioactive waste.

Victorians have every right to be dissatisfied with the way the state is being run by the Labor government but One Nation would increase state debt. We are blessed with renewable energy assets, solar being the cheapest way to make electricity that humans have invented. The world would take us for fools if we neglected this opportunity.

Derek Ryan, North Geelong



Stop stoking fear

Waleed Aly (Comment, 28/8) recently wrote that to One Nation and sadly its supporters, details don’t matter. This was chillingly accurate. It doesn’t matter that Pauline Hanson, Barnaby Joyce and David Farley espouse different numbers on their immigration policy or that they have no coherent education, health and aged care, foreign affairs and trade or social services policies.

Some of the media’s failure to scrutinise One Nation to the same degree as is done to Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor and the constant portrayal of a country in ″⁣crisis″⁣ has fed the masses. Even though we still face challenges, you wouldn’t know we still have a triple A credit rating, envious universal healthcare including a life-saving PBS. Public education remains strong as do opportunities in multiple fields of employment. Ironically, we are have arguably the world’s most successful multicultural society, although One Nation exploits this as a division rather than economic, cultural and societal strength, as it is. But once again, details and facts don’t matter for some, but you’d hope sections of the media would do better than to stoke fear and anxiety.

Craig Jory, Albury, NSW Joy of live music

David Crowe’s tribute to the live music he enjoyed in a Dublin pub struck a chord with me (″⁣Traditional music still strikes chord for fans″⁣, 1/9). I am lucky enough to live near the Merri Creek Tavern in High Street, Westgarth, where there is an old-time music jam every Saturday afternoon. There fiddlers are joined by guitarists and banjo players, the man with the double bass and one playing the mouth organ. The group of players can add up to between a dozen and 20. The music spills into the street and passers-by stop for a while to listen, with some even venturing in.

May it continue to give us joy.

Janna McCurdy, Northcote News from the street

On Sunday, I fell on the footpath and then fainted. I came to with three concerned strangers around me, one ringing for an ambulance. Two men and one woman, they all stayed with me until the ambulance arrived. They deserve the warmest thanks. It was such a good experience, when the news is so full of street violence.

Robin Burns, Ivanhoe Dangers of algorithms

The damage that social media algorithms do is not confined to children and teenagers.

While the belated efforts of government to regulate harmful and addictive business practices is welcome, social media algorithms are still the enabler and amplifier of grievance politics.

Before social media, it was difficult for extreme views to take hold. Now, the scrutiny and fact checking of traditional media can be bypassed by those seeking to harness dissent.

Algorithms that feed on difference and conflict are driving consumption of content by adults that undermines rational debate and threatens democracy.

Turn off the algorithms and the content will wither.

Greg Williams, West Footscray Work for the soul

I can see positive outcomes in involving low-risk prisoners in road maintenance support roles. Prison existence is a dull, aimless, daily grind of nothingness. Some inmates who have almost done the time for their crime are going to be released soon. Rather than a traumatic hit from the mainstream world upon release, an incrementally controlled contact program with the real world would be of great therapeutic value. I reckon it’s a terrific initiative. And satisfies my belief in the philosophy of Jeremy Bentham, whose tenet was ″⁣The greatest good for the greatest number″⁣ is the way to go.

Ray Bannister, Somers



Little meaning

The word science derives from the Latin ″⁣scientia″⁣, which means ″⁣knowledge″⁣, ″⁣awareness″⁣ or ″⁣understanding″⁣. With climate change having catastrophic effects on our planet already, and with worse to come, it’s obvious that with One Nation pushing fossil fuels, they have none of the three above.

George Djoneff, Mitcham State’s black holes

According to many local British councils, a hole becomes a pothole when it measures about 40mm deep and 300mm wide. In Victoria, forget about holes and potholes, we now have superholes to which there’s no limit on size.

Lyn Bayley, Kyneton Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Potholes

With all the discussion about potholes on Victorian roads, I am not reading about the danger to motorcyclists. If you think a pothole is dangerous to car drivers please spare a thought for us on two wheels.

Peter Sherry, Maidstone



Having travelled extensively across Australia, I can assure you that potholes don’t stop at Victoria’s borders.

Kathy Diviny, Coburg One Nation

Pauline Hanson’s coffin representing the end of our emissions reduction pledge is the height of bad taste, given the glacial collapse and loss of lives in Nepal.

Greg Curtin, Nunawading Words have consequences, says Pauline Hanson. Well, yes.

Maureen Goldie, Blackwood, SA Matt Golding’s cartoon (2/9) certainly tells it all. How to vote for nothing.

Doug Shaw, Sunbury Secret Harbour is the latest in a growing list of electorates that have shown there is no such thing as a ″⁣safe″⁣ seat for either Labor or the LNP. Take your electorate for granted and out you go.

Belinda Burke, Hawthorn



Few will vote for One Nation when it expresses support for the cruelty of the live animal export trade.

Ronald Elliott, Sandringham Funny how One Nation has selected orange as its colour when the US has an at-times orange-coloured president.

Michael Brinkman, Ventnor Furthermore

While our planet is either drowning or burning, it’s good to know we can buy a toothbrush that takes film only your dentist can see. And, it’s only $799.

Myra Fisher, Brighton East I’m longing for the day when Niagara Falls becomes Trump Falls.

Tony Andrews, Seacliff, SA Is it too late to turn Dan Andrews’ unfinished statute into Dolly Parton?

Peter Venn, East Bentleigh

World.title: ‘We’ll be a team to the finish,’ said Dom Perrottet of brother Charles. This looks like the finish
World.content:
PoliticsNSWOperation Rosny Opinion ‘We’ll be a team to the finish,’ said Dom Perrottet of brother Charles. This looks like the finish Alexandra Smith Senior writer September 2, 2026 — 7:50pm

September 2, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A fresh-faced Dominic Perrottet had no qualms about playing favourites when it came to his 12 siblings. “I would like to particularly single out my brother Charles, who has worked alongside me in politics,” the newly elected MP for Castle Hill told parliament in 2011 in his inaugural speech. “We have been a team from the start and will be a team to the finish.” It’s highly unlikely that the once-formidable Charlie-and-Dom team, as it has long been known, remains intact. Charles, just 13 months younger than Dominic and the one-time “muscle” of the conservative wing of the withering Liberal Party, is a star of a corruption inquiry. He is also a liar by his own admission. Charles, Dominic and Jean-Claude Perrottet. Former premier Dominic, meanwhile, is in Washington DC with his large family, working for BHP after a dignified loss in the 2023 state election. Time was against Perrottet, as were some shockingly ill-disciplined members of his team, when he attempted to convince voters to give the Coalition another four years in power. Charles is a central figure in the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s wide-ranging inquiry into whether fugitive developer Jean Nassif made illegal political donations to the Liberal Party. And Charles has clearly decided that his best defence is to say he made up rubbish to keep Nassif on side. Not the odd white lie, but repeated fabrications, Charles has told the commission.



He may be confident that argument is sound, given Nassif has a long history of colourful, bordering on erratic, behaviour. This was the man, after all, who gave his then-wife Nissy a yellow Lamborghini for Valentine’s Day several years ago and boasted about it on Instagram: “Congratulations Mrs Nassif. You like?” So while it was a surprise for the many keen ICAC watchers, it was also on-brand when Nassif’s name popped up on the commission’s witness list for this Friday. Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny The 11-word text that exposed a ruthless Liberal Party ‘black op’ It disappeared almost as quickly. A medical certificate from a doctor in Beirut, where Nassif is hiding out to avoid serious fraud charges in Australia, says the disgraced developer is not well enough to appear via video link from Lebanon. He is happy to reschedule, apparently. So that leaves Charles, whose evidence has been extended by an extra two days, to continue insisting that the political fixes he was promising Nassif – from getting rid of the then building commissioner David Chandler and his political nemesis, former police minister David Elliott, to sorting out bothersome councils – were fibs. And why? He was worried that Nassif was being too tardy in paying bills owed to his political apparatchik mates, Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis, who ran the lobbying firm Beckington. “That’s what friends do,” explained Perrottet, a top executive at BP who is contractually obliged not to take on outside work.



The commission’s formidable counsel assisting, Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, has not been buying it. She has reminded him, more than once, that “the great truism about telling a lie, Mr Perrottet, is you have to be really good at remembering it”. There was, however, one refreshing moment in his evidence when Charles said what many of us suspect. “In politics, sometimes you say things to people that aren’t 100 per cent the truth,” he told Dwyer. That did not seem to surprise her. Related Article Updated

Operation Rosny Jean Nassif pulls out of ICAC appearance but vows to reschedule There is an uncanny resemblance between Dominic and Charles, even for brothers. Same voice, same mannerisms, same slim build (although Charles has shed weight). Dominic is not a person of interest and has not been called to give evidence. But there is no doubt that having his family feature in a blockbuster corruption inquiry – the youngest Perrottet brother, Jean-Claude, is also a person of interest – would be making his stomach churn. By all accounts, Dominic had a charmed run in politics. He was the chosen one in the Perrottet family to be elected to parliament and Charles was instrumental in making that happen. Dominic’s first ministry in Mike Baird’s cabinet was the low-risk portfolio of finance, which set him up to be treasurer. When Perrottet wanted to swap seats to Epping (he had already shifted once to Hawkesbury as part of a factional deal), his life-long family friend and fellow right-wing warrior Damien Tudehope stepped in to help. Tudehope shifted to the upper house and surrendered Epping to Perrottet, who worried the commute from Hawkesbury would be too long with a young family.



And Perrottet survived a political near-death experience when Nigel Freitas, his devoted chief of staff, became the casualty in a scandal involving the scandal-ridden insurance body icare. Freitas resigned over revelations that the salaries of two of Perrottet’s ministerial staff were paid by icare. Ultimately, it did not hold Perrottet back. The Perrottet clan in 2000, when all ran in the City to Surf. Dallas Kilponen Eventually, he replaced Gladys Berejiklian as premier in October 2021. And it was his teammate Charles who Dominic credited with his success. “He thanked me for everything. Not just this weekend. But the last 20 years to get here,” Charles told his wife, Anita, in a text message which has formed part of the ICAC inquiry. Anita responded: “Well it’s definitely true that he couldn’t have done it without you!!” Alexandra Smith is a senior writer and former state political editor of The Sydney Morning Herald.

World.title: Fewer Kiwis contracting sexually transmitted diseases
World.content:
The number of New Zealanders contracting sexually transmitted diseases has fallen, a newly released report shows.

Syphilis rates have had the biggest drop - about a quarter - and have fallen everywhere except the South Island.

PHF Science analysis on the country's sexually transmitted disease rates in 2025 shows there were drops across all of the three reported diseases - gonorrhoea, chlamydia and syphilis.

Health authorities had been worried about syphilis when it spiked in 2023 but it was now on the decline.

There were 605 cases of infectious syphilis notified last year, a 27 percent drop the previous year, and the lowest rate since 2022, the report said.

The South Island did not improve on the previous year, however its rate of 11 cases per 100,000 was the same as most of the country.

The Northern region - Auckland and Northland, had 13 cases per 100,000.

For gonorrhea, the rate of cases fell by 17 percent last year, with 6306 cases reported.

The Northern region had the highest rate at 1.7 cases per 1000, with the South Island on the lowest at 0.6 per 1000.

Chlamydia rates were down by 13 percent.

The Northern region had the highest rate of five cases per 1000, and the South Island had the lowest at 3.8 per 1000.

PHF's report said the decrease in STIs was likely due to better prevention, testing and management of contacts.

Some at risk people were sometimes prescribed preventative antibiotics.

The report showed New Zealand had had its first recorded case of a super drug resistant strain of gonorrhoea known as XDR neisseria.

The case was linked to overseas and there had been no transmission in New Zealand but it showed the country needed to keep up good surveillance, the report said.

The number of gonorrhoea cases that were antibiotic-resistant to a lesser degree was growing.

World.title: Earthquakes hit near Milford Sound
World.content:
A series of earthquakes struck near Milford Sound on Wednesday evening, the first hitting soon after 6pm.

They began with a 5.5 magnitude quake at 6.13pm, followed by a 5.6 at 6.57pm.

Those two were followed by weaker quakes - 4.8 at 7.12pm, 4.6 at 7.39pm and 3.8 at 8.05pm.

The first quake hit 40km northeast of Milford Sound. The first two were listed on Geonet as moderate in intensity, while the third and fourth were light and the fifth, weak.

All five were relatively shallow, at five kilometres deep.

Within 10 minutes of the first earthquake, 6000 people had reported feeling it on GeoNet.

Some people on social media described it as a "decent shake", with one person in Invercargill saying they felt a jerk and swaying.

One person in Alexandra described it as "quite scary".

"Loud boom here before the shake arrived."

Another said it was "short and sharp compared to the one a couple of months ago".

"Loud rumble, cracking noise and windows rattled. Something in the pantry fell to the floor."

Historic bridge closed for inspection

Queenstown Lakes District Council said it would close Edith Cavell Bridge overnight

"As this bridge is a historical asset with heritage status, an inspection is required following earthquakes like the one we just experienced," it posted on social media.

Traffic from Arthurs Point will need to detour via Malaghans Road in Dalefield, the council said.

"Engineers will inspect the bridge at first light tomorrow morning and we'll provide a further update when we know more.

"Please also take care around our alpine passes like Crown Range Road as debris caused by the recent earthquake could be possible."

The area has experienced a few light shakes in recent days, of up to magnitude 3.3.

World.title: Reserve Bank hikes official cash rate to 2.75%
World.content:
RBNZ raises official cash rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent

The rate rise followed a similar-sized rise in July and was widely expected

The monetary committee says inflation has likely peaked and a economic recovery is likely to gain pace

A recovering economy does not need same stimulation of low cash rate

At least one more rate rise is expected this year - future rises will be guided by numbers and global events

Further rate rises are expected next year

The Reserve Bank has raised the official cash rate (OCR) for a second meeting in a row to tackle inflation pressures, and has signalled more increases could be coming this year.

The Monetary Policy Committee raised the benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 2.75, percent following a similar sized rise in July.

The move upwards was widely predicted by economists.

The committee said inflation had surged because of the Middle East war, but discounting the spike in fuel prices was on the way down.

"Excluding vehicle fuels, annual CPI inflation decreased to 2.9 percent in the June quarter. Most measures of core inflation are within the 1 to 3 percent target band."

It said higher fuel prices would drop out of the annual inflation calculation, and along with the slack in the economy and gradual rises in the OCR then inflation would hit the desired 2 percent rate by the end of 2027.

It said the economy has shown signs of recovery after being knocked off track by the US-Iran conflict.

"After lacklustre growth in the June quarter, New Zealand's economic recovery has most likely resumed, but remains uneven."

It said strong exports were boosting incomes and investment in parts of the economy and in the regions, which was being offset by weak income growth, job insecurity and flat house prices which were weighing on household spending.

The committee said global events posed risks to recovery and tackling inflation and would be a factor in setting rates.

But it signalled further rate rises to come.

"The committee judges that gradually removing monetary stimulus is appropriate to return inflation to the 2 percent target mid-point while supporting growth and employment.

"Future policy decisions will depend on the committee's judgement of the balance of risks to medium-term inflation."

Reserve Bank hikes official cash rate Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

The committee has two further meetings this year, in October just before the election and December.

Interest rate guidance in the statement suggested at least one more 25 basis point rise to 3 percent by year end, and possibly two more rises by the middle of next year.

'Positive news for New Zealanders'

Finance Minister Nicola Willis told media at Parliament that the central bank's statement showed the "economic recovery broadening" and that job creation and consumer confidence was looking to strengthen in the coming months.

"That is positive news for New Zealanders who are looking forward to more prospects in the months ahead, although we fully acknowledge that the uncertainty in the Middle East is impacting inflation and will remain with us potentially for some time." she

Willis said banks had previously lifted their interest rates in anticipating of OCR hikes but it was important banks "don't get too far ahead of themselves" and "bring on more difficulties to the economy".

"Anyone who's got a mortgage doesn't want to be paying more interest on their mortgage - it's that simple - you don't need to be a chief executive to work that out." she said.

She said she was "very satisfied" with her government's policies aiming to grow the country's economy and New Zealander's were "smarter than some of my opponents give them credit for".

"They know that it's not for Chris Luxon to tell Donald Trump to get out of the Middle East because it's affecting inflation and interest rates here at home, those are decisions for Donald Trump, not for us.

"We need to control what's in our control and we will continue to do so." she said.

ACT leader David Seymour put the blame for rate hike squarely on the "catastrophe" of the Iran War and said it would be a "double catastrophe" if Labour were in power at the same time.

Asked if he feared a "Halloween hike" in October, Seymour said the prospect was "spooky" but ultimately up to the Reserve Bank.

"Standard and Poor has visited, they spoke to a lot of people about the New Zealand economy and they said they're going to put us AA+ with a stable watch.

"That's a very positive thing and so let's see where the Reserve Bank gets to at Halloween, but hopefully they're not going to spook the markets or the election for that matter," he said.

'We like it'

Economists broadly regarded the statement as softer or more 'dovish' than expected, based on the gradual and little changed track for the OCR.

Kiwibank chief economist Jarrod Kerr, a long standing backer of no rate changes to support the economic recovery, was heartened by the decision.

"We like it. Given where we've been, and where we're likely to go, slightly lower interest rates that don't move above a neutral setting, is good news."

He expected one more rise to 3 percent by year end and then a prolonged pause.

ASB senior economist Mark Smith said the central bank decision was the line of least resistance, but it clearly remained wary of inflation risks, and global uncertainty.

He maintained for now ASB's previous forecast of two hikes this year, and m ore next year.

"We expect 25 basis point hikes in October to 3.0 percent and December, with the OCR ending the year at 3.25 percent, which we adjudge to be at broadly neutral levels."

He said the RBNZ might look to increase rates more slowly than expected depending on events and data.

The perceived softness of the statement and unchanged rate track hosed down expectations of the cash rate hitting 4 percent, as some economists were forecasting.

World.title: Family of young woman killed by truck driver fight for law change
World.content:
Call for stronger accountability for preventable road deaths Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Preventable deaths on our roads deserve stronger accountability - that's the message from a family grieving the loss of a daughter and her unborn child.

Jade Evans, 18, was killed near Palmerston North in November last year when a truck driver drove through a stop sign.

The driver pleaded guilty to careless driving causing death, and was sentenced to two months' community detention. He also lost his licence for 12 months and must pay reparations of $8000 to the family.

The maximum sentence possible under the law is three months' imprisonment. But Jade's mother, Kathryn Stothers, says that does not reflect the seriousness of the driver's deliberate - and fatal - choice.

She told Checkpoint on Wednesday the next part of the family's healing process was an initiative called Jade's Law.

"Jade's story has shown us that a preventable road death has devastating consequences for us as an entire family and also in the community, so we really want to turn that loss into meaningful change and make New Zealand roads safer."

She said at present, the law does not differentiate between genuine mistakes and deliberate decisions.

"The level of accountability is just the same if there was an accident that resulted because of water on the road or sunstrike, or anything like that. There's no deterrence for somebody that has deliberately breached road rules."

On 18 November, Jade was on her way to her parents' for dinner. The truck driver "looked left and right and continued to drive through" a stop sign, Stothers said.

"The truck driver has collided with our daughter Jade, and upon impact she's received devastating brain injuries and lost consciousness instantly and never regained it again."

Stothers said police and the courts did "everything they can" to hold the driver accountable, but the law did not differentiate between careless driving causing injury, and careless driving causing death.

"This is why we're pushing for stronger accountability to close the legislation gap. There's a gap in our current law when a fundamental road rule is broken and someone loses their life. This is to strengthen deterrence and restore public confidence that the law reflects the seriousness of a life lost.

"We don't want to make it that every single offence is charged at a higher charge. What we're asking for is to have more of a tiering section in the law so that the police and the court can charge appropriately when something like death occurs, because there's been a breach of a fundamental road law. We're not trying to take away from genuine accidents."

Stothers said Jade was a "strong, young, energetic, enthusiastic person" and her death left a hole in their lives.

"What we want to prevent is for other families to be in our situation where we're looking across the dining room table where there's a person missing. We want to reduce the possibility of other families sitting in the place we have, because it's a terrible place to sit."

World.title: Higher interest rates add to pressure on struggling retailers
World.content:
Retail NZ says the latest interest rate rise could put further pressure on businesses already facing a difficult trading environment.

The Reserve Bank has increased the official cash rate to 2.75 percent, saying it needs to reduce economic stimulus to tackle high inflation.

Retail NZ chief executive Carolyn Young said retailers were dealing with high costs, tight margins and weak consumer demand.

"It's just another blow that we know is really difficult and a really fragile economy."

She said higher mortgage and rent costs were likely to make households more cautious about spending.

The sector showed some signs of recovery at the end of last year and early this year, but Young said that recovery had been disrupted by the conflict in Iran.

Carolyn Young. Supplied

She said she spoke to one retailer who had been in business for 18 years and described this as the hardest year they had faced.

Large retailers had been restructuring and cutting staff, while smaller businesses were also struggling with rising costs and weaker demand, Young said.

The current situation was unusual because inflation remained high despite unemployment being at an 11-year high and consumer spending being weak, she said.

Retailers had largely been absorbing higher costs rather than passing them on to customers, but higher interest rates would add to their debt costs.

World.title: Cattle farmers hoof it to Auckland's first inner-city bull auction
World.content:
Inner-city cattle auction attracts farmers from across North Island Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

It's a bull rush.

A cattle auction at Epsom's inner city Cornwall Park has attracted farmers from across the upper North Island.

The farm is known for its quiet and friendly animals, who've adapted to the buzz of urban life.

When she heard about the herd, Dargaville farmer Cynthia hoofed it.

"This sort of event is always very popular in any district, but this is a really different sort of experience coming to the city," she said.

"And it's the first annual, so I've got my souvenir bull catalogue to put in with all the others."

Each of the 20 specially bred Simmental bulls is worth thousands of dollars.

Even with four stomachs, such a beefy price tag is hard to digest.

Having a munch Felix Walton/RNZ

"Well, actually... We were just looking at the scones and sausage rolls, because we think the bulls are going to be out of our budget," Cynthia admitted.

But some brave bidders were ready to take the bull by the horns.

"I've looked through the catalogue and spotted some favourites," Rebecca said.

"I'll have to see once the bidding starts, I hope I don't get carried away, stupidly."

Repeat customer Ray was keeping his cards close to his chest.

"I do have a budget... But that's my business," he laughed.

That attention was good news for farm manager Peter Maxwell.

It was his first time hosting an auction, and with beef prices at an all time high - the steaks are even higher.

A troublemaker escapes the lot. Felix Walton/RNZ

"The beef market's really strong, so it might be a good year to have a first go at an auction like this," he said.

"These are breeders, these will go onto some possibly purebred herds or to some crossbred herds, that's the big thing about Simmental cattle, they cross well with a lot of other breeds."

For auctioneer Cam Heggie, this wasn't his first rodeo.

He had sold cattle from Cornwall Park for a number of years, but said it was a novelty to host an auction on the farm itself.

"I've been fortunate enough to deal with Cornwall Park for a number of years, but there's a lot of people who don't even know there's a Simmental stud in the middle of downtown Auckland," he said.

Auctioneer Cam Heggie and farm manager Peter Maxwell. Felix Walton/RNZ

"So to run an auction here, it's actually pretty cool."

He said the bulls, raised in a fast moo-ving urban environment, were among the calmest he had met.

"Unbelievable temperament, on not only the bulls but the cattle her at Cornwall Park in general," he said.

"I could probably say, without fear of contradiction, these would be the quietest cattle I deal with day to day. Look at them in the paddock there, they just wander up to you, just incredible."

At a rapid-fire auction, the bulls sold for an average of $5,615, the highest for a whopping $8000.

A bidding agent talking to his client over the phone. Felix Walton/RNZ

Peter Maxwell was pleased with the results.

"We haven't sold a bull for that sort of money before, so that's pretty cool."

"That was a pretty amazing sale, to be all over in 30 minutes with a high average like that, a lot of work went into that so I'm pretty pleased about it."

World.title: Floating rates rise after official cash rate increase
World.content:
Banks have started to move their floating rates, after Wednesday's official cash rate increase.

Westpac says it is increasing variable interest rates for borrowers and some savers, after Wednesday's increase to the official cash rate.

The OCR was lifted by 25 basis points, to 2.75 percent.

Westpac's variable home and business lending rates will increase by 0.25 percent, effective Monday for new customers and Thursday for existing customers.

Its Bonus Saver and Business Online Saver, will also increase by the same amount from Monday.

"New Zealanders have shown resilience in the face of cost pressures and uncertainty, and our data suggests they remain well-placed to manage further rate rises," said managing director of product, sustainability and marketing, Sarah Hearn.

"Most of our home loan customers are on fixed rates and there are no changes for them today.

Is there any point in KiwiSaver if I'm on a total remuneration package? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

"However, we recognise some customers will be worried about rising rates. We're here to help borrowers and savers manage their money through an increasing OCR cycle and we encourage them to contact us if they need any help or advice."

ANZ also lifted its floating rate.

Managing director for personal banking Grant Knuckey said the Reserve Bank's decision came against a mixed economic backdrop and a broadly flat housing market.

He said when reviewing interest rates, ANZ considered a range of factors, including the OCR and changes in wholesale interest rates, while balancing the needs of borrowers and savers.

More than 90 percent of home lending was on fixed rates.

"Fixed home loans are influenced more by wholesale rates and expectations of where the OCR is heading next," Knuckey said.

Mortgage adviser Campbell Hastie said few borrowers would be surprised by the OCR increase.

"We were all expecting the rate to go up... I don't think anyone wants to hear that interest rates have gone up but I think there is a general expectation that this is going to happen and it'll eventually flow through into fixed rates.

"I think that's what people are expecting. Whether it happens or not is a different question but I don't think it's going to be a surprise to anyone."

He said interest rates were unlikely to rise enough to go back to their levels of two years ago.

"It's more than what it was six months ago but not like what it was two or three years ago."

Cotality chief property economist said the increase was not likely to have much of an effect on the housing market.

"The mood amongst buyers and sellers certainly remains fairly cautious, and those with mortgages will be wary of the recent interest rate increases on popular terms such as the two-year fix," he said.

"That being said, although floating rates may well shift higher to some extent after today's OCR rise, it's arguably already been priced in to prevailing fixed rates, so they might not show too much movement in the coming days.

"Of course, looking out over the next few months, there still seems a greater likelihood of higher mortgage rates rather than flat or down.

"The resilience of employment ...will tend to offset the housing effects of higher interest rates to a degree. But the looming election is another key factor at the moment, especially for property investors as they wait any indications from the opposition about interest deductibility."

World.title: Methanex closure to have ripple effect across the region
World.content:
New Zealand's largest gas user Methanex is to effectively close its plant and sell off its gas contracts.

Methanex said a lack of natural gas and a clear pathway to new supplies meant operations in New Zealand were no longer sustainable.

The Canadian-owned company said it had now entered into an agreement to sell all of its New Zealand natural gas contractual entitlements, commencing in the first quarter of next year.

It said it then planned to safely idle and preserve the facility for long-term optionality, should future circumstances support a restart of operations.

The company has in the past been responsible for taking around 30 to 40 percent of all of New Zealand's natural gas production.

ln recent years the country's natural gas production has declined rapidly with little new supply coming on board.

The company, which employs around 200 people, not including contractors and suppliers, said it would work closely with employees, contractors, suppliers, customers, and government stakeholders during the transition period.

Rich Sumner, president and chief executive of Methanex Corporation, said the company had been preparing for this eventuality, given declining gas availability in the country.

Sumner said the company was now focused on supporting its team members during the transition period, and safely operating the plant over the next several months.

New Plymouth Mayor Max Brough said the announcement was disappointing but not unexpected.

"They've got no continuity of supply. They don't have enough gas coming and they're making the best of a bad situation.

"They recognise New Zealand has a gas shortage. This will free it [gas] up for other users, but the price will go up. You need a baseline consumer to keep the price down for others because make no mistake, they've subsidised New Zealand's gas at a retail level and for other users for decades."

He said many people who would lose their jobs as a result of the closure would struggle to find similar work.

"There's no alternative here for those roles.

"They will be heading to where [they can] support their families, and it probably won't be in New Zealand. So that's very disappointing."

But he was optimistic about other gas exploration projects in the city.

"I've rolled out the red carpet and the welcome mat actually, because New Zealand needs gas.

"Whatever your political persuasion is, the reality is, we still need gas to power industry in a lot of places in this country and earn export dollars."

The Taranaki Chamber of Commerce said the decision of Methanex to mothball its Motunui plant would have a widespread impact on the local economy.

Chamber chief executive Arun Chaudhari said while the move was not unexpected, it would have a ripple effect across the region.

"They'll be impacts across almost every sector as we've known it.

"Methanex obviously employ a lot of people, so we're going to have unemployment to some extent.

"Obviously, the hospitality industry, the visitor industry will all get affected by a huge employer like Methanex leaving the region."

Chaudhari said a silver lining was that the plant was being put into hibernation rather than completely decommissioned.

"The good thing is that they are idling the plant which means there is some hope that if there is gas that can be used commercially to manufacture methanol again that is what will happen."

Chaudhari believed the decision gave people a clearer picture of the road ahead.

"The positive side of it is that there is more gas that can be used by Genesis and it means we have more energy security when we cannot rely on renewable energy in times of no sun, no wide and low lake levels."

He was optimistic new gas exploration permits would uncover gas supplies significant enough to allow Methanex to be rebooted.

Port Taranaki said it was "saddened" that Methanex - its single largest customer - was closing its New Zealand operations.

Chief executive Simon Craddock said the Canadian-owned company had been a long-time and important customer of Port Taranaki and a key contributor to the Taranaki economy.

"With the challenges in the gas sector, we have been preparing our business for this decision to ensure we remain sustainable in the long term.

"We are saddened to see their New Zealand operations close, and thank Methanex for their decades-long commitment to our business and the region.

Craddock said his thoughts were with the Methanex team and their families as they navigated this challenging period.

Resources Minister and NZ First MP Shane Jones told Checkpoint the closure was no surprise - although the exact timing of it was not previously known - and would shore up gas supplies in the short term.

"Obviously there's going to be a a wave of gas available. I mean, Genesis have told me that they're in a position to purchase it," he said.

"In the very short term, it creates an opportunity for more gas to come into the market to assist industrial users such as the the producers of fertiliser and other industrial market users - and obviously for electricity. Last year, I think a third of all the gas got exhausted by electricity producers."

Global methanol producer ceasing Taranaki operations Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Methanex seemed to have been engaged in "secret negotiations with Genesis", he said, and the government had brought in new regulations recently to "get more information as to what's happening with the various contracting activity".

Jones said the government's LNG import facility was still needed.

"I understand where the Green Party is coming from, but the level of need that the country has for gas well into the future goes much beyond this short-term fill-up of gas available associated with the shuttering."

Asked what support the government could provide to those losing their jobs as a result of the closure, Jones said the Defence Force needed to boost its resources and he was working with local engineering firms to provide that new kit - and such firms could employ them.

"Taranaki is at the front of the queue."

Minister blames Labour

Energy Minister Simeon Brown said the former Labour government was at fault.

"The reason why we're in this position is because Labour decided to ban oil and gas exploration, crashed a sector, thousands of jobs in our regions lost, particularly in Taranaki, and today even more being lost."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins denied there was any link.

"New Zealand hasn't had a significant find of new natural gas for over 20 years, the oil and gas ban didn't change that reality," he said.

"People were out there looking for gas, they couldn't find it. That's the reason why Methanex have made this decision."

Ditch LNG import facility - Greens

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick RNZ / REECE BAKER

The Green Party said the closure left the government no reason to push on with its plans to build a liquified natural gas (LNG) import facility.

The government has set out to build the $1 billion terminal, saying it is necessary to shore up energy supply.

"Methanex leaving takes the country's largest gas user out of the market and frees up gas supply through to the end of the decade for electricity generation," said co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick.

"The 'gas shortage' the government has been talking up to try and justify this fossil fuel project is now about to be a great deal smaller."

Swarbrick said if the government did not cancel its plans, it should at least return to the drawing board before signing a deal.

Brown said the government would push on because it was still necessary.

"Some of that gas will become available to the electricity sector, but it's not going to be enough in the long term," he said.

"We still have a significant lack of backup energy."

Finance Minister Nicola Willis said the government had factored in the likely closure of Methanex when it planned for the LNG import terminal.

"Therefore we accounted for the additional gas that would come into the market if that closure occurred," she said.

"Even with that additional gas coming into the market, we would still face a dry year risk, a shortage of gas in years when there isn't enough water in the hydro lakes."

Meanwhile, Genesis Energy said it had secured additional gas supplies from a third party for the period of March 2027 and 2029.

It has not said who it got it off. It was 11.4 Petajoules (or PJ), about 10 percent of national gas production.

In addition, Genesis said it had exercised its right of first refusal in respect of the Kupe gas supply, securing access to up to 8.6 PJ.

World.title: AFL boss backflips by scrapping controversial 'Opening Round' experiment
World.content:
The AFL has scrapped the Opening Round experiment after three seasons and will return to a traditional nine-game first week.

League boss Andrew Dillon today confirmed the demise of the much-criticised concept that featured four games played exclusively in Queensland and New South Wales between only a selection of eight clubs.

Designed to build a foothold in rugby league heartland, it instead drew criticism given the fixturing created a staggered start and early-season byes.

Defending it in March, Dillon said Opening Round was "key" to growing the sport north of Victoria, citing record attendances and membership rises.

Australia and England will play a one-off Test next year at the MCG to celebrate 150 years of Test cricket, pushing the AFL season back. (Getty Images: Robbie Stephenson/PA Images)

"What we've found in the last couple of years is that focus on NSW and Queensland is helping to grow awareness in NSW and Queensland and at the same time it hasn't taken away from our round one," Dillon said at the time.

But, with the season to begin a week later next year due to the MCG hosting the 150th anniversary cricket Test between Australia and England, it has been taken out with the trash.

"We have been working through alternative options to deliver the start of the AFL season," Dillon said in a statement.

"After important feedback from fans and stakeholders, and consultation with clubs and broadcasters, round one will see the return of a traditional nine-game round played across the country."

The first round will be played from Wednesday or Thursday, March 17 or 18, just days after the final day of the historic Ashes Test.

The 24-round home-and-away season will conclude on Sunday, August 30, with the five-week finals series beginning with two wildcard finals in the first week of September.

The grand final will be held on Saturday, October 2 and Gather Round in South Australia is locked in for April 8-11.

AAP

World.title: Police speak with four men over Sydney Swans scandal
World.content:
Victoria Police detectives have spoken with four Sydney men as part of their sexual assault investigation linked to the Sydney Swans.

In a statement, police confirmed they travelled to NSW this week.

Sexual Crimes Squad detectives spoke with a 26-year-old Randwick man, a 30-year-old Maroubra man, a 25-year-old Randwick man and a 25-year-old Paddington man.

Investigators say the interview process with the four men has now concluded.

The allegations relate to events at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel where it is understood players were joined by several adult entertainers in the early hours of August 17.

Three women subsequently made a report to police.

No-one has been arrested and no charges have been laid.

Authorities say they also spoke to, or will speak with, three men also believed to be in the hotel room, who are being treated solely as witnesses at this time.

The club stood down five players — vice captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordan, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey — for breaching club standards for drinking and bringing women to the hotel in the hours after the team's round 23 clash against Essendon.

Police now believe they have identified all parties who were in the room at the time of the alleged incident.

The investigation into the alleged incident remains ongoing, and Victoria Police said it does not expect to provide any further updates for about eight weeks.

Detectives believe they have identified everyone who was in the hotel room at the time of the alleged incident. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The club released a statement acknowledging the update on Wednesday afternoon.

"The wellbeing of those impacted remains of paramount importance," the Swans said.

"The club again extends its sincere apologies to our members and fans, sponsors and the wider community, along with all of our staff and players across both the women's and men's programs, for the distress and disappointment this matter has caused."

Two separate law firms have been engaged to represent three women considering civil action over the alleged incident.

Their lawyers have previously alleged the women are suffering severe stress and anxiety and may pursue damages.

World.title: Clarkson sacked as Kangaroos hunt 'coach for the modern game'
World.content:
North Melbourne says "gaping holes" within Alastair Clarkson's game plan led to the club parting ways with the veteran senior coach.

Clarkson was contracted with the club until 2027, but the Kangaroos opted to end his tenure early.

Kangaroos president Sonja Hood and head of football Todd Viney both pointed to key game plan issues when questioned on the reasons behind the decision to not proceed with Clarkson into the final year of his deal.

"I think if there was one thing that Clarko did was he tried too hard in trying to fix that, and then therefore what happens is we get into more meetings, more information, and the players at the end of the day become a little bit confused, and we don't get the cohesion that we need to win more games," Viney said.

"There's still parts of our game plan that we haven't been able to improve in the four years, and that's some stuff that we need to get right when we talk to the next coach to bring us in line with where the modern game is right at the moment."

Viney also conceded that Clarkson had been run down by the investigation into racism at Hawthorn under his tenure.

"I'm not sure the scars have fully healed, to this point. He's gone through enormous trauma," he said.

"I'm not sure of the exact impact, but I know it's had an affect. He's been through a lot and he's managed it well and coached us well, but it's definitely had an affect.

" He's not the same bubbly person that I knew early days. "

Despite former Kangaroos stars-turned-coaches Adam Simpson and John Longmire both being on the market, Hood said North Melbourne will run a full process to find its next coach.

Hood added that assistants already at the club who worked under Clarkson are also welcome to throw their hats in the ring for the full-time role.

When questioned over what type of coach the Kangaroos are after, Hood said: "a coach who can coach for the modern game".

Clarkson was blindsided by the club's decision to not proceed with him into 2027, with Hood saying he was "upset" by the call.

Despite Clarkson being Hood's star hire four years ago, she envisages continuing in her role as president, while Viney also said he was prepared to remain at North Melbourne.

Former Swans premiership coach John Longmire (pictured) has been linked with the Kangaroos vacancy, but will need to go through a process if he wants the job. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Clarkson released a statement in response to his exit via his manager James Henderson.

"My time as coach of the North Melbourne Football Club has come to an end," he said.

"We set out to stabilise the club and lay the foundations for a return to playing deep in September.

"The challenge was a difficult one that I embraced with my whole being.

"My family and I have been privileged to be involved in AFL football for over 40 years, but it is now time for a new chapter."

The Kangaroos will begin their coach search next week, and Hood said there is no timeline on when an appointment should be made official, despite the trade period taking place next month.

Hood said the Kangaroos were in a better position now than when Clarkson took over, but the club wanted more success over the next four years.

"We asked Alastair to give our club stability and strength and help return us to the top of the AFL ladder," she said.

"Four years later, we have created an environment where our staff and players want to be at our club. This is a testament to the culture Alastair has helped create and the belief that he has built in this group.

"Although we have clearly made progress and won more games, we won't shy away from our desire to want more from this talented group.

"We are incredibly grateful to Alastair for the work he's done over the last four years and we wish him all the very best for his next chapter."

Live Moment Look back at North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney's press conference after Alastair Clarkson was relieved of his duties as Kangaroos coach. What was going to happen next year? Did the North Board refuse a contract extension prior to the 2027 season? Did the want Clarkson to coach for his future? - Roos Member From what Hood said, they determined that they weren't going to extend Clarkson beyond 2027, therefore believed that it would be unfair to expect him to coach next season. Is it time for Simpson or Longmire? I think it's the right thing to do. He has laid a foundation but it needs a new voice to get that bit more. I prefer Simmo to Horse and think he could really push this group forward. - Nathan Hood wasn't prepared to say they're the preferred candidate, but both of their reactions will be interesting. The stuff about a modern coach makes me think they'll go for a highly-credentialled assistant. Should the players be blamed? Why get rid of a 4 time premiership coach with 1 more year left. Makes no sense. Maybe players should be held more accountable. - Davo It is interesting, Davo, that the players often seem to skirt responsibility with this kind of stuff. I guess it's easier to remove one employee than multiple. At the end of the day, this is a players' league. Show more

Under Clarkson, North won 20 of its 82 AFL matches, including nine this season. Clarkson took over the Kangaroos after the club had collected back-to-back wooden spoons in 2022 and 2021, while also finishing second-last in 2020.

North has not made the finals in a decade, when the club made consecutive preliminary finals in 2014 and 2015 and an elimination final in 2016 under Brad Scott.

The 2026 season was North's best under Clarkson, and most successful since 2019, with the Kangaroos finishing 14th on the ladder with nine wins.

World.title: Ferrari's Schumacher-inspired livery, F1 leader to cop penalty in Italy
World.content:
Ferrari will be celebrating the legacy of Michael Schumacher this weekend at its home race, with a special livery dedicated to the seven-time Formula 1 world champion.

This year marks 30 years since Schumacher joined the Scuderia, and 20 years since his final F1 victory in the 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix leaves the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

With Schumacher at the wheel, Ferrari rose to the top of F1 after years spent without championships.

Ferrari's constructors' championship win in 1999 ended a 16-year wait in the teams' competition, while Schumacher's drivers' championship triumph in 2000 made him the first Ferrari race to become world champion since Jody Scheckter in 1979.

Schumacher won five of his seven drivers' championships with Ferrari, from 2000-2004.

This weekend at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza, a race Schumacher won five times with Ferrari, the Scuderia has a one-off livery which pays tribute to the F1 champion.

Among the features are seven stars on the nose of the car, representing Schumacher's world titles, and drivers Lewis Hamilton — the sport's other seven-time world champion — and Charles Leclerc will wear racing suits that also feature the seven stars and Schumacher's logo.

F1 championship leader to take grid penalty at Monza

Kimi Antonelli has celebrated his 20th birthday as the Formula 1 drivers' championship leader, and heads into his home grand prix with a significant 59-point advantage over his two nearest rivals.

F1 drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli is set to start the Italian Grand Prix from the back of the grid. (Reiters: Benoit Tessier)

But the youngest-ever leader of the F1 championship heads into this weekend's race at Monza knowing he has work to do to be near the front of the grid.

Mercedes announced during the previous race weekend in the Netherlands that Antonelli will take an engine penalty this weekend.

F1 teams have an allocation of power unit components they can use in a season. When a driver is fitted with a power unit component that exceeds the allocation, they are handed a penalty at the first event that new part is used.

Mercedes has had multiple power unit issues this year, with Antonelli failing to finish in Barcelona and teammate George Russell suffering issues in Canada and Belgium.

Despite the Italian Grand Prix being Antonelli's home race, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said now was the right time to do it for the championship leader.

"Our calculations say that that's the best track to take it," Wolff said.

"Obviously, algorithms don't take their nationality into consideration. We're here to fight for a championship and not get the most PR. So yeah, that's what we're going to do."

Monza, known as the Temple of Speed, is expected to be a strong track for Mercedes, which is likely why it is taking the penalty now.

With long straights, there should be plenty of opportunities for Antonelli to pass with his impressive Mercedes power unit.

Monza has been the scene of impressive drives through the field in recent years.

Pierre Gasly won from 10th on the grid driving for AlphaTauri (now Racing Bulls). Max Verstappen won in 2022 after taking a five-place grid penalty, while Lewis Hamilton charged from the last row on the grid to place fifth.

Last year, Isack Hadjar started in the pit lane for Racing Bulls and was able to finish 10th.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Italian Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 6.

World.title: Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header announced as sevens added to ticket
World.content:
Australia's sevens teams will share the stage in a scheduling first, with the Wallabies and Wallaroos creating a Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header in Sydney.

The Stadium Australia Test against the All Blacks on October 17 already had a support act secured, with the Wallaroos due to host Scotland for the first time in their WXV Global Series clash.

Kick-off times for Bledisloe Cup in Sydney Wallaroos v Scotland, 12pm

Australian sevens men v Fiji, 2:05pm

Australian sevens women v New Zealand, 2.25pm

Wallabies v New Zealand, 3:45pm All times in AEDT

Now two more fixtures will be added to the ticket, with Australia's world champion sevens women to face rivals New Zealand and the men up against two-time Olympic gold medallists Fiji.

"This is an historic moment for Australian rugby, with all four of our Teams In Gold competing on the same pitch, on the same day, on an unmissable occasion," Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh told AAP.

"The day will showcase the very best of rugby with our elite male and female players across the XVs and Sevens formats taking on famous rivals from around the world in an unprecedented line-up of international rugby.

"We look forward to celebrating this extraordinary occasion with our great Australian rugby community and we thank our friends from New Zealand Rugby, Fiji Rugby Union and Scottish Rugby for helping make this day a reality."

The Wallaroos will begin the action before the men's and women's sevens outfits take the field, followed by the Wallabies, who will complete the four-course menu with a late afternoon kick-off at the venue set to host next year's World Cup final.

AAP

World.title: Thea Frodin, Serena Williams's body double in movie, makes US Open debut
World.content:
Making a US Open debut as a teenager is a daunting task, but American Thea Frodin is no stranger to the bright lights.

The 17-year-old played at her home slam for the first time, going down in straight sets to world number two Elena Rybakina 6-3, 6-2.

There were plenty of fans at Grandstand who were there to see Rybakina, this year's Australian Open champion, but Frodin was a mini-celebrity in her own right.

Frodin, from California, was a body double at the age of 12 in the 2021 film King Richard, a movie starring Will Smith about the rise of Serena and Venus Williams with the help of their father, Richard Williams.

Fordin was the body double for actor Demi Singleton, who played Serena in the film, and is now forging her own path at Flushing Meadows.

There was no Hollywood screenwriting for Fordin's debut, with Rybakina never troubled in the win that came after a near three-hour rain delay.

Fordin was not disgraced in the straight-sets defeat. Down 1-5 in the second set, the teenager fired four aces, saving three match points, to extend the match just one extra game.

"She played really well today, and she has great shots," Rybakina said of her teenage opponent.

Fifth seed comes from behind to avoid another US Open boilover

Italian fifth seed Flavio Cobolli has rallied from two sets down to win his first-round match at the US Open, avoiding another early upset on the men's side.

Flavio Cobolli needed more than four hours, and five sets, to make it to the US Open second round. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The French Open runner-up beat Francisco Comesana 3-6, 2-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, finishing his match that lasted 4 hours, 12 minutes, not long after some sun had broken through the clouds and allowed play to start on all the outside courts after a morning of rain.

Cobolli made his first career two-set comeback to avoid joining Novak Djokovic (fourth seed) and Arthur Fils (10th seed) among early losers in a men's draw that was already missing top-ranked Jannik Sinner due to injury.

Cobolli said he took a bathroom break after the second set and decided to change everything.

"So I changed all the dress that I started with today and it works," Cobolli said.

"In grand slams it's never done. You have to fight until the last point."

Ninth seed Taylor Fritz, the 2024 runner-up, rolled to a 6-3, 6-2, 6-4 victory over 18-year-old fellow American Darwin Blanch.

Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.

Madison Keys was the only other player to move into the second round early in a tournament where rain threatened to hamper the schedule for a couple of days.

Showers that began Monday night, local time, and could be on and off through the middle of the week delayed play on all the outer courts, allowing action only in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, which have retractable roofs.

Keys, the 22nd seed, beat 19-year-old Alina Korneeva 7-5, 6-4 in the leadoff match in Ashe. The 2017 US Open runner-up was knocked off in the first round last year in Flushing Meadows.

"It's always tough playing someone young and up-and-coming, and they're going after their shots," Keys said.

"And it's so hard to play a first round of a Grand Slam, so nervous and just wanting to do so well. So, really happy I was able to kind of fight through that and win today."

Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open champion, 17th seed Alex Eala, and men's first seed Alexander Zverev are scheduled to play later on the final night of round one matches.

ABC/AP

World.title: Aussies march on at US Open, De Minaur washed out, Kokkinakis withdraws
World.content:
Diminutive Dane Sweeny and qualifier Tristan Schoolkate have stormed into the US Open second round to continue Australia's excellent start to the season's final grand slam.

Sweeny was leading the crafty Corentin Moutet 7-6(4), 6-4, 3-0 when the Frenchman retired injured on Tuesday, local time.

Schoolkate then celebrated like Lleyton Hewitt when he finished off American qualifier Nishesh Basavareddy 7-6 (4), 3-6, 6-3, 6-4 in a tick over three hours.

The 25-year-old Sweeny marked his maiden appearance in the US Open main draw with a first-ever victory at an overseas grand slam.

The wildcard next faces either Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti or rising Brit Arthur Fery for an improbable place in the last 32.

Schoolkate is into round two for a second time and will next play Italian fifth seed Fabio Cobolli, the 2026 French Open runner-up.

Sweeny, who only stands 170 centimetres high, and Schoolkate give Australia at least seven players in round two, joining Taylah Preston, Kim Birrell, Maya Joint, Alexei Popyrin and James Duckworth.

Men's sixth seed Alex de Minaur will have to wait another day to try to follow suit after more rain in New York wiped out the day-three night session.

De Minaur did not even make it onto The Grandstand for his first-round clash with Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri.

Injured Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball

Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.

Kokkinakis formally withdrew from the season's last grand slam after being unable to take the court for his scheduled first-round clash with Spanish wonder boy Rafael Jodar because of an ankle sprain.

Thanasi Kokkinakis has pulled out of the year's final grand slam. (Getty Images: NurPhoto/Robert Szaniszlo)

The Australian suffered his latest injury in Cincinnati two weeks ago and has been racing the clock to be fit for the Open ever since.

He ran out of time and, after a decade battling endless back, shoulder, abdominal, knee and arm injuries, Kokkinakis admits he is losing patience.

"It is a possibility for sure," the 30-year-old told AAP when asked if his US Open career might be over.

"I'm not going to say never. The thing is, I feel like the tennis part, I've still got a lot of good tennis left in me.

"On the limited matches that I've played, I've shown that I'm more than good enough to still compete and then beat some good players.

"But, to be honest, I'm sick of going into tournaments not feeling like I can do it physically and everyone asks me how my body is."

The 30-year-old used — or "wasted" — the fifth of nine injury-protected ranking entries available to him to make the US Open draw.

The one-time Roger Federer slayer now plans on continuing his recovery and trying to be fully fit for the Australian summer.

"I want to go into it being confident in myself and, if I do win, give myself a chance to back up and try and play again," Kokkinakis said.

"That's always the thing. So it's about feeling strong in myself.

"I'll definitely obviously give the next Aussie a crack and see where I'm at after that."

AAP

World.title: Adelaide MotoGP project is more than the track. Here's what's planned in the parklands
World.content:
Headline announcements have a habit of overshadowing, if not totally obscuring, finer details, and the future of the Australian MotoGP has been no exception.

On Sunday, the SA government released its long-awaited plan for the design of a $96 million Adelaide street circuit set to host the race from 2027 — a development that will involve the cutting down of nearly 400 trees to make way for the new track.

The announcement came amid environmental acrimony. The government is currently facing protests and a federal court challenge over its actions in another part of the Adelaide parklands to redevelop the North Adelaide Golf Course.

But the MotoGP project will be about more than the track and the trees — the government is promising what amounts to a sweeping upgrade of the areas around Victoria Park in Adelaide's eastern parklands.

Here's a look at the plan that is currently out for community consultation.

Canopy and habitat

Of all the ramifications of the MotoGP project, the impact on the environment is perhaps the most politically sensitive.

But the government has been keen to spruik what it has described as a "nature-positive outcome" and has promised to plant many more trees than it removes, "meaning a net increase of at least 3,393 trees".

It has also committed to a $15 million environmental spend on "greening, rewilding and revitalising projects to restore habitat and strengthen biodiversity".

Shared-use paths are part of the concept plans. (Supplied: SA government)

Those projects will include work to reduce pollution entering the River Torrens and to support wildlife such as local butterfly populations.

Asked about how soon the works would be completed, SA Premier Peter Malinauskas spoke of "the next few years".

"We've got a timeline that we want to work within in terms of the release of that funding," he said.

"There'll be capacity constraints about when some projects will be delivered.

"Some of the projects will require a fair bit of design work around the stormwater work that we're doing … to be able to help grow the tree canopy at a faster rate than what otherwise [would be] the case."

Grey-headed flying foxes — which are prone to summer heat stress — will get improved cooling infrastructure and habitat regeneration.

Bat Rescue SA's fundraising coordinator, Judith Bemmer, welcomed the commitment, but also expressed concern about habitat loss as a result of the removal of trees.

"We're worried that there's the potential for starvation of the baby bats, because they won't have some of those trees to fly out to," she said.

"Having said that, the trees close in to the parklands, where their colony is, and the fig trees are all still there.

"We're very hopeful that in the future, as these other trees mature, it will provide both cover and forage for these bats."

Grey-headed flying foxes at Adelaide's Botanic Park. (Supplied: Craig Greer)

Mr Malinauskas said environmental works would also include steps to contribute to platypus rewilding efforts in the Torrens by ecology group Green Adelaide.

"We are putting funding in place to accelerate that work and get it done. There is a bit of work that is required here," he said.

Adelaide Park Lands Association president Mat Monti said that, on their own, tree planting, revegetation and environmental investment were commendable — but that, when coupled with tree removal, they amounted to "greenwashing".

"We don't want them to do it just to excuse the destruction of the eastern parklands for MotoGP," they said.

Fringe benefits

The design for the new street circuit will see MotoGP bikes race along Rundle Road, between Rymill and Rundle parks.

During Adelaide's so-called Mad March festival season, those parks are occupied by Fringe venues Gluttony and The Garden of Unearthly Delights.

Rundle Road — an extension of Rundle Street — will host part of the race. (Supplied: SA government)

The government said the venues stood to gain from the redevelopment works, through upgrades to water, electricity and sewerage infrastructure.

"When Fringe and Gluttony set up down in the East End around Rymill Park, there is often temporary infrastructure they have to bring in at substantial cost," Mr Malinauskas said.

"If we can put some permanent infrastructure in the ground, that makes it easier for them to set up and pack down."

Sport and recreation

The main part of the MotoGP circuit will be in Victoria Park, which currently hosts Adelaide's Supercars races and formerly hosted the F1 Grand Prix.

The heritage grandstand in the park — a hangover from its time as a horseracing venue — will be closer to the race, thanks to a track redesign involving a revised turn-off from Wakefield Road.

The redevelopment could accommodate new playing courts. (Supplied: SA government)

But the government is also promising other works in Victoria Park for community benefit, such as an upgraded soccer field, with lighting, and community space near the grandstand.

It said there would be new running tracks through the eastern parklands, including a 2-kilometre loop in Victoria Park itself.

It also said there would "potentially" be a new skate park and playing courts near Fullarton Road.

"They could be pickleball courts, they could be basketball courts, they could be netball courts," SA Motor Sport Board chief executive Mark Warren told a parliamentary inquiry on Monday.

Mark Warren says the redevelopment will include playing courts and a cycling criterium circuit. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

A new water jump will be installed for the Adelaide Equestrian Festival — an annual three-day horse trials event and Olympic qualifier held in the eastern parklands.

"This will give our event a bit of a boost because we won't now have to fund it ourselves, which is great news," board member Karlene Maywald said.

"We're also working closely with the Motor Sport Board and the government to ensure we can deliver our event next April."

Pedal power

Several of the elements of the new design relate to cycling — including plans for the Tour Down Under.

The government said the Victoria Park circuit would be hosting the return of the Tour Down Under classic, a pre-tour street race, from 2028.

The heritage grandstand will be closer to the action because of a track re-design which will also accommodate cycling events, the government says. (Supplied: SA government)

The Motor Sport Board said a new 1.2-kilometre criterium loop would provide space for cycling races and Pedal Prix events.

"That's quite critical because right now the criterium loop that exists has a crossover between park users," Mr Warren said.

"It was important to, in the design, look at how we can have an unobstructed cycling criterium loop, and we believe the current design as it's been put out for consultation will achieve some of that. There's been some discussion already with cycling clubs."

There are also plans for new shared-use paths, and a pedestrian and cyclist refuge on Wakefield Road.

Consultation on the plans is open until September 20.

Tech.title: Is this the future of America?
Tech.content:
InIn 2007, the US was on the cusp of an economic recession, and Buddy Rizer was tasked with finding Loudoun County, Virginia, a new way to make money. Rizerâs earlier career as a radio DJ didnât exactly make him an obvious candidate to find a solution, but he was looking for what he called a âreal jobâ and stumbled into a role at Loudounâs economic development authority.

This new gig came with urgency thanks to the bursting of the housing bubble: More than 80 percent of the countyâs revenue came from residential real estate. The goal, at the time, was to raise the commercial tax base from about 19 percent of revenue to something like 23 percent, Rizer recalls. Today, just over half of the countyâs tax revenue comes from commercial sources. To jumpstart that turnaround, Rizer turned to the carcasses of another recent bubble burst â those of the dot-com era.

The county had been home to the headquarters of AOL, which by 2000 was the USâs largest internet provider. Combined with its proximity to the nationâs capital and access to resources including water and electricity, Loudoun quickly emerged as the physical manifestation of the internet, the place responsible for how the majority of Americans got online. Estimates suggest that as much as 70 percent of the planetâs internet traffic passed through Loudoun County.

But after the collapse of dot-com stocks in 2000, followed by AOLâs disastrous merger with Time Warner, much of that industry dried up, and Loudoun was left with hulking, empty buildings and miles of fiber optic cable already laid in the ground. Where some people saw abandoned infrastructure, Buddy Rizer saw opportunity: âAnd so I thought if we can fill those, that would be a good start,â he says. Rizer soon realized that the same factors that made Loudoun County attractive to AOL could once again make it a hot spot for technology. It still had an internet exchange point, lots of land, a government eager for investment, and a capable local electricity utility. âAnd so we came up with this plan to attract data centers.â

Buddy Rizer, executive director for economic development in Loudoun County, has become known as the âGodfather of Data Centersâ for courting the massive data center buildout to the area.

Today, Loudoun County has another moniker: Data Center Alley. Over just a small portion of its roughly 515 square miles, itâs home to about 250 data centers, the densest concentration in the world. For a long time, residents there recall only a passing understanding of this, if they realized it at all. The development of data centers in Loudoun was just something going on in the background of many residentsâ lives. They noticed construction along main roads, paid an increasingly lower property tax rate, and sent their kids to coveted public schools.

The countyâs data center boom arrived as tech companies expanded into the cloud, a sanitized name for the blocky buildings that house rows and rows of servers. And with that business came prosperity: 22 new schools built in just the last 15 years, tax revenue from data centers alone that exceeded the countyâs operational budget by $35 million in 2024, and a decline in real property tax rate for residents from about $1.29 to 80 cents per $100 in assessed value since 2008.

Some longtime residents never heard of their countyâs nickname until recently, when the effects of data centers on the community started to become impossible to ignore. What had been a relatively quiet boon locally was starting to foment a national backlash elsewhere, and starting to disturb daily life in Loudoun, too.

The current, massive US data center buildout has been accelerating thanks to the widespread adoption of generative AI, which has created a growing need for the physical infrastructure to run tremendous amounts of âcomputeâ â the industry term for processing power. There are already 3,000 data centers in operation around the US, according to an April analysis by the Pew Research Center, with 1,500 more in development. When Rizer began recruiting companies to build data centers in Loudoun, he sat on conference panels for secondary markets. Now when he attends data center conferences, Loudoun is the biggest market there, and âthereâs more economic developers than there are data center companies, because everybody sees the opportunity.â

Loudoun County residents are also starting to take notice. Within the past few years, data centers have been elevated from an unremarkable part of daily life in Loudoun to something that many residents now think about every day. For some, itâs the constant hum they hear from their decks; for others, itâs the transmission towers that loom over their favorite green space, or the surprise call from their energy utility that one of those towers could go up in their own backyard. While residents recognize that data centers have brought a lot of prosperity to the county, theyâre beginning to wonder how much more they can take.

As communities around the country begin recognizing the potential opportunities of building data centers, the efforts have also faced immense pushback. Opposition to this development is shaping strange alliances across the political spectrum and has become a central issue in this yearâs midterm elections.
