Tech.title: Are We There Yet? Startup Wants to Launch an 80,000-Year Mission to Alpha Centauri
Tech.content:
A group of executives and entrepreneurs led by Starcloud co-founders Philip Johnston, Adi Oltean and Ezra Feilden teamed up to develop humanity’s first interstellar spacecraft. If everything goes according to plan, it will launch in 2029, headed for Alpha Centauri, the closest star system to our solar system. But it won’t reach its destination for about 80,000 years.

Known as Fermi Explorer, this non-profit mission aims to build a 10cm cube weighing about 1 kilogram (about 2.2 pounds). Once the cube is built, they plan to attach it to a propulsion system, take it to space and launch it toward Alpha Centauri. It’s the technological equivalent of taking a hefty rock into space, throwing it at Alpha Centauri and waiting for it to get there.

“The mission is intended to make the idea of interstellar travel real, and to encourage more people to confront one of humanity’s biggest unanswered questions when we look beyond our planet,” the group said in a post on X. The post is accompanied by a video showing the Fermi Explorer being overtaken by hundreds of faster spacecraft also bound for Alpha Centauri.

The wait for this mission to go interstellar is unreal. The exact wait to mission completion is 79,800 years, according to the Fermi Explorer mission calculator, which means once this thing gets underway, it won’t be the problem of anyone currently living, or anyone else, for a few thousand generations.

Just getting out of the solar system will take longer than any road trip any human has ever taken. The spacecraft is expected to circle the sun for 12 years in an oval orbit. The boosters will fire when the spacecraft gets closer to the sun, a process called the Oberth maneuver, thereby gaining speed through multiple orbits as it approaches escape velocity. Once done, it’ll launch itself and keep going, and going, and going. The Fermi Explorer’s technical feasibility assessment says it should leave the solar system by the early 2040s.

It’s quite a different mission from what Starcloud’s co-founders usually work on: putting data centers in space to power AI. The company plans to launch its first such full commercial data center, called the Starcloud-2, in 2027, but it did send an Nvidia H100 GPU into space via Starcloud-1 in 2025.

More symbolic than scientific

We hope they packed enough snacks, because that’s one long road trip. Fermi Explorer

Interstellar travel takes so long that humanity has focused far more on speeding up the journey than actually making it. One of the big projects addressing this was Breakthrough Starshot, a multi-billion-dollar initiative that would’ve used laser-based propulsion to propel a ship to another star in a matter of decades rather than millennia. That project collapsed in 2025 with no launches.

The only other interstellar missions ever conducted, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2, entered interstellar space in 2012 and 2018, respectively, over four decades after their launches.

According to the non-profit group, the purpose of the Fermi Explorer is to just toss something into the cosmos and see what happens. It sounds silly, but it’s the truth. The group’s thinking is based on the Fermi Paradox, which seeks to explain why there are so many stars and planets yet no signs of extraterrestrial life.

One potential reason is the Fermi Great Filter, which suggests a barrier so hard to cross that intelligent life rarely survives long enough to be detected.

There are dozens of potential filters, ranging from the various steps of abiogenesis — the natural process by which life arises from non-living matter — to technological filters such as the inability to get into space, or, once there, the lack of motivation to search beyond a species’ host star.

“By launching the Fermi Explorer mission, we can for the first time tick two possible Fermi Great Filters off the list,” the group wrote on its website. “That it is impossible for an intelligent species to leave their nearest stars (and) that all intelligent species decide not to leave their home star for some reason.”

The goal is to fund and build this entire project for about $15 million, using existing technology and piggybacking on a commercial rocket, such as SpaceX’s, to reach orbit. This project exists only to prove that humans can and are willing to do it, even if it’s something no one alive today is ever going to witness.

Tech.title: Acer Recommits to Repairability With New Vero 16 Laptop
Tech.content:
Acer is a brand closely associated with budget workhorse machines — the company largely manufactures laptops for entry-level gamers, students and office workers. It’s an admirable (and tough) niche to fill at a time when RAMageddon is inflating hardware component prices and even sub-$700 laptops feel like a dying breed.

Maybe that’s why the company is continuing to throw its weight behind the right-to-repair movement with the fourth-generation Vero 16 revealed at IFA 2026. If you’re going to be shelling out more cash for a so-called “budget laptop,” it makes sense that you’d want it to stand the test of time. The repairable and upgradable Vero 16 is one way for the company to adapt to changing market conditions.

While that more modular Vero design is one of the laptops Acer is positioning front-and-center at the show, its other clamshells certainly aren’t being ignored: Two new lightweight Swift laptops are making their debut at IFA 2026.

The latest Vero 16 doesn’t look quite as distinguishable as its predecessor. Whether that’s a good thing is up to you. Acer/CNET

Vero 16

When Acer revitalized its Vero laptop line last year, sustainability was the name of the game. The 2025 version of the Vero 16 had a chassis composed primarily of recycled post-consumer plastic waste and oyster shells. It was a gritty, textured clamshell shot through with gray-blue specks — a spectacle piece, to be sure. And while vague commitments to sustainability and repairability are great, there wasn’t anything especially interesting going on aside from the computer’s oceanic aesthetic.

The next-generation Vero 16 brings the sustainability theme to one of its natural conclusions, and the company ended up with a more interesting computer in the process. The 2026 Vero 16 is an even more repairable laptop, allowing you to swap out or upgrade parts. That could cut back on some waste — and additional expenses for you, the laptop owner.

Parts of the chassis (including the bottom cover, hinge and I/O port covers) are removable, granting Vero 16 owners access to the laptop internals for quick repairs. You’ll be able to swap out a bad battery or SSD on your own, and the device is designed to support processor upgrades for the next two generations. You still might need to bring the computer into a repair shop for more serious maintenance, but there’s a lot here that you can service completely on your own.

While Acer isn’t the only computer manufacturer hopping on the repairability trend, the Vero 16 feels like it fills a niche for folks who might not feel technically savvy enough to benefit from, say, one of Framework’s fully modular computers. This laptop even has a visual repair guide engraved on the chassis to help owners feel more confident about completing simple swapouts. Hey, who knows, maybe that’s what it’ll take for your dad to phone you for computer help a little less frequently?

Every fourth-generation Vero 16 configuration has an OLED panel, with 2.8K (2,880×1,800-pixel) and 2K (1,920×1,200-pixel) resolution options available. The 1,920×1,200-pixel panel will support an optional touchscreen. This clamshell will house up to an Intel Core Ultra X9 388H processor with integrated Intel Arc B390 graphics, up to 32GB of LPDDR5x memory and 512GB of storage.

The diminutive Swift Blade is a durable 14-inch laptop. Acer/CNET

Swift Blade 14

Acer’s Swift laptops might not be quite as funky-looking as the Vero 16, but the two new additions to the company’s more premium lineup are some of the sleekest laptops ever from Acer.

The Swift Blade is the more compact entry. This 14-inch laptop weighs just 1.76 pounds and is half an inch thick, making it appreciably lighter than the Swift Edge 14 AI. The Swift Blade 14 can be configured with up to a 2.8K OLED panel, an Intel Core 7 350 Wildcat Lake processor, 12GB of LPDDR5 RAM and 1TB of storage.

With Acer laptops, you’re usually making build quality compromises, as many of the company’s computers have plastic chassis. That’s not the case with the Swift Blade 14, which will be built from a magnesium-aluminum alloy and carbon fiber. These lightweight metallic build materials are crucial for a thin laptop to withstand accidental stress, so I think the Swift Blade could carve out a meaningful place in the brand’s lineup, depending on its price.

The Swift Air 16 is a refresh of one of Acer’s more premium lightweight clamshells. Acer/CNET

Swift Air 16

Unlike the Swift Blade 16, the Swift Air isn’t an entirely new entry into Acer’s sleek laptop lineup. In fact, this 16-inch laptop refresh is rather beefy compared to the rest of the Swift lineup, weighing in at 3.3 pounds. Perhaps that can be attributed to the all-aluminum build, since Acer ditched its magnesium alloy for this particular clamshell.

Like its predecessor, the Swift Air 16 features an up to 2.8K display with OLED and IPS options — certain IPS panels will offer touchscreen support. This laptop houses up to Intel Core 7 350 silicon, 16GB of LPDDR5x memory and 512GB of system storage.

Acer has neither confirmed when its new laptops will be available for purchase nor the prices for the Vero 16, Swift Blade 14 and Swift Air 16. Stay tuned for that information in the coming days.

Tech.title: Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Could Come in Black, but Skip Silver This Year
Tech.content:
Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are expected to be unveiled at the company’s Sept. 9 launch event, and a new rumor appears to be firming up the three-color lineup for these phones.

According to leaker Fixed Focus Digital on Weibo (h/t MacRumors), the iPhone 18 Pro is now in full production and is set to come in sky blue, pure black and burgundy models. Prior iPhone 18 rumors have pointed to these colors, although the names have varied (dark cherry instead of burgundy, for instance).

For anyone hoping for a silver or gray shade, this report suggests Apple may skip that color this year, instead bringing back black after abandoning it on the iPhone 17 Pro series. Last year, black was available on other iPhone models, such as the iPhone Air, the base iPhone 17 and the iPhone 17E.

With just about a week to go until Apple’s official event, it’s likely that reports on the iPhone 17 Pro’s looks will continue to leak.

Even more prescient than the color of the iPhone 18 Pro will be its cost. The tech giant has hiked prices across other Apple products amid the ongoing memory shortage that’s making consumer electronics more expensive.

The new Mac Mini with an M6 processor, for instance, starts at $899, which is quite a bit higher than the $599 Mac Mini with an M4 processor it replaced. It’s entirely possible that the iPhone 18 Pro line could have a higher starting price than the $1,099 iPhone 17 Pro, should Apple follow this trend. We’ll find out more on Sept. 9.

Tech.title: PlayStation Gamers Sue Sony Over What ‘Buying’ a Digital Game Really Means
Tech.content:
Sony caused a stir among gamers in July when it announced the phase-out of physical PlayStation game discs starting in 2028. In California, a group of gamers sued the company over its practice of selling digital games on its storefront. However, this isn’t the landmark case some are hoping for that would bring back physical media.

A lawsuit filed in June on behalf of four gamers alleges Sony violated California’s AB 2426 regarding digital purchases. According to the complaint first reported by Aftermath, Sony “misled” customers who purchased games via the PlayStation Store by not making it explicit that they were only buying a license for the game. Sony’s defense is that the links about the license are made available to those buying games, and it’s clear that the ones buying the games don’t own them.

California’s AB 2426 was signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2024. It requires sellers of digital goods such as music, movies, ebooks and video games to clearly disclose when consumers are receiving a license for the content rather than ownership. It also restricts those sellers from using terms such as “buy” and “purchase” for licensed digital goods without having proper disclosures made during the buying process.

The lawsuit, which seeks class action status, argues that the terms “Buy Now” and “Confirm Purchase” are found while buying Resident Evil Requiem, NBA 2K25, Five Nights at Freddy’s 4 and other titles. The gamers suing Sony say they didn’t realize they were receiving a revocable license and alleged they paid more than they otherwise would have.

In its motion filed on Aug. 21, Sony cites Section 8.4 of its PlayStation Terms, saying when a customer purchases a product from the PlayStation Store, they buy a personal license and therefore “do not own the product.” Sony then points to Section 10.1, which says terms such as “own,” “purchase,” “sale,” “sold,” “sell” and “buy” do not imply a transfer of ownership. It also notes that the license is “revocable.”

Last month, Sony sent an email to PlayStation users reminding them of the terms of service and that digital games are licensed, not purchased. The mass email campaign appears to have happened right after Sony filed its motion.

The gamers are asking the court for an injunction to stop Sony from conducting the alleged deceptive practices, a change to how the company’s wording is used at the point of sale and are seeking damages for California residents affected by the practice. There is no indication in this lawsuit that they are asking Sony to bring back physical media, as this suit was filed before the company made its announcement.

Sony’s filing requests that the court dismiss the case or have the individuals file their own claims individually. As part of the PlayStation Terms of Service, those who agree to the terms also agree to arbitration for any claims, along with waiving rights to a class action lawsuit.

A similar lawsuit was filed against GameStop in January for allegedly violating AB 2426. That legal action is still ongoing.

Tech.title: Razer’s New $100 Game Controller Folds Right Up for Your Pocket
Tech.content:
Razer has been making mobile game controllers for a few years now, but the new $100 Prio ultracompact controller could be its most portable yet. Whereas prior controllers like the Razer Kishi are so large that they need to be in a tote bag, the Prio folds up so it can fit inside a pocket.

That on the go convenience could be a selling point for this controller on its own. Standard mobile controllers help make your phone transform into a gaming handheld, but they’re typically not pocket-size. And if you’re already carrying a bag for a controller, you might as well bring a full-size Nintendo Switch 2 or a Steam Deck.

Razer says the Prio weighs 101 grams, roughly the same as a bar of soap. When folded, the controller almost resembles a small wallet. When unfolded, Razer says it can attach to larger phones like Apple’s iPhone 17 Pro Max and Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra.

The gaming controller connects directly over USB-C and includes a full-size controller layout with two thumbsticks, a four-way D-pad, face buttons and shoulder button triggers — similar to most video game console controllers.

Razer’s Prio is launching just as Samsung and Google have finished unveiling the rest of their Galaxy and Pixel phone lineups for 2026, and as we await Apple’s Sept. 9 event that’s expected to focus on higher-end iPhone models like a rumored iPhone 18 Pro Max and a folding iPhone Ultra. The Razer Prio is compatible with both iPhone and Android mobile devices.

The Razer Prio is able to fit in a pocket like a small wallet. Razer

This tiny mobile gaming controller comes as consoles keep getting more expensive due to the ongoing memory shortage driving up the cost of electronics. Nintendo’s Switch 2 just rose $50 to $500, Microsoft’s Xbox Series X with a disc drive is now $800 ($300 more than its $500 launch price) , and Sony’s PlayStation 5 with a disc drive is now $650 ($150 more than its $500 launch price).

With prices like these, it could be a lot more affordable to get a portable controller to game on a phone instead of owning a video game console.
